case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- for the purpose of this, right?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: But -- I would agree. But the point I guess I would come back to at the start of your question on this would be -- is that in a tax foreclosure due -- or, excuse me, takings context, the obligation of the government under Cherokee Nation is to have reasonable, certain, and adequate provisions to reach just compensation.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Right. And the just compensation is the difference between what the government sold his -- was forced to sell his house at on the tax sale and what it owed -- what he owed in taxes. So they gave it back to him, right? They sold it for $70,000 or whatever it was, gave it back to him, and I would think they're done. You're saying they had an obligation to not sell it for the 70 or to reach into the public fisc and pay the difference between the 70 and what it would have sold in a fair market scenario, and I don't understand where that comes from.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Where it comes from is the obligation that if you're taking property, which is -- here, the property interest is not the auction proceeds.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: The property interest here is the value of the equity that was taken.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: One last time. They're not taking property like a person who -- like a government who wants to build a railroad. You know, the government wants to have a -- a sidewalk or a park. They're taking property because he didn't pay his taxes. And so, to me, that context makes the just compensation analysis different.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Respectfully, I would say that the --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: You disagree?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: I disagree.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Okay.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: And I would -- I guess I would finish by saying that takings law doesn't turn on moral fault. And -- and the reality is is the -- the balance --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: But I thought we were doing just compensation.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Well, but --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: There is equity in this, right?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: But the -- but the balance of the fairness was decided at the adoption of the Fifth Amendment. The tradeoffs between the government and the citizen was already weighed and -- and the obligation was put on the government by putting fair -- just compensation obligations on the government itself.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas, anything further? Justice Alito?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Let me come back to the point that Justice Jackson was just making. Typically, if a property owner doesn't pay real estate taxes, the jurisdiction will send a notice and say you've got -- you didn't pay your taxes, and maybe they'll send several, and they'll -- they'll warn, you know, if you don't pay your taxes, we can foreclose on your property and sell it at a tax sale. Now, before any of that occurs, I still don't understand why the taxpayer cannot -- a taxpayer who's in a situation like your client, and, again, assuming there was proper notice here, take steps to prevent a tax sale from taking place. If you've got $190,000 of equity in a house and you owe $2,000 in taxes, can you not get a loan using your equity as collateral?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: It -- it is difficult to do that. There is off-ramps that -- that individuals can try to do. In fact, Mr. Pung tried to do that in this case at -- at numerous parts with interactions with the tribunal, with the Tax Tribunal, and -- and things of that nature. To answer your question is there are steps they can take, but if they cross that Rubicon, if the government takes that property --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Yeah, but, before the government takes the property, there are steps that can be taken.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: But, if those steps aren't taken for whatever reason --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well -- well, if the taxpayer doesn't take them for whatever reason the taxpayer has, then perhaps one shouldn't feel so sorry for the taxpayer when the tax sale occurs. There are a lot of outfits that will buy houses sight unseen for cash.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: I guess --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Isn't that another option?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: I don't think that's another option because, you know, Mr. Pung didn't want to leave his home. The ability -- this is the home that he wanted his -- his nephew's son and his family to be able to have and retain. The idea that we'd vacate from the family home because of a tax that's being challenged in this aspect strikes me as not -- as being kind of counterbalanced to the equity that we shouldn't be forced to sell something that we shouldn't necessarily --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, on that, I mean, that's another argument about whether monetary compensation is always sufficient to constitute just compensation when there's an emotional attachment to a house, which is a serious thing. But that's not the issue here.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Well, but the issue is here ultimately -- is that there is a piece of property that has been uncontested by the government to be worth, you know, approximately $200,000. Once the government has decided that it's going to take more property than what the actual value of the debt actually is, that's what triggers the takings obligation. And if it's not a takings obligation, of course, we've also argued it's an excessive fine.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: What is the -- what sorts of personal property do you think the government has to go after first before it goes after the -- the house?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Well, in this case, with a tax debt of about 2200 bucks, it could have been the Peloton bike that was in the house.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: You think a Peloton bike today is worth $2,000? (Laughter.)

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Well --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: If you go on Facebook Marketplace and you try to sell a Peloton bike today for $2,000, I don't think you're going to be very successful.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Tradition --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: How are they going to know that he has a Peloton bike?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Traditionally -- joking aside, traditionally, there are a lot -- there are a lot of different options. There's bank accounts, there's personal property, the vehicle, there's lots of other --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: All right. There are vehicles -- there are vehicles and bank accounts. Maybe they can find out about that. Other personal property, how are they going to know what he has? I mean, do they have a right to go in the house and inspect everything --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: The govern --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: -- and see whether there's a, you know, a valuable gigantic TV that might be sold?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: When -- when the government is acting in a debt collector capacity, this was what -- and when I'm not paid a debt, that's the obligation I have when I'm collecting on a debt from someone that hasn't paid. The government is no different.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: If we start to -- to set out all sorts of rules for these tax sales to make them fair, how many years and how many cases do you think it's going to take to flesh out all of these details without any historical support for the procedures that you seem to think are required?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: We think that the -- that the government has excellent models that are already in place that they could utilize. For example, Michigan's mortgage foreclosure process is well-established, over a hundred years. It's already a known market. It's already a known process. They could adopt that on its own and -- and would have the back-end protections that are necessary so that fair market value is reached in all circumstances, whether it's an auction or a post-auction shortcoming.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: All right. Thank you. I appreciate it.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Sotomayor?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I -- I think your fallback position or your main position is just compensation under the Constitution requires fair market value?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: If I disagree with that and I believe just compensation should be defined the way Justice Scalia did in BDP, which is what's reasonable under the circumstances, and I believe that a fair -- that a valid auction is a reasonable compensation, you lose on your main argument, correct?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: We would -- we would -- if -- if you do not believe that fair market value is the standard, correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And so, if we believe that a valid auction -- and by valid, it has to be fair, it has to be permitted. I don't know about the personal property issue at all. I haven't looked into it. It hasn't been briefed, and it's a very bad place for us to make such a huge decision. That would be up to the court below, correct?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. Now, with respect to fairness, Justice Alito asked are there -- or said are we going to have to wait for every court to decide what's fair, or is there a standard of fairness that we can look to. Not a particular Michigan, but provide me with a case that talks about what a fair auction for a tax fail -- a tax sale would be.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: We would point you to three cases, in fact. One would be Slater versus Maxwell, which provides that tax foreclosures have to be provided for with entire fairness, and that's the -- the trigger word from there, that they have --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I'm not asking you for words. I'm asking you to point me to cases that set forth the parameters of what that fairness would look like.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: That's the high -- that's -- Slater is the high water mark of tax foreclosure we would point to. As a practical multiple-factor aspect, we would point to Ballentyne and Graffam, this Court's prior decisions, which we've -- we have briefed.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Okay. Thank you, counsel.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kagan?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Mr. Ellison, wouldn't your primary position effectively stop states from using foreclosure scale -- sales? Because I'm just thinking that if you accept the proposition -- I guess I am going to ask you to accept the foreclose -- the proposition that foreclosure sales usually depress prices so that they're lower than the fair market value. If I'm -- if I have to give you the fair market value, you, the homeowner, aren't I -- am I not going to lose money if I'm the state on every -- on -- on every transaction like this? I mean, let's take a -- an example. Suppose you don't have this mismatch that you have here between the very small debt and the -- suppose you have a hundred thousand dollar debt, right, and a foreclosure sale is going to get you $110,000, and then the state takes the hundred thousand dollars that it's owed and it gives you the $10,000 back, right?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Okay.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: But then, if you say: Well, no, the fair market value was really $150,000, so I'm entitled to $50,000 back, right?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Right.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, that's just going to cut into what the state gets to take and it's going to mean that the state doesn't get the debt satisfied.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: So my response is that the Fifth Amendment requires just compensation. And -- and somewhat -- what seems to be baked into some questions today has been whether this is best compensation, but assuming your hypothetical, where the --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, I'm just saying that the state is never going to get satisfied in the -- in the -- in that situation where a foreclosure sale will lead to less than the fair market value, so the state is going to say: Well, we can't use foreclosure sales anymore to satisfy debt obligations.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: I would agree they can't use this style of tax foreclosure sale. There are plenty of tax foreclosure sale systems in place that can reach just compensation or even the -- the best compensation in the foreclosure circumstances.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: What you're saying is that there are plenty of foreclosure sale systems that can reach fair market value?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Yeah. And I -- I guess -- I -- I -- I guess I think how could that possibly be? I mean, if you're selling a house on foreclosure in an auction, you're just not going to get the fair market value as if that house had never been foreclosed on and you were selling it in an open market.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: But acknowledging the -- the -- the assumption you want me to make, which is the fact that the foreclosure itself can depress the price, it can't depress the price, I think, this far. Now it could be a factor. It could be a piece of evidence. And we could offer contrary evidence to say, even in this foreclosure-type environment, the price that it was actually sold for was not good enough. And this is our -- this is our Graffam/Ballentyne challenge that's there that says, in this circumstance, the particular system that the government's created in this particular type of auction sale unreasonably and unfairly depresses the price too far because we've got this counter-evidence, whether it's market appraisals, professional evidence, you know, information -- even the government's own assessments about those values are can say what you got at the auction is not enough in that circumstance --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: -- for that system.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Gorsuch?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Is there something incongruous about the fact that when your property is taken by the government for -- to -- to enhance it in a way that's going to increase its value radically -- I take a house, I'm going to put a skyscraper on it, I'm going to rezone it -- that the property owner doesn't get the upside?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: But, here, we're debating about how much of the downside they're going to get.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Correct. And I would go as far as to say that the government -- this Court has always said the government does get the upside. It's well-established takings law. The problem that I see here is is that even if this is not a takings -- if we -- if we take it out of the takings context and we put it in the excessive fines, what we have here is a government that says, for a very small debt, we are going to take and destroy vast majorities of the equity that's valued at the time that we took title to the property itself. So, even if the takings part of this doesn't provide the answer, the excessive fines in particular circumstances, which where the delta is so high here, can provide alternate relief.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And then I -- I -- I do want to understand just a little bit better this principal residence exemption, the -- the -- that -- that led to this tax, this $2200 or whatever it is. You won in front of an ALJ who said that the family doesn't have to pay this.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: The county then went ahead and assessed it anyway and used that as the basis for this foreclosure.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Correct. So --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: How did that happen?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: I don't think you have a long enough afternoon to explain the story of what happened here. (Laughter.)

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: But the very short version of it is is that the PRE credit was determined by -- in Michigan, we have a Tax Tribunal that determines this.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah. No, I -- I've read -- I've read the briefs.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Yeah, yeah.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I got that. I'm just curious, why -- why would the county pursue a $2200 debt that their own ALJ said wasn't owed to this extreme?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: We can't figure that answer out. We don't believe it's due. And the reality is is, by the time the tax assessor actually informed Mr. Pung that the price was actually -- that she had put the PRE credit -- had taken it way, denied it once again, the time -- the very limited 35-day window in which a Michigan taxpayer can activate the process of the tribunal, to go back again --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: After he's already won.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Had already gone.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: And so we're in a weird circumstance here where the tax is legally technically owed but actually isn't owed in these circumstances. And it's -- it's a -- it's a terrible position to be in for a homeowner who's trying to keep their home.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah, if you want to talk about what's just.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: I think it's an important -- we've been talking about the equities on the government's side. I think the fact the tax isn't owed is a major equity on the govern -- or on the property owner's side in this circumstance.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kavanaugh?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: On the possibility of remand for consideration of fair process, the Solicitor General says, as part of that, the courts below could consider whether and to what extent Petitioner has preserved the issue. If he has, he'll bear the -- bear the burden of showing that the sale was not conducted fairly. Do you agree with that?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: We believe that's the first correct step that -- at least one theory that can be challenged, but it's not the only theory that could be challenged on a -- on a remand.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: What are the other theories?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Well, the other theory is inadequacy of price, combined to this as well, so -- because you could have a sales auction or a sales auction that is entirely fair but still doesn't reach just compensation.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But do you agree you would have to show that you preserved the issue and that you would bear the burden of showing that the sale was not conducted fairly?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: As someone who represents property owners, we always want to put the burden on the government whenever we can. This Court has not --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: That's why I'm asking the question. Do you --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: The Court has not spoken to that answer yet at least as I can see.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay. So you don't -- you don't necessarily agree, is what --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: We don't --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: That's fine. That's fine. I just wanted to clarify what you thought about that. And then, secondly, Justice Sotomayor a few times has brought up Justice Scalia's opinion in BFP, and that does speak, as you know, very generally and broadly at the end about foreclosure redefines the market, and given that altered reality, the only legitimate evidence of the property's value at the time it is sold is the foreclosure sale price itself. And I just want to hear your succinct response to BFP and how you distinguish not only the holding but the reasoning and rationale of BFP.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Of course, the first answer, of course, is always to point to Footnote 3 in -- in BFP and say, in the -- in the Constitution --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Which is a standard footnote, but -- that we use, but -- but the question is the rationale and why it wouldn't apply more -- more generally.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Because, in the bankruptcy context -- well, two -- two answers to that question. One is, in the bankruptcy context, Congress has given separate authority to reallocate the burdens of debt between private debtor and creditor in those circumstances. So this is an Article I, Section 8 question. We're not here on Article I, Section 8. We're here with the government with a takings-style claim. So we think that easily distinguishes in that aspect. Importantly, BFP on the facts itself -- and I won't get into it in tremendous detail -- but the foreclosure occurred pre-bankruptcy. In California, at the time that that foreclosure occurred, they had a challenge process that they could have challenged the unfairness of the foreclosure before it went into the bankruptcy process. And the property owner didn't opt to utilize that process, presumably thinking that the price got fair. And, apparently, the bankruptcy attorney thought differently once they got in there. So, in addition to the -- just we're in different constitutional worlds, I think the facts that led up to the foreclosure and how the question was framed before this Court got there in two totally different paths and are not -- are not congruous.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Barrett?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So, counsel, I -- I want to echo what Justice Gorsuch said. I mean, it seems like there was some real unfairness to your client. I mean, frankly, reading the briefs, it sounds to me like the tax assessor was like Inspector Javert, but it was even worse because Jean Valjean hadn't stolen the bread. I mean, you didn't even -- (Laughter.)

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- you didn't even owe the tax, and it's this small tax and -- and the big -- you know, the big loss of the family home and -- and of the money. So it -- it does seem that there's some unfairness there. But I'm struggling to see how it fits into the takings framework. Can you tell me of a case that we have that treats the foreclosure of a house as a taking? I mean, Tyler treats the pocketing of the surplus as a taking, but I'm not aware of a case -- I just don't know if it fits this framework. I'm not aware of a case of ours that says that when the government forecloses on the house, as opposed to when it pockets the money, it's -- it's taken the house.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: The best I can point this Court to is Tyler. And I think Tyler was specifically written with the words about value as opposed to surplus proceeds if we look at the -- many of the passages in Tyler itself. What's important, I think, is that historically, under the common law, under debt collection schemes that are developed by states, there's always a back-end protection on the former property owner. There's a sales confirmation. There's a review process. There's a challenge. So we knew --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: But none of that -- none of that answers whether it's a taking. And -- okay, well, let me ask you this question. You say that it should be fair market value. You also say the taking happens when the government forecloses on the property as opposed to when it sells the property at auction?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: In this circumstance, yes.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Which is the right date for gauging the fair market value --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: When they --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- if there's a gap of a year?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: They -- when they take title. When they assume full and complete title, that is the taking because the govern -- the person is dispossessed of the ownership of that property at that point.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So the -- the property falls in value, and that's the government's risk?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: It is, but it's also the government's benefit if it goes up in value, as Justice Gorsuch points out as well. It's -- it's the time -- it's always -- this Court has always said we measure precisely at the time of the take, is what the value of that property is.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. So let's say I don't think Tyler settles the question whether the foreclosure is a taking, that I think Tyler leaves open and might treat just the pocketing of the surplus as the taking. Why couldn't I view the foreclosure of the house as just an exercise of the taxing power and not a taking?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Because the government is taking more property than necessary to fulfill the debt because, at that point, they're no longer a debt collector anymore. When they've taken that much property over the debt itself, they've become a confiscatory government now as opposed to a debt collector. When -- when a -- if a client doesn't pay my bill, I don't get to go seize their whole entire house. I can only collect on the piece of the debt that I'm entitled to do so. The government has different powers. They can act as a super debt collector, and they're utilizing their takings power to be able to take more property than necessary. And when you trigger that taking obligation, here -- again, what's taken is not the surplus; it's the equity that's in the home at the time of the taking -- that's what triggers the obligation to pay just compensation because the Fifth Amendment requires it.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Jackson?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Can I just get clarity on the tax-isn't-owed scenario in this situation? I mean, ordinarily, in the tax system, if you have -- if you're contesting that you owe the taxes, you pay them and then you go through some sort of process to get refunded by the government. So is that not the case here?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: This is a -- I have to acknowledge this is a unique case in that --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Okay.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: -- the tax isn't owed. This is the worst of all examples of government -- I think government run amok on --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: But the government says it's owed. That's why they're foreclosing on your house. So the dispute is, I guess, over whether it's owed. And the question is whether it can be collected before that dispute is resolved. And in other tax schemes, it can be, the --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Right.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: So why can't it be here?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Because Michigan has this very unique system, the PRE, as I was engaging --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: -- with Justice Gorsuch. The PRE has this very narrow 35-day appellate window that when the assessor says, I'm taking away the PRE credit, you have 35 days, even if you know it or don't know it --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: -- if you don't trigger the Tax Tribunal's review in that, you're barred from challenging that tax from being -- whether it's owed or not owed in that circumstance.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And you couldn't bring some sort of, under Michigan law, a collateral attack on the fairness of that process?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: That is correct. And I have --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: That has not been -- yeah.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: And I have certainly tried as part of the federal case here to bring that fact, detail in, but as the Sixth Circuit and the trial court both below said, is we don't consider any of the factors outside of surplus as categorically fair market value. And they went no further than that in any further analysis.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: All right. One -- one final question with respect to Justice Alito's type analysis. I mean, I do understand the concept of we have a fairness problem because this is a really small debt and a lot of equity in the house. But, to the extent that the homeowner has notice that the government is intending to use this particular tool to recover its debt, I wonder if the fairness questions that you are raising don't get resolved because the notice gives the homeowner a chance to prevent that terrible outcome. It -- I hear you if there's no notice, there's no opportunity, there's no chance for Mr. Pung to run in and pay the $2,000 so the government doesn't steal his -- steal, from his perspective, his family home. But, when the government says clearly, this is how we intend to solve the problem of you not paying your taxes, why isn't it incumbent as a matter of justice for the taxpayer, if they want to avoid the thing the government is threatening, to just pay the taxes in some other way?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: I -- I believe, if Mr. Pung knew he was going to be at the United States Supreme Court arguing about $2200, he would have paid that many years ago, but the answer to your question is is that at the point when the government takes more property than necessary --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: I'm before that point. I'm before the taking. I'm at the government threatening --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Threatening.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- to take your house. And when they do that, the question is what comes next as a matter of fairness and traditional tax policy, et cetera. And the reason why I keep getting hung up on your ultimate this-is-so-unfair point is because I see a very clear opportunity for the taxpayer, who, by the way, is the original problem because he hasn't paid the tax, to solve the problem. And when the government just follows through with what it said it was going to do because it's owed this money in its view, I don't understand how the taxpayer gets to say it's unfair that the government didn't do all I think it should have done to get my house valued at the highest possible price. And, in fact, if they put it in a tax auction, which is just standard, they've got to actually go and pay me the difference. That seems like real unfairness the other way to the, like, rest of the American people, that we are paying you because you didn't pay your taxes and the government had to foreclose on your house.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: The best answer I can give you is governments have a lot of tools in their tool chest to collect debts. They can use lawsuits. They can use, you know, the Peloton bike example I was using earlier. They have a lot of tools in their tool chest. If they're going to utilize a process that captures way more property value than what the tax debt is, the Takings Clause does not have a moral fault. The Takings Clause has balanced those interests already and has put that burden onto the government.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Philip L. Ellison
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Mr. Liu.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: In Tyler, this Court looked to history and tradition to conclude that a taxpayer is entitled to just compensation when his home is sold for more than he owes. The same history establishes what compensation is just. As long as the sale is conducted fairly, just compensation is the surplus proceeds. According to Petitioner, compensation should instead reflect a property's fair market value. But, as this Court recognized in BFP, foreclosed property is simply worth less. Petitioner's approach would defy that reality and spell the end of tax sales in this country. As for the Excessive Fines Clause, it's simply not implicated here. Any taking that's justly compensated for can't be a fine, can't be punishment, and can't be excessive. I welcome the Court's questions.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: Mr. Liu, you seem to put a lot of weight on fairness of the process. How do we determine that? Do we look at history and tradition? Do we look at, as Petitioner argues, at least as a part of this the end result, whether or not the price is a fair market value? The -- what should be our gauge for that?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: I do think we look to history and tradition to determine what a fair sale looks like. I would -- I think some helpful guideposts are the Cooley treatise, starting at page 334, that goes through the historical practices of jurisdictions at the time. I think the federal government's 1812 statute is also a helpful guidepost. And I think, if you look at those guideposts, there are basically three minimum ingredients of a fair sale. One is public notice, notice that contains the time and date of the sale, a description of the property. The second is that there must be a public auction. It can't be a secret sale. It can't be a private sale. And the third ingredient is that the auction must be competitive. There must be an opportunity for bidding and sale to the highest bidder. And, of course, you can also look to history and tradition to also figure out what is the amount of the tax debt that can be subtracted from the sale proceeds to yield the sur -- the surplus proceeds. But do I think the inadequacy of the price bears on that? I'm not going to dispute that a truly grossly inadequate price should cause a court to look more closely at the procedures. But the fact that the -- the price is inadequate is not alone enough to justify setting aside the sale, and -- and -- and it never has been for -- for the centuries that tax sales have been conducted.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: Has the taxing authority and power of the government superseded that of the constitutional right to private property?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: No. I don't -- I mean, if I'm hearing the question correctly, no. The -- the -- the government's authority to foreclose on property doesn't supersede any -- any private property rights. I think the taking -- what the Taking Clause reflects is a really important guarantee of what happens when the government does take property, and it's the guarantee of just compensation. That's -- that's the balance the founders struck.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: Are there more protections in mortgage foreclosures, for example, than there are in tax foreclosures?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: There -- there may well be. You know, if you -- if you -- to contrast some of the cases my friend cited, he cited Graffam and Ballentyne, I mean, those -- those were not tax sale cases. They did mention this concept of gross inadequacy of price. If you look at the Court's on-point opinion on tax sales, which is Slater versus Maxwell, the Court rejects the notion that tax sales could be challenged based on a mere inadequacy of price. So --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: That's not what I'm -- I'm not talking about that.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Okay.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: The -- it seems as though, when we talk about such things as mortgage foreclosures, which we, of course, know are contractual, but there are all sorts of built-in protections --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Right.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: -- for the homeowner. Are there similar built-in protections for the taxpayer in tax foreclosures?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: I think there are, but I don't think they're constitutionalized by the Takings Clause. I think federal and state statutes have long proven perfectly capable of protecting the process and exempting certain property from levy in the tax sale context, and so they've provided the protections that may exist outside.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: I think my point is rather that you're looking at a contract, a private contract when you're looking at mortgage and there are these built-in protections. You're looking at a constitutional right as -- with respect to private property as it relates to the government. It seems as though that if you're looking at protections, they should be at least similar.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Yes. And -- and if you -- I think it's a pretty good sign that the -- the -- the tax sale procedures are constitutional in that they provide -- the -- the -- the tax sales that are conducted by governments look very much like the private mortgage foreclosure sales that banks and private lenders --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Mr. Liu --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: -- conduct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- you -- you -- you say that we should vacate and remand, correct?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: So we can't -- we can't affirm because none of these arguments about history were developed in the Sixth Circuit. They just went off on the idea of a foreclosure sale's automatically good enough. And -- and you don't support that view?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Correct.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: We think the right way to go is vacate and remand for consideration of any arguments that have been preserved as to the process.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And it really would be any arguments about what history and tradition might require in your view that we -- that they should consider, that are preserved?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Exactly. So long as they're preserved --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: -- all of those arguments can be considered.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: So -- so, for example, you know, Cooley also says, don't take more property than you need to, right? That's another rule that might be -- a court might want to look at?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: That is certainly fair game on remand.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And they say, you know, if you get -- if you can take the Peloton rather than the whole house, you should take the Peloton. I mean --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: If it's preserved, that could be considered too.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: All right. All right. Thank you.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Do you have a position on whether those things are required? You're just saying, if they're preserved, they can be litigated below. Do you think they are required?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: I don't think they're required by the Takings Clause. To take the personal property hypo, there's no need for such a rule that says the government needs to exhaust the personal property.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, if you want to play with history, if you want to invoke history, you've got to -- you can't -- you can't cherry-pick it, Mr. Liu. And, you know, the history there is pretty clear that, you know, Cooley's -- Cooley's -- if you invoke Cooley, you -- you -- you've got to eat your Cooley, it seems to me. (Laughter.)

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Yeah. So I -- I read Cooley differently. I -- I -- I know -- I know that that's --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. All right. That's fair. But you -- you would accept that you have to deal with the whole of the history, you don't get to cherry-pick here?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Oh, of course. And -- and that passage from Cooley is a rule about divisible property. What it says is, when property is divisible --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Sure.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: -- that the government shouldn't take more of the parts than it needs to. Now, here, the property was indivisible and everyone agrees that it was necessary to take the whole property. You couldn't take just the backyard or just the front yard, and so that rule is simply inapplicable.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, how about, Mr. Liu, that -- a rule that would say there's the house, but there was also a car, and the car could have satisfied the $2,000 debt?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: We don't think the Takings Clause constitutionalizes that rule. We think the Takings Clause doesn't address the antecedent question of what property can be taken for public use. Gather -- rather, it addresses the -- the -- the subsequent question of, if you take property for public use, what is the just compensation. But I -- I just want to address the merits of this personal property exhaustion rule. There's no need for such a rule because, if the taxpayer wants to sell his Peloton bike to satisfy his tax debt, he is free to do so any day of the week. In fact, our foreclosing on it would make it more difficult for him to sell it. So, if, indeed, Mr. Pung thinks the way to satisfy my tax debt is to sell my Peloton bike, there's no need for a rule that forces him to do that. And --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, what if the only thing he has to sell is his house?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: If the only thing that he has to sell --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Does he -- he doesn't have to do that, does he?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Well, he -- he -- he can sell his house and he's free to do so to -- to pay the price. If it's a situation where there's a financial hardship or it's --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: If -- well, what do you mean if there's a financial hardship?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Well, in Michigan --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: It's usually not a defense to paying your taxes.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: No, but in Michigan and -- and -- and in many other jurisdictions, taxpayers who truly are unable to afford their taxes are given installment plans, offers in compromise. They're -- they're -- they're given --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: What if the --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: -- opportunities to --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Oh, sorry, go ahead.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Well, they're just given opportunities to -- to find a way to pay their taxes. And -- and one of -- one of them is, indeed, to ask the -- in the case of the IRS, to discharge the house from the federal lien so that the taxpayer can sell it. And what happens at closing in that open market sale --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: -- is they simply cut a check to the IRS.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, what if the validity of the tax assessment is still under challenge?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: So, if -- if it's still under challenge, under the IRS rules, we cannot levy on the house, so that challenge can go forward. I think what's unusual about this case is that instead of paying the tax and then challenging it, Mr. Pung just -- just wanted to litigate all the way through without paying the tax at all.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you. Justice Thomas? Justice Alito?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: There are some suggestions in the many briefs that have been filed in this case, although not in Petitioner's brief, about specific things that could be done to make the process fairer. For example, one of the briefs points to statutes that have been enacted in Oregon, Maine, and Massachusetts, and they say that under those statutes, the -- the jurisdiction that is attempting to collect the taxes must first list the property for sale at market value via real estate brokers or real estate agents, and then, if the realtor listing is unable to proceed, then a public auction is allowed where the minimum strike price at auction is two-thirds of the fair market value, et cetera, et cetera. So some of those things seem like possibly good reforms that would make the process fairer, but what concerns me is getting into the determination of which -- the details of this scheme that are minimally necessary to comply with the Takings Clause.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: We -- we share that concern as well, Justice Alito, and that's why, at the outset, in response to Justice Thomas's questions, I provided a few things that we think provide the constitutional floor. But, above that floor, I think states have leeway to adopt other procedures that -- that, in their view, may or may not close the gap between the for-sale price and the fair market value. But it -- it -- it's up to them to adopt those.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: I don't think the Takings Clause speaks to those issues. I mean, to the extent the --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So what would?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Well, I think these sorts of issues about when a foreclosure is appropriate have typically been the province of federal and state statutes, and those statutes have proven perfectly competent in addressing those issues --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Not here.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: -- for centuries.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Not here. That's the claim. Not --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Well, I think the -- what the facts of this -- this case show is that Mr. Pung was given notice of the delinquency. I mean, he face-to-face was told by the township assessor that he owed the tax.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And he went to tax court, and the tax court said no, you don't.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: That --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And he presented the government with that notice, and the government said bye.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Right. And -- and I think this is a -- an unusual feature of this case, that while Mr. Pung did appeal the denial of the principal residence exception as to certain years, he didn't appeal that denial as to the year at issue here. I don't know what explains that choice, but it is what --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: -- creates this case.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I have one final question. Given the three minimums of fairness, are you saying those are the only ones, or are you leaving open the door that there are potentially others?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: We are leaving open the door that there are others. I think, as -- as has been mentioned this morning, this is not an issue that has been the focus of the briefing. So one of the reasons we think a remand is appropriate is for any preserved issues like this to be addressed. The reason why I say it's not an exhaustive list is because, while there are certain procedures that you can point to that will provide fair procedures, there's any number of things a state could put on top that would actually make those -- you know, undercut those same procedures. So I -- I don't think it's -- it's -- it's as simple as going through and saying there's X, Y, and Z. I think you need a catch-all that's something like: And a state can't do anything else to kind of undercut all -- all the procedures on that list.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So --

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice -- oh.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- the other side is saying you can't do anything that undercuts fair market value. That -- that's how they would answer that question. And so how should we answer it if not that way?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
text: Right. And -- and I -- I -- I don't think the mere fact that a -- a procedure is or is not going to have an effect on fair market value can be enough to decide whether it's okay or not.

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But should it be a factor?

case_name: Michael Pung, Personal Representative Of The Estate Of Timothy Scott Pung, Petitioner, V. Isabella County, Michigan, Respondent
speaker: Frederick Liu
