case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Correct.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But, if no one has actually done the analysis whatsoever --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Correct.   And I think it is a fair point, you know, I think it's a correct concession on the government's part that the Controlled Substances Act does not reflect a determination that every substance that is labeled a controlled substance is too dangerous for people to regularly consume.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, didn't Congress --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: In fact, it represents the opposite.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: We can't -- we can't make that -- given for all the reasons that Justice Barrett pointed out, all the different scheduling, you can't really say that every single drug on there Congress could have reasonably, rationally, whatever.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Congress, I mean, the point of the scheduling is to say some of these substances, even though controlled substances, are capable of being used regularly in moderation without making somebody a walking public safety risk. So, if you are serious about ensuring that the modern, you know, the modern law fits that historical understanding, this law doesn't even reflect Congress's determination that everything designated a controlled substance is inherently the kind of thing that cannot be used responsibly or in moderation.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And, Ms. Murphy, I thought your point --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Ms. Murphy --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: I thought your point was that even if it had, even if it did, deferring to Congress with respect to that kind of judgment is what Bruen tells us we're not supposed to do, that you would be abandoning in a sense the Bruen test to kind of take the Chief Justice's what I think reasonable view of, you know, thinking about what Congress has said and assessing what Congress wants to do in evaluating whether it's doing it in a -- a narrowly tailored way, if we're doing that, then what work does the historical analogue have to do? I thought we had to look at the historical analogue to constrain Congress in its ability to disarm people today.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: That is -- that is exactly -- I mean, that is our core submission. And the government said multiple times today that they agree that they have to actually map onto a historical tradition, and if that is the principle --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And so the question is, how does that mapping happen?    At what level does that mapping happen?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Sure.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And I hear the government saying it happens just at the level of the old cases were looking at people and making judgments about when they were dangerous and should be committed or whatever.    And it can't be that broad, I think.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: We certainly don't think it can be that broad.    I think it has to be attached to a principle.    So the principle in Rahimi was not simply Congress decided certain people were dangerous.    The Court focused in particular on the fact that that part of (g) -- of 922(g) required an individualized determination of dangerousness. Now we're not saying that's the only way you can map onto historical tradition, but it was that.   The Court didn't stop at the high level of saying a determination -- you know, that -- that there was just a legislative view of dangerousness.   It looked at that individualized inquiry.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Here, I think that you'd have to say, okay, you know, what was -- what was the historical principle surrounding dangerous substances, intoxicating substances? And when you have a tradition that's all about ensuring that the regular user doesn't get swept up with the habitual drunkard, I don't think you can point to that tradition and say this is our tradition that allows us to bring the regular user in along with the person whose abusive use is actually impairing their ability to function in their day-to-day life.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Can I ask about the tradition with respect to addiction?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Yes.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Because I think you and the government agree -- I want to find places of agreement here.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Yeah.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I think you and the government agree that there is a tradition of prohibiting gun ownership, possession, by those who are addicted to drugs, correct?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Yes.    We agree that the historical -- I mean, you know, we agree that the historical tradition of habitual drunkards can support laws with respect to addiction, which is -- I'm happy to talk about the state laws -- is really the dominant approach that's just taken -- had been taken.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well, as my questions indicated, I think you have a strong point there on -- on that being the dominant approach when it -- when it started up. Now then, on this statute, so taking what you just said and applying it to this statute, this statute does cross-reference the Controlled Substances Act, which then does define "addict" as a habitual user so as to endanger the public morals.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Yeah.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I'll just leave it at that.    And my question is, is that definition of "addict" good enough in your view to satisfy the tradition of prohibiting gun ownership, possession, by addicts, and, if not, what is the delta?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Yeah.   I think that definition pretty -- pretty well maps onto the historical tradition.     It's a little bit of an unusual definition because it has these two prongs.    It refers to a habitual user as someone whose habitual use either is essentially because they're addicted or just is endangering public safety. But I actually think, you know, while that may be a bit of an odd way to think, like --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: It says endangering the public morals too --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: It does say I think some --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- which means anything.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Yeah.   Look, if we were here in an "addicted to" case --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Right.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- there's some discussion to have about whether some of that language is a little bit broad and a little bit --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Right.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- problematic from -- from maybe just -- but I think what the -- what the definition is getting at is, if your use is so excessive either because you're addicted or if it's a product of choice, either way, if your addiction is rendering you a threat to yourself and others -- your use is -- your habitual use is rendering you a threat to yourself or others, I think that maps onto historical tradition --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: So you're good -- let me just summarize.    You're good with addiction being a tradition and with this definition of "addiction" being good enough?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: The only --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Is that correct?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- minor caveat I will give you is the government has, in fact, accused my client of being a drug addict, so I don't want to foreclose, like, literally any argument that might be made about the "addicted to" prong, but, as a conceptual matter --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: As a legal matter.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- we don't have a problem with the historical tradition supporting the use -- as supporting laws that prohibit drug addicts from possessing firearms.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: The government didn't accept that.      They said that that definition doesn't control.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: The -- I think what I heard --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well, they --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: So --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: In fact, they said it had to be more focused.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- I think what I -- if I understood the government, I think they're focused on the fact that the definition specifically refers to narcotic drugs, which is a narrower category than controlled substances. We aren't suggesting that the definition has to be read, like, literally in haec verba into the -- the -- you know, 922(g)(3).    I think you could say the standard that the definition of "addict" is accomplished -- is -- is setting out for addiction can apply as to a controlled substance. And this is actually the way -- when the government does prosecute under "addicted to," several courts use this as the jury instruction to give content to what the conduct is.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: So you think we could --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I want -- we interrupted Justice Barrett, and I want to make sure you get back to her.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Justice Kavanaugh, you can finish.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Go ahead.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: I was just going to give you a variation of Justice Kagan's hypothetical.    I have never heard of the drug that she was -- is that real?     Okay. (Laughter.)

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Let's imagine that it's marijuana, okay?    So let's say that you win this case and Congress comes back and says -- you know, it conducts hearings, it hears all this evidence about the concentrations of THC and marijuana that's made today, documents that marijuana users who use it several times a week have a proclivity for violence, violence with firearms, and then passes the same statute with findings along the lines I just sketched out. Can Congress do that consistently with the Second Amendment?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: So I think you'd have to look at that evidence yourself and decide does it suffice to show that someone fits this pattern.    If they could show that --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: I have to look at the evidence to see if the person satisfies the pattern or I have to --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: No, the category.    If Congress wants to say we're going to do it at a categorical level, then I think you look and say, did they get the category right?        I think that --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay.   How do I make that judgment?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: By look -- by thinking about the -- the test that was applied historically.    Is it -- has the government demonstrated that anybody who uses at the degree of this -- you know, that substance in that amount in that frequency is actually a danger not even just when they're using but in their day-to-day life?    Are they unable to care for themselves and their affairs?    That's the language --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Do I have experts?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I mean, if the government wants to do it on a categorical basis, it is going to have to prove up its case.    If they don't want to do it that way, then applying the same test on an individualized basis should get you to the same result if they define the category correctly.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So the judge would then conduct an evidentiary hearing, hearing from experts on both sides about whether marijuana actually --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: If --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- poses a risk of gun violence?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I mean, if the government wants to say we want to set a categorical rule, I don't think it's too much to ask to hold them to put it --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Meth?   Like, could it do that for meth?     Could it --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I don't -- as to some substances, I think it's not going to be that hard.    It's just marijuana, you know, we're all here and these cases arise because marijuana, boy, it would be difficult for the government to make that showing when it is the considered judgment of 40 states, the District of Columbia, three territories, and the President --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: But you concede --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- that it's not that kind of substance.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: But you concede that there are some substances that the government would have a pretty easy time on a categorical basis?    Maybe cocaine, maybe meth?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Absolutely.   We are not here to suggest that you couldn't ever have a categorical approach as to a particular substance.    It's just that if the government wants to do that, I think it has to do it under Bruen, not just --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So it could have a categorical approach with respect to Justice Kagan's drug?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: They can come make their case and then you decide -- you know, I think the right test to apply is, did they define the category close enough to the habitual drunkard concept?    Maybe -- you know, maybe the level of generality is enough to capture your drug, but it's not going to be enough to capture something that is the type of thing that people regularly all throughout the country lawfully use a few days a week and most states and the President have made the judgment that that is not so categorically addictive or --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, your --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- dangerous that nobody can use it safely.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Your -- the -- the trial you're contemplating after Congress has gone through whatever it's gone through in establishing the record and making the determination, and then it's going to be relitigated in a trial, the fact that your client wins in one trial there doesn't mean there's not going to be another trial in another district and the -- the --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: If --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: -- develop -- case law developed until I suppose there's a conflict among the circuits, and then we would have to evaluate the scientific record.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I mean, for one, the government does have to do this anyway as to its scheduling determinations, which can be challenged through APA review.   The only difference is they want a lesser burden of proof, which they get in the APA context, than they would get under Bruen.   They have to defend them in exactly this way.    They don't just get to say trust us, we got it right. Now, if the government's getting it right, I just don't think this is going to be that hard as to the substances that it's pretty clear can't be used on a regular basis by anybody safely.   And that's why you're not seeing these cases come up to you, and -- and you're not seeing the lower courts struggle as much when it's somebody who's admitting that they take heroin every day. You know, nobody's -- nobody's getting as concerned about the scope of the statute as applied to certain substances.   But applying the test ensures that the government doesn't make category mistakes in the way that the President himself seems to think the government currently has done as to marijuana.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Do you think the statute when -- with the word "habitual" added -- you make a big deal about that in -- in your brief -- really does then reduce to addiction?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: So it certainly captures -- the addiction prong would be irrelevant at that point because you have to be a habitual user to fall within the definition of addiction. And it would be particularly odd because that's not enough to make you addicted to.   You need to be habitually using so as to either endanger the public health and safety, et cetera, or to have lost the power of self-control.   So it's really, you know, the "addicted to" prong is designed to kind of be narrower, yet all of a sudden, you'd have this unlawful user prong that's so broad that it renders that prong irrelevant. I -- I don't think that that's really an available interpretation, a -- kind of a coherent interpretation of this statute when Congress set out two different concepts that it was trying to get at.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Ms. -- Ms. Murphy, I wonder, do we need to get into much of this about how the government could proceed or -- with categorical versus individual or how it applies to addicts?      He wasn't charged under that part of 922(g)(3). And all we know -- I mean, the -- the only thing we know in the record is he uses some marijuana, we don't know how much or in what potency, a few times a week.     And why isn't it just enough to say whatever else may be true, that is not an habitual drunkard?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: We would be happy for the Court to resolve the case on that narrow ground.    I mean, I'm trying to be very responsive.    I appreciate the Court wants to think about this statute as a whole, but you really don't need to answer any of the questions about the "addicted to" prong today. And, really, even as to the unlawful user prong, all you have to say is either, whether the government's thinking about this individually or categorically, they just can't get there simply by saying somebody uses some unknown quantity of marijuana some unknown time of day a few times a week.    We're -- we are very happy to prevail on that narrow ground.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Which sounds to me very much like it is sounding in traditional understandings of this category being overbroad, that to the extent that we are concerned about the match -- the -- the -- the perceived mismatch between historical drunkards and regular users, it really is just that Congress's purpose here, which is to prevent dangerous people from having guns, is not, you say, furthered by including this kind of person in that statute.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: That's right.   And that's --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And so it's just an overbroadness kind of -- right.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: And -- and -- and, you know, I think, under Bruen, the right way to say it is it's overbroad as to the historical category.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Right.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: But I think you could kind of get to the same place by saying, even if you were doing means-end scrutiny, it's overbroad.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Right.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: It's just overbroad in the sense that this particular -- at least as to what you've got before you in this case, it is overbroad even under a traditional conception of giving the government a little bit more room for deference on its determinations.   That doesn't mean the government might not have a much stronger case with somebody who regularly uses a different substance.   If you apply the same principle across the board, the government's going to win when it got those categorizations correct.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: So you think the government could say someone's an unlawful user but not an addict as to particular kinds of drugs, and that would be sufficiently connected to a historical tradition that it would satisfy the Second Amendment?    That's what you're saying?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I think the one way to understand this statute, which isn't the easiest statute in the world to completely understand, but would be that the "addicted to" prong is focused on people who -- who -- who use so excessively and routinely as to fit the habitual drunkard category is focused on people who do that out of physical or psychological compunction, and the unlawful user can reach the people who do the same thing out of choice. And so, either way, you have the same ultimate principle, but you could read this statute as saying one is about addiction in the most traditional conception of addiction, and the other is about abuse of use even if it's just that somebody chooses to spend much of their life in a drunken stupor or intoxicated, you know, high on drugs.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas? Justice Alito?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: You say that there is not a problem with, at least I understand what you're saying, that there is not a problem with prohibiting everybody who is addicted to a controlled substance from possessing a gun.        Is that correct?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: We do not have a problem with that.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: And that applies to everything, every controlled substance?       So that would --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I think the concept of addiction, the determination that's made to show that someone is addicted to something is, I understand, the kind of determination that's going to show that somebody is engaged in the kind of use that renders them a risk all the time. So I just want to be very clear about, you know, we're not conceding at, like, some generic level, it's because the consequences --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Seriously?    You think that being addicted to every single drug in the schedule renders that person a -- a danger?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: You would be willing -- you -- you don't think arguments can be made that being addicted to, I don't know, the illegal use of Ambien --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I'm not sure you'd be able --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: -- somebody's charged with that, that person couldn't come in and say, whoa, that doesn't make me dangerous --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Sure.   And --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: -- I'm doing this while I am sleeping?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: And this is where we might have a marginal disconnect about, you know, when I think of what would be necessary to prove that someone's addicted to some -- something, it's going to need to -- it's going to incorporate something like the definition of the Controlled Substances Act that's asking about whether you are a threat to yourself or others. And maybe there are some substances you just can't make a showing that somebody's addicted in that sense, but -- but -- but, if you accept so --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Can an addict -- can an addict as to every substance in the list insist on an individualized determination or not?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: The statute requires that.    I mean, you can't figure --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: So there has to be an individualized determination?     So --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: There -- there --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: -- the mere fact that someone is addicted to something that is a controlled substance is not enough for Second Amendment purposes?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I don't know how you determine that someone's addicted to a controlled substance without engaging in an individualized inquiry into their use.       Once you've determined that someone's an addict, you've determined that they fit into --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: No, not -- not as to what their -- not as to their use or even their reason for the use but whether their -- their situation renders them dangerous.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I mean, that is what the definition of "addict" in the Controlled Substances Act contemplates, that you have to assess somebody's use by reference to the impact it is having in their life. So I don't think it works under the statute to say someone's an addict without having engaged in an individualized inquiry into the nature of their use.    And that's what -- what's required all across the country. If you want to adjudicate somebody, a drug addict, who can be subject to confinement or guardianship, you have to actually individually assess their use of the drug --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: If -- if an individual --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- and the impact it has on their life.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: I'm sorry.    Are you finished?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: No, no.    Go ahead.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Yeah.   If an individualized determination is required under (g)(3), is it an individualized determination as to that particular individual, or is it as to the drug across the board?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: So I think the individualized inquiry is to whether you are addicted to a controlled substance.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, no, I'm not talking about addiction now, just -- just use. Whether somebody -- someone is -- is prosecuted for being a user of drugs.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Sure.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: And you say, you can't do that, you have to have an individualized determination as to something.   And what is this thing that there must be an individualized determination?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I -- I -- I want to be clear, again, we are not actually saying that the only way to do this is through an individualized inquiry.   For addiction, I think it is because I think the -- the concept of addiction requires it. But, if the government wanted to say that there is a particular degree of consumption of a particular substance that it considers virtually anybody who -- who consumes in that quantity to be someone who cannot possess a firearm, we are not asking you to rule out the possibility that the government could make the showing that that category is categorically analogous to the concepts that the habitual drunkard laws reflected. We are not saying the only way they can do it is by coming in and making a case-by-case determination.      They can proceed either way.    It's just that if they want -- whichever way they want to do it, they have to meet their burden under Bruen of proving that they did, in fact, make the right determination; they put either the person or the substance use into the correct category.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Yeah, I -- I struggle to figure out how these individualized determinations can be made in the context of a criminal prosecution.       The whole -- the way in which criminal prosecutions are conducted makes this extremely difficult. Now the Third Circuit issued a very thoughtful opinion about what they thought is required in an individualized determination, and what they said was that the test is whether disarming a drug user is needed to address a risk that he would pose a physical danger to others. Is that the test that you would apply?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: That's not necessarily the test.    We would ask you to apply a test more akin to the historical one, but I -- I just --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Okay.   What is it? What is your test?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Sure.   The test is whether somebody's use is rendering them a -- unable to function in their day-to-day life all the time, whether it's because they're always intoxicated or because their use is such that it's impairing their ability to function in their day-to-day life. That is what the civil commitment laws ask.   They said is someone a drunkard incapable of taking care of himself or his property, where you had to prove that a person, by excessive drinking, is unable to attend to business or has lost self-control.      You had to prove these things.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: I -- I -- I'm just puzzled by -- by most of your argument. Suppose somebody -- I just don't understand what you're arguing for. Suppose someone regularly takes a drug, and during the period when that person is taking the drug, that person is super dangerous.   Congress couldn't -- the Second Amendment would not permit Congress to say that's too risky?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: It might.   And if you look at the laws, the definitions that were used historically, some of the cases talked about it in terms of is somebody the type of person who's going to take the substance, you know, going to drink to excess whenever the opportunity presents themself? They're focused on that question of saying not just are you always drunk, but are you so habituated to it that you are drunk a lot of the time and we can't trust enough for you to just, you know, be around the one day a week, that's why we're going to commit you or have guardianship or have these severe consequences. And so we don't think -- I mean, you know, the traditional way the addiction prong is applied is to give juries the instruction from the CSA definition which requires a jury to make an individualized finding about whether somebody's use is impacting their day-to-day life.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: All right.   Well, speaking about -- speaking of jurors, this is -- these are the factors that the Third Circuit said an individualized determination should entail:    The length and recency of the defendant's use during and shortly before his gun possession; the drug's half-life; whether use of the drug affects a person's judgment, decision-making, attention, inhibition, or impulse control; whether the drug may induce psychosis; the drug's interference with a user's perception of his own impairment; the long-term physical and mental effects of the use of that drug. Are -- are those -- in a criminal case, would those be submitted to the jury?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: We are not suggesting that juries would need to be instructed to consider all of those things, but I certainly think the government would -- would say that's the type of evidence we should be able to present when we want to show that a drug was --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: So experts --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- correctly categorized in this way.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: -- would -- experts would testify on all of these matters and the jury would decide whether the person met the -- the -- the test for being a dangerous person?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I don't think the government's going to need to do that when it comes to a lot of cases and a lot of substances, but --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, maybe not always, but if -- if that's at issue, is that what's going to be required?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Again, I mean, the government can't even put a substance on one of these schedules without having to withstand if somebody wants to bring a challenge to that. They're going to have to prove it up.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: We're talking about criminal prosecutions and what needs to be shown in a criminal prosecution.   I don't know where the line -- the Sixth Amendment line is as to all these things, but even -- let's assume that some of them, all the ones that go to questions of science, for example, you would have every single -- potentially every district judge in the country would make a finding, and I find -- as to all of these drugs, I find that this -- that the use of this drug being a -- that users of this drug are dangerous or they're not dangerous.   Every district judge before whom that issue comes up would make a determination on that scientific question?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: No.   I think you can give the jury a standard that asks whether somebody's use is impairing their ability to function, and the government can then choose to present evidence.   They can present evidence about their life.   They can present evidence about the nature of the particular substance and the fact that it is a substance that carries with it effects for days at a time. It can present evidence, and the jury can make an ultimate determination, just as the jury has to do as to the addicted person.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: It's been said that Congress never made a judgment about the dangerousness of using all of the substances on the controlled substance list.   Is that right?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: I don't think Congress has made a determination that anybody who uses those substances regularly is a public safety risk.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Isn't that what Congress did when it enacted (g)(3)?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: No, because Congress only applies that if somebody's use is unlawful. And so somebody can be using a controlled substance regularly under the Controlled Substances Act, and Congress deems them not to be a public safety risk so long as they got the prescription for the sleep aid and they aren't the spouse who didn't.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: One final question. In the cases in which we have previously held that the Second Amendment prohibits certain government regulations -- Heller, McDonald, Bruen -- there have been a lot of "the sky is falling" arguments about the consequences of that for public safety. In Rehaif, I said that I think that 922(g) has a more direct and severe bearing on public safety than the issue of whether a law-abiding citizen can possess a gun in the home or even, as in Bruen, carry the gun outside the home. Do you disagree with that?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: No.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Here, we're talking about disabling people like -- people who have committed felonies.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Sure.   But I would note that under 922(g)(3), it's only about five prosecutions that are under (g)(3).      The vast majority of them are under provisions, other provisions, and about 80 percent are under (g)(1).    So I don't think the arguments that we are making today would vastly endanger the government's prosecutorial efforts under 922(g).

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Sotomayor?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: If you look at the statute, there's two components, unlawful user of a controlled substance and someone who's addicted to any controlled substance. "Addiction" is defined by the statute, correct?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: It's defined by the Controlled Substances Act --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Yeah.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- not by the Gun Control Act, but --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But it's --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: -- there is a cross-reference which suggests Congress intended the statutes to be read in pari materia.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Means any individual who -- this is the definition -- habitually uses any narcotic drug so as to endanger the moral -- public morals, health, safety, or welfare, or is so far addicted to the use as to have lost the power of self-control. That would go to a jury?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: That does go to juries often in cases.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And it has to go to the juries.    So --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: That goes to juries in these cases, yes.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- Justice Alito's concern about each jury determining is inherent in the definition, correct?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: It's inherent in an "addicted to" prosecution.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Now, with respect to who is an unlawful user, I've been surprised that in your cert petition and even in this brief, in your briefing, you haven't really raised the vagueness issue. But it seems to me that the government is sort of giving "unlawful user" a definition that's not present in the statute, correct?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: Correct, which is why we -- you know, we -- we did lead with a lengthy argument in our response brief that we think the statute has an independent vagueness problem that is sort of baked into trying to analyze whether the statute is constitutional under the Second Amendment.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And -- and --

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: If you don't know exactly what it means, that's its own problem.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- historically, the only thing that was ever given meaning to was a habitual drunkard, correct?   And that had maybe a common-law background definition, but there's nothing in the -- in any of our history or tradition that has created a use definition, correct?

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Erin E. Murphy
text: That's right.   And if you take the early statutes from the 1920s and '30s, none of them had an "unlawful user" prong.   And even today, there's only eight states that have an "unlawful user" prong. Almost all of them are focused on addiction or focused on it through the lens of, even more concretely, things like have you been adjudicated to have a substance disorder or committed for treatment for a substance use disorder.

case_name: United States, Petitioner, V. Ali Danial Hemani, Respondent
speaker: Sarah M. Harris
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice: I'd like to contrast where this Court might go with respect to people who present a special danger of misuse.       Our position is Congress made a judgment in 922(g)(3) itself that it is, in fact, dangerous to mix firearms with habitual use or addiction to controlled substances. That is backed by the historical habitual drunkard tradition, where there weren't these sort of fine-grained lines that Respondent appears to be drawing as to exactly how incapacitated you are.   It's sort of a common-law approach that starts with magistrates and justices of the peace in making these determinations. Over time, there's more consensus, but I find it ironic that they're focused on modern-day civil commitment laws to try to superimpose on a body of sort of case-by-case determinations of a justice of the peace do you fit into the category of habitual drunkard or not some sort of unifying theme. What they on the other hand want to do with respect to these hundreds of prosecutions a year under 922(g)(3), not a mere five, and most of which are for the unlawful user prong, the lion's share for sure, is to revert to what I think ends up being individualized determinations all the way down. These seem to say you have to as a constitutional matter, I think, on the strength, again, of these modern laws, have individual determinations for every single addict under that prong, and, otherwise, they seem to sometimes say category by category is fine for some drugs, but I really don't know how that would hold up. What they seem to be saying is actually even for categories like heroin, like PCP, whatever it is, you still would have to have a chance to say what is your frequency, what is your mix of drugs in the mix, what are other things that make you dangerous. I think all that collapses.     And that is a rejection of what the Court accepted in Heller onwards, which is there can be some categories on a category-by-category basis of a special danger of misuse. I think where does this leave the rest of the inquiry, it certainly creates a mess of 922(g)(3).   I think what we've heard about are mini-trials in every single case in an attempt to capture Justice Kagan's hypothetical of, like, the hallucinogenic, non-addictive drug, is that sufficiently similar to the effect of alcohol on founding-era generation people who were sufficiently drunk sufficiently amount of the time in the same way as alcohol to be sufficiently dangerous for this purpose? I don't know how anyone would figure that out.    But, certainly, what's happening now is not district courts finding an easy time of it.   As Chief Judge Colloton's recent dissent in Ledvina indicates, it's just remands all the way down with no really good way to proceed and making all these kind of pharmacological judgments that are very, very difficult for district courts and really do end up being individual determinations. Where does this leave the rest of 922(g)?    I think that's a real problem also with Respondent's approach.    It's not just apparently for 922(g)(3), where there has to be what will back into individualized tailoring and a mess of a position. I think this is all the way down from (g)(1) felons, every single category of felons, even a serial murderer, you would have to be able to second-guess is that person really dangerous, is that a good proxy, how many people, what are the kinds of offenses, to (g)(2), the fugitive, if you're just out for a couple days, are you really a dangerous fugitive who should be disarmed, to (g)(4) with respect to mental illness. I think the questions just cascade from there and make an absolute hash of the 922(g) framework, which has been something the government has relied on to deal with -- with -- with more than -- as Justice Alito's dissent in Rehaif notes, something that is a cornerstone of violence prevention. Third, I don't think you can shortcut to who knows what a habitual user is and how -- I think courts of appeals have provided a good yardstick for this.    There is no confusion on this.    The distinction between a habitual user and an addict is both very real and important. A habitual user, again, is judged by the frequency of their use.    We're at the indictment stage here.    The government will have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt to a jury that the frequency of use here, which, again, is concededly multiple times a week of an illegal substance, marijuana, is, in fact, habitual use under the way courts of appeals have interpreted this. I don't think that's confusing.    I think the knowledge requirement presents a large amount of checks, and I think that does real work vis--vis the addict prong, which deals with people who can't control their urges even if they're not currently using the substance. The two work in tandem, and the fact that Respondent seems to acknowledge that perhaps lots of these unlawful users can, in fact, be constitutionally prohibited from possessing firearms at least only during the period of their habitual use, I think, is a problem for Respondent's position because, if all they have at that point is this mess of individualized determinations, then the category-by-category approach is out the window for every single drug no matter how dangerous, no matter how different it is from alcohol, even if it is the most dangerous hallucinogenic drug, that even if you use it once a week causes hallucinations at unpredictable periods going forward. I think that is the approach that is risked here, and the better course is to say habitual drunkards are a valid tradition.    You do not have to exactly match the degree of alcohol impairment to fit in that tradition. Thank you.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: All contracts are subject to defenses. So appeal waivers are also subject to defenses and can be excused in more circumstances than the two recognized below. The government argues that no contract defense can apply to knowing and voluntary appeal waivers, no exceptions. But, if appeal waivers bind defendants under contract principles, they can be excused under contract principles. A contrary approach is anathema to our criminal justice system. No appeal for sentences above the statutory maximum based on race, religion, national origin, tribal status, or pure vindictiveness. No appeal for pregnancy bans, castration, or compelled church attendance either. These scenarios are all real cases. Or take this case. Only the most paramount government interest overcomes the fundamental right to refuse medical treatment. But Hunter was sentenced to a mandatory medical condition even though he had no mental health issues, let alone one connected to the crime or related to any sentencing goal. Defendants bargain for caps on their sentencing exposure. Those bargains are destroyed by plainly unlawful sentences that are totally outside the realm of plausibility of either party. Now floodgates concerns are belied by decades of experience in the 11 circuits that reject the Fifth Circuit's rule. Applying defenses to appeal waivers maintains the status quo. Contract defenses are narrow by design and rarely satisfied. Appeal waivers will continue to bar the vast majority of alleged sentencing errors, guidelines miscalculations, insufficient explanation, or misbalancing under 3553(a). But contract defenses may be satisfied in the rare case of clear legal error and punishment unauthorized by statute or that violates the Constitution. At a minimum, this Court should remand on the second question presented. I welcome questions.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: Ms. Blatt, if you can waive constitutional rights or statutory rights, why can't you waive these contractually rights that are statutory here?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: You absolutely can waive the -- the -- the right to appeal and there's a appeal agreement, but the issue here is, absent this plea agreement, which is a contract, the defendant could just walk away. The only thing that is binding him to the waiver, and the government is asserting, the enforceability of the appeal waiver by contract. I don't think there's any dispute that the plea agreement is a contract. If you waive your right to trial when you -- at -- at the arraignment and just say I waive my fundamental right to trial, that's a pretty big waiver. Tomorrow, you can get up and say, you know what, Judge, I think I want a jury trial. You can just revoke it. But, here, there's a plea agreement. There's a contract. The government has to rely on the contract principles. The government gets out of plea agreements by relying on contract defenses. And there's just no rational -- or it's just inexplicable that you would not apply contract defenses to this contract when you do to all others.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: Could -- in this case, could the government simply void the agreement and proceed with the 10 counts?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah, I -- I don't think so, but here's why. The government has in many cases asserted frustration of purpose and did exactly what you said. I think, here, because the government has no interest and is not defending the mandatory medication condition, there's just no countervailing principles. Now the government has not disputed it can allege a breach of the plea agreement, and that would result in an invalidation of the plea. The government just doesn't dispute that. That's why defendants so rarely bring these appeals, is because they run a substantial risk of exactly what you're saying. We would try to argue that there's no breach based on the fact that the judge told him he had a right to appeal. And even if it is a breach, you know, it's -- it's justified by defending the contract exception, and the government doesn't have any countervailing interest to invalidate the whole agreement. And that's all the stuff we would fight on remand. Here, we're cut off because the -- the Fifth Circuit has this categorical rule that, although it's a contract and you're denied the benefit of the bargain with sentences that exceed the statutory maximum, it allows no other exceptions.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- a known right. You haven't argued that. case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. Guideline errors are just going to be out. And they've been here for --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I know. But -- but don't give up so easily, okay?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Let me just break it down and --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: No, no, no, let me just come down to --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Oh, sure. Yeah, take it.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Let me finish my question, okay?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. I'm sorry.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I know you want to correct me along the way, but --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: No, you're -- it's wonderful what you're saying, so keep going. (Laughter.)

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: The reason why Justice Alito's arguments about trial errors doesn't work is because you are giving up some known defenses to a trial. You can look at all of those things, you can imagine them, and you can say whatever they are, I'm going to give them up. So those are never considered, the trial-related errors. What we're talking about is sentencing errors, which is at a time where you don't know what the judge is going to do and so you have to make certain presumptions. One of them is they're not going to act outside of their constitutional or statutory duty. That's your argument, isn't it?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. I -- I can tell you I did think about what you said because you can make an argument, like, in all your cases -- Mezzanatto is the best one that explains what you can waive -- and, basically, personal rights -- this goes to Justice Alito -- personal rights can be waived. Now you get to a certain point where there's a public interest in the actual right. And what we were trying to say when courts go so outside the bounds of what anyone could have been thinking, government can't even defend it, it's implausible, there's something to be said for the criminal justice system not bringing itself into disrepute and having these embarrassing sentences out there. And the judiciary has certainly the authority or duty to correct them. So you can --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: -- analyze it under Mezzanatto, but it just seemed like a higher -- higher hill to climb.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Just one brief question. case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Because there's -- there's no fiduciary duty to say, and it's not just within the realm of plausible, ineffective assistance of counsel is you're waiving the right to appeal. I don't -- you would have to say, and I just don't think it makes sense, is that I have a fiduciary duty to tell you this judge may impose the death penalty and order castration. That's just not --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, that's why I said --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: So --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: -- that's why I said in many cases, not -- not all of them. I mean, for -- I don't know, for example -- maybe this is a good example, where the -- the counsel presumably knows a little bit about his client and he could advise him, look, you have to understand that if you accept this agreement, they may require you to take medication. And if he doesn't, then maybe that's something that can be brought --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: But that --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: -- as an ineffective assistance --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: With all due respect --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Maybe I'll finish the sentence.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. Okay, sorry.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: You know, if it doesn't, maybe that's something that could be brought as an ineffective assistance claim that would allow him to get out of the sentence.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: I don't think that would succeed because it was not ineffective and this guy doesn't -- there was no mental health condition. He did it for the assistance of -- the probation officer just said it might be easier if this guy were medicated. That's preposterous. I mean, it might be easier if you were medicated too for my job. It just -- that's not how you get to medicate people.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Okay. Thank you. Justice Thomas? Justice Alito?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, let me begin with Justice Sotomayor's rebuttal of what she took me to be asking about regarding constitutional rights. Now she will have the right to surrebuttal, which I won't have a chance to answer under this questioning regime that we have now. The Fourth Circuit test, which you seem to agree with, as I understand it, was any important constitutional right. So that wouldn't be limited to sentencing errors, would it? It would encompass all of the things I was asking about before.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: No. We're just talking about the appellate right on the sentence.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Okay. We're just talking about the sentence.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. That's all -- every circuit, the whole circuit split is about when you can appeal sentences. So, as Justice Jackson said, these are all things you -- you know, you -- you wouldn't --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: So anything that couldn't -- wasn't known prior to the time of sentence.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: At sentencing. Again, I tried to say with Justice Gorsuch it has to be clear. So, when you have an unconstitutional right to not go to church, and just it seems ridiculous that a -- a lawyer would say, by the way, you're sentencing this, I know you're religious, so there might be a chance at supervised release he's going to think you're a religious fanatic and say don't go to church. And all we're saying is come on.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Okay. What if it's a sentencing issue that was known by the parties before entering into the plea agreement?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. So all of that would be factored into any contract defense. It would be factored into miscarriage of justice. That's why guidelines are all out, is because it's known at the time of sentencing that, you know, you could be sentenced up to the statutory maximum. It really doesn't matter what the guidelines say.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: What about guidelines issues during the period when compliance with the guidelines was mandatory?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Oh, I think that that would have been -- I mean, now you're taking me back to --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: That's a sentencing error.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah, you're taking me back to pre-Booker. So, no, I don't -- I --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: No?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: I don't think so. Sentencing guidelines is just something that happened. Now we could talk --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: I mean, it was above the statutory maximum because the statutory maximum was defined by the mandatory guidelines.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. And we -- look, we could talk about that, but we don't need to because it's advisory and all courts have said sentencing errors are out. And if you write this opinion, you can say that too. So that way you just --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: What if the guidelines call for a sentence of six months' imprisonment, but the -- but the judge says that's woefully inadequate and anyway, they're not mandatory, so --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Thirty years.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Right, right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: The statutory maximum? If you want to say they -- they so misapplied the -- the criminal, whatever it's called, the -- the criminal career offender one where you get this massive bump, I just -- courts really don't want to see those. They just want, look, up to the statutory maximum, guideline errors are out.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Okay. One final question. If we're -- well, maybe not the final one. But, if we're going to apply contract law, what body of contract law do we -- do we look to? It's not the same everywhere.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. You look to the same that you would look every time you apply contract law, including in Rumery. You look to the Restatements, you look to centuries of case law.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: We look to the Restatements?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: That's what you did in Rumery. You cited Restatement 171, and that's what all the courts have done. I mean, you have -- the Court said -- held we'll apply, you know, general common law to contracts. But you have so many cases and plenty of collective bargaining agreements, we cite a lot of cases in the brief where you're applying contract law. Remember, the government is always applying contract law. I don't know where they're citing the state that they're in or they're citing -- I don't -- I don't think the cases really care. All contract defenses are so narrowly circumscribed that -- and the court of appeals, if 34 years, not even a trickle? Much less a flood, a river.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Thank you.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS

speaker: KAVANAUGH
