case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Absolutely not.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And if that were to be the case, presumably, Congress or the Rules Committee would have to do that.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. I mean, you'd have to go through the analysis Justice -- Justice Sotomayor said, and you already had that Brady case that says you can plea. So I think it's just not going to win.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And then, notwithstanding an appeal waiver, you can appeal a condition of supervised released if -- if you could fill in the blank, just to summarize, not --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah. Not with -- I mean, the easiest for me is just it was not within the realm of plausibility of either party. So I would take into account the government's expectation that supervised release is no fun, but you have these -- some of these conditions and we've talked about them. It can't include who you get pregnant with. That's just -- no.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But, obviously, you want a broader standard than that. Is there a phrase you would use for the broader standard?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Oh, yeah. Just violates the Constitution and it was not within the realm of plausibility, government has no justified expectation in the enforcement of that condition. I mean, all these conditions, the government would look ridiculous saying, well, yeah, no, we really need to do that.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And then, last, I just want to confirm this. You just said this to Justice Alito, that misapplying the guidelines, procedural or substantive unreasonableness would not be a basis.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Not under any contract defense or any -- like, any public policy or not miscarriage of justice because it's always within the reasonable expectation that the court could veer off from the guidelines and impose under the statutory maximum. And this is what the courts of appeals have held, so I'm just parroting what's already been held.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I -- I agree. Thank you.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Barrett?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So there's a lot of intuitive appeal to the contract analogy, especially because it's used for the underlying plea agreement. One thing that concerns me, however, is that at least on this question of appeal waivers, I don't understand any of the courts of appeals to go all in on this contract analogy.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Fair.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: And it wasn't fleshed out below in the Fifth Circuit. And I think you've had a lot of questions today exploring how there could be difficulties with it. So it seems kind of risky to go all in on this contract thing.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: So I guess three responses. One, as always, you're correct. It's fair. Only eight circuits have applied contract law to plea agreements generally. And they're not -- I think maybe only the Tenth Circuit and the Second Circuit has talked about this in terms of defense. So you're just a hundred percent correct. Number two, ironically, that is the Fifth Circuit. The Fifth Circuit's rationale for all of this is you can always appeal above the statutory maximum because the defendant didn't get the benefit of his bargain. I mean, that's too broad and it kind of -- it -- you know, it makes the Fifth Circuit's decision just not defensible. But they say over and over again that's not what the defendant bargained for. So we've already gone down that crazy, you know, open-ended route, and so I --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Well, but Judge Bibas wrote an opinion in the Third Circuit that located the statutory maximum thing and separation of powers and said you'd be going beyond the sentence. So just because the Fifth Circuit said this would be beyond reasonable expectations of the bargain doesn't mean that that is, you know, what we would have to say is the rationale for that exception if we accepted it.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: I -- I think separation of powers is good. It's just, you know, for the Constitution, you have to get a little more tricky with why that -- you know, outside of Article III power for a supervisor -- you know, a supervised -- condition of supervised release, it's just absurd, unconstitutional.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Well, and -- and here's another question I have about the contract analogy. It doesn't seem to me like a lot of the exceptions that we're batting around really fall within contract defenses. It's almost like we're trying to shoehorn them in.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: I disagree because I've argued two cases in the Delaware Supreme Court, and they're all about expectations of the parties, and one side usually wins as I expected the contract to be enforced as written. The other side has to really get out of it by saying it's so outside the realm of industry standard or so outside the realm that anyone could have thought of, that anyone could have perceived.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Yeah, but what about the other ones? Like, what's the analogy for miscarriage of justice or -- I mean, that -- that -- that is grounded, I think, in systemic concerns, maybe constitutional concerns.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: That reflects the fact that this isn't a pure contract between the prosecutor and the defendant, but the judge is involved because the judge signs off on it. But that doesn't map on.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: And I think the statutory maximum thing, you know, okay, well, maybe we can talk about it. I mean, nobody's really put it in those contract terms. Maybe the Fifth Circuit has gestured that way.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: And I think --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: But then what -- what -- what -- let me just finish this part of it.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Sure.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: What rationale would there be for us not taking every possible contract defense that could come along or limiting it to certain ones? I take it you would say no, any contract defense from the Restatement would be on the table.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Justice Barrett, with all due respect, whatever the government can do, the defendant should be able to do. The government doesn't get to just say I can only look at three principles of contract law in interpreting the contract and the defendant has a different rule. I mean, that's just -- just whatever Elon Musk could get, a criminal defendant has to be able to get under a contract.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. But -- but, Ms. Blatt -- and I haven't looked at all the cases in which the government is saying that or alleging breach. You know, I -- I -- I know Judge Easterbrook said that before and invited the government essentially to -- to allege that there was a breach when the defendant appealed. But, in all of these contract analogies, you're looking at the term itself and asking if the term itself is, say, unconscionable. And you're not arguing here that the term, that the waiver of the statutory right to appeal, that term is not void against public policy.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: It's not unconscionable. You're talking about one narrow circumstance, which is the application of that term. So it's not really like the contract itself.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Well, so, A, you're absolutely correct in terms of what Justice Kavanaugh said, but in every contract, again, over and over, we cite cases involving government contracts where a third party has to apply that provision, and there's just defenses that apply when the third party goes off the rails. But unconscionability, I think you're right, it's tricky. So the only way we would get there -- unconscionability I haven't seen applied. The only way you would get there is, in the government's view, this contract literally says you waive your right to appeal no matter what, no matter how many body parts they remove for you and no matter what the court sentences, no matter what the contract says. And all we're saying is, oh, come on, there's got to be a contract defense to that somewhere.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. Last question. This is just a factual one. As I understand the record, the district court said at sentencing when he objected to this medical condition, medical condition of supervised release --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- that, listen, if you go and get treatment and they do prescribe drugs that you have to take, talk to your probation officer, and if that's not fruitful, you can come back and see me. Did he go back to see the district court?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: No. He just got out of jail and he now is under an ordered mental health treatment program. Again, if -- I'll get a really bad law if all women have to --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: I -- no, no, no, no. I mean, like, I just wanted to know. I wanted to clarify that factually --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: You are correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- that's what happened because I do think then that gives him some recourse to go back to someone in the judicial system to ask. So I just --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Not really because, if the court says no --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: But the court didn't say no here. He didn't go back.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Correct. But there's -- again, he has a threat of imprisonment if he doesn't take the drug. I mean, that's bad.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. Thanks.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Jackson?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: So, when I'm thinking about this, I am mindful of the narrowness of the question presented as you have set it forth. You say whether the only permissible exceptions to a general appeal waiver -- waiver are for claims of an ineffective assistance of counsel or that the sentence exceeds the statutory maximum.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: I suppose we could answer no --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yes.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- to the extent that we see other exceptions that some of the other circuits have accepted and we think those should be allowed as well. This questioning that you're getting is, I think, an effort to say what -- we could offer more than that --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- what exactly are circuits supposed to be doing. And you point to contract principles, but I guess that doesn't necessarily have to be where we go with this, right?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Correct. I mean, the question presented is the Fifth Circuit is obviously wrong, please reverse and let us try to get a defense, but -- because there was questioning about, well, what will that mean on remand. But, no, you just need to say the Fifth Circuit's rule is indefensible.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Yes. And -- and I guess let me just add -- add one thing or ask one thing about the conversation you had with Justice Kavanaugh. I guess I'm not sure that Congress or the Rules Committee would necessarily be the only body that could determine whether these kinds of waivers are categorically unenforceable. I would think that based on our case law and sort of standing principles about knowing and voluntary waivers that this Court could perhaps avoid the concerns about picking a particular set of waivers, which -- I mean -- excuse me -- exceptions, which ones, are they contract principles or whatever, if we could be, enough of us, persuaded that in a circumstance where the defendant is pleading guilty and we know a sentencing hearing will happen, it is not sufficiently knowing to have a waiver of any errors that are going to happen in that sentencing proceeding, that it's just not an enforceable thing consistent with our understanding of knowingness and voluntariness with respect to the exercise of one's ability to make a waiver.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: So, A, correct, and, B, that's the law that Congress passed in 1984, which is you could bring appeals. Appeal waivers didn't even become boilerplate until the late 2000s. So we had a world in which you could just appeal your sentence. There was no flood.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And it's hard to see really -- and I'll ask the --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: But I -- I'm not going to get any votes for this, so --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: No, I understand. You don't want to waste your time because you feel that it is not --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Oh, I think you can get there.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And my point is -- my point is that when we're thinking about what a waiver is and we're trying to understand the circumstances and we're balancing the public policy issues on both sides, I'm going to ask the government, what are they gaining out of ensuring that people don't appeal obvious waivers -- obvious errors in their sentencing.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: Yeah.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Like, what's the public policy interest in that.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: My --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: So all of those things might lead one rationally to think it's really not worth the candle for us to try to parse out exactly what kinds of waivers in which situations we would allow or not allow as opposed to just saying we're not going to allow this sort of thing because of the knowingness and voluntariness problem.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: I mean, as I sit here, I kind of like what you're saying, and I -- I actually think it's a way of looking at it because nobody brings these appeals. I think, from the government, just putting the government hat on, they just don't like the guideline appeals because people get -- you know, they're advisory and if the court goes above it. But you could just -- you could get all the same way and say, well, that has to be knowing because everyone knows that the guidelines are advisory. Just in terms of the state of the law now, it's just not that bad for the government. They just don't --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Thank you.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Ms. Jacoby.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Knowing and voluntary presentence appeal waivers are enforceable bargains, and no doctrine of contract law calls for a different result based on the subsequent sentence that the defendant receives. Petitioner asks this Court to create new substantive limits on the enforceability of those knowing and voluntary waivers, but he's provided no administrable limits on which waivers should be in or out. The litigation that would inevitably follow under his front-line approach would essentially eliminate all appeal waivers. As a fallback, Petitioner proposes a safety valve to appeal waivers for the most egregious sentences. But, without more real-world evidence of the most farfetched hypotheticals, this is a solution in search of a problem, and it's a solution that comes with costs. An amorphous exception for egregious sentences will also invite litigation over what is egregious. Such litigation will deprive the government of the benefit of its bargain, thus making appeal waivers less valuable as bargaining chips for defendants. In all events, this Court should make clear that there is no exception that would permit Petitioner's appeal rather than simply remanding, as Petitioner suggests. No injustice would be worked by dismissing Petitioner's unripe due process claim, but remanding would signal down on that score to lower courts and litigants, opening the floodgates to garden-variety waived appeals like Petitioner's. Finally, this Court should reject Petitioner's argument as to the second question presented. The district judge's statement that Petitioner had a right to appeal was accurate under the terms of the waiver and circuit precedent, but even if it were not, the government's non-objection to a misstatement by the district court did not modify or waive the parties' written appeal waiver. I welcome the Court's questions.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: If the -- if this Court says that the agreement is void, would a remedy that would eliminate the underlying agreement be that you totally eliminate the plea agreement?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes, I do think there is a possibility that if this is -- you know, this is an essential part of the bargain, and if we are not getting our part of the bargain, then we don't have to enforce our -- our end of the bargain either. I think Petitioner has argued that the possibility that we'll, you know, reinstate the dropped charges is enough of a disincentive to stop the floodgates of dismissed appeals, but -- sorry -- pardon -- of -- of waived appeals. But, in practice, that's not actually much of a deterrent because it's not some -- it's not an option we avail of our -- avail ourselves of all that often because our whole point in bargaining for an appeal waiver is we want to bring finality to the proceedings and we want to stop spending resources on it. So the idea of having recourse to go back and reinstate the charges is kind of at that point --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: So, in this case --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Lisa S. Blatt
text: -- counterproductive.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: -- though, just confining it to this case, what's the disincentive to allowing an appeal here?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I mean, that is our whole concern, is that if you open the -- the floodgates to sort of a broad miscarriage-of- justice exception, there isn't really a powerful disincentive, and we will, in -- in various cases, be deprived the benefit of our bargain because we'll have to be litigating whether this exception, amorphous exception, to appeal waivers applies.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And you're -- you're asking --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: So I thought --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Your -- your --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: I thought you said that it wouldn't apply in particularly egregious cases. Did I mishear that?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: That's correct. I mean, our front-line position --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Correct that I didn't -- but --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct that you didn't miss --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Correct that I misheard it or that --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Our front-line position is that there should not be an exception for -- for even egregious miscarriage of justice because the Petitioner has argued this case based in contract doctrine, and we don't think there's a basis in contract doctrine for that. If this Court goes the route of wanting to have a -- a miscarriage exception for reasons other than contract law, maybe some kind of, you know, sort of federal common law policymaking or -- or constitutional, we would very strongly urge this Court to define whatever that exception would be very narrowly and to make clear it doesn't apply here.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: So all of the hypotheticals that Ms. Blatt presented us, you're comfortable defending all of those?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Our front-line position, yes, is that the appeal waivers in --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, you keep saying front-line position.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yeah. Sure.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: To me, that conveys the notion that you're ready to retreat.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: No, I -- I'm not -- I am not ready to retreat. I'm not ready to retreat. Our position is that the -- the appeal waiver is enforceable.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: So the order that you only -- only make your wife pregnant or what all the -- all the other examples, you say that's fine? We're --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes. Our position is that that's enforceable. And I recognize that sounds like a very harsh result, but I don't think it's a real-world concern that this --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: A -- a racist sentencing judge?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Again, our position is that it is enforceable. There are a few --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: A -- a sexist sentencing judge?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Someone who is biased against religious minorities?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes. The appeal waiver is enforceable.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: All of that -- all of that stands?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Because the -- the -- the point is that at the time that we're deciding whether to enforce the appeal waiver, all we have is a claim that there has been this particular type of error. And what the -- what the defendant has given up --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Why wouldn't that -- why wouldn't that bring --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- as part of the bargain is the right to bring that claim.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- the sort of disrepute on the federal judiciary that Judge Posner talked about, if you held a trial with 12 orangutans was his example, that that would have to be resolved. And I think we would all agree with that, right? But, here, you say any sentencing error of any kind.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So, to be clear, an appeal waiver is not an agreement to receive an unlawful sentence. You couldn't agree to receive trial by 12 orangutans. That would be an unlawful bargain. It is an agreement that the final decisionmaker --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Why isn't this an unlawful bargain?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: It's an agreement that the final decisionmaker on your sentence will be a district court rather than a court of appeals, and that is a bargain that the law tolerates.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: It's a district court who says I'm going to let an orangutan pick a sentence out of a hat?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Well, again, it -- it --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
