case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: The -- the district court remains oath-bound. It is a bargain that at the time you're entering into it, all you are agreeing to is that the district court will be the final decisionmaker.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: That is not a bargain against the law. The law already tolerates the possibility of even egregious sentences going unreviewed because it has given defendants the choice whether to bring an appeal or not. If the law did not tolerate that, we would have a system of automatic appeals, as many states do, for example, for capital cases.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Counsel, can I -- you talk about opening the floodgates, but you're the one who's proposing a theory that no circuit has ever accepted. Yours is even more limited than the Fifth Circuit. You're saying only IAC as it relates to a knowing -- knowingly or not knowingly enter a plea is cognizable. The statutory maximum, you're saying, is not cognizable either unless the plea agreement tells you that the judge will sentence within the statutory maximum because the logic of your argument is, if I agree, if I say in the plea agreement the judge can sentence you any way he wants, that would not be cognizable, correct?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So -- so our position, yes, is that if in the plea agreement you expressly say I am waiving my right to appeal on the grounds that the statute -- that my sentence is above --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Now every other circuit has something broader than the Fifth Circuit. Virtually all of them have something for constitutional errors of the nature that Justice Gorsuch was call -- talking about either under a miscarriage-of-justice rubric or under a plain error or unconstitutional violation. So this is not floodgates that are opening. Whatever is being appealed now is pretty narrow. It -- it's a small fraction of the plea agreements are being appealed, and those that are, there's an even smaller fraction where there's any time being spent on them. So waiving a flag talking about floodgates opening seems rather exaggerated by the government.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So the burden that we experience in the circuits right now really depends on the way that this exception is described in the circuits. In the circuits that have open-ended exceptions for, you know, all constitutional claims, the U.S. attorney's offices do report that to be a significant burden because it's quite easy to characterize even garden-variety claims as a due process violation, as I think this case illustrates. In case -- in circuits that more carefully circumscribe their exceptions to two or three discrete situations, it is -- it is admittedly less of a burden, but the problem is that whether we get the benefit of our bargain, which was to not have to litigate an appeal, just turns entirely on the defendant's choice because, if the defendant chooses to raise a miscarriage-of-justice exception --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Well, if you don't -- if you're not happy with the bargain, do what she -- what you're threatening to do, which is go ahead and prosecute them.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: But, again, our -- our whole purpose of --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Your -- your -- your -- your --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- entering into the appeal waiver is that we didn't -- we wanted finality and we didn't want to have to keep litigating.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Well, but the problem with finality is that you're basing it on the good faith of a third actor, meaning you're -- you're depending on a district court judge to not -- or they are, a district court judge to follow their constitutional and statutory obligations. I would think it's unenforceable to enter a contract that says you are going to be sentenced by a judge who does not have to follow the law.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: That is -- that is very much not what an appeal waiver says.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: That's exactly what it says.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: An appeal waiver says --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Well, but that's -- that's exactly what you're saying.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Not at all, Your Honor. An appeal --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: That's exactly what you're saying, which is, if the judge uses impermissible race factors, impermissible sex factors, religious factors, that can be waived. That's saying that a judge -- you're entering a contract that says, if your judge is biased, if he doesn't follow the Constitution, if he breaks plain -- if he makes plain error judgments that are clear and undisputed, there's no remedy for you.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So -- so, again, an appeal waiver is not saying you can be sentenced however you want by a judge. The judge is oath-bound. The judge has to follow the law all the time.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But that's what you're saying.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: The -- the appeal waiver is just saying the final decisionmaker is the district court, and, by the way, that was the system that existed for a hundred years in this country. We didn't have sentence --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Ms. Jacoby --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: If that -- if that really is --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Ms. Jacoby --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Sorry.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: -- just out of curiosity, what's your back-line position? (Laughter.)

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Sure. So we -- we think -- we think that if this Court is going to go the miscarriage-of-justice route, again, we don't really see a basis for that in contract law, but if you're -- if you're going to go that route, our strong preference is that you follow the circuits that have, you know, basically done what the Fifth Circuit has done but just with one or two more exceptions that seem to capture some of the concerns that people have here. So we like, for example, the Seventh Circuit's test. I would put a little bit of a gloss on it for precision, but what I would say are the three circumstances that would be qualifying as -- as a miscarriage of justice would be a sentence that's explicitly based on a constitutionally impermissible factor like race; two, a sentence or condition that is categorically unlawful for the statutory offense of conviction; and, three, a sentence reached without even a minimum of civilized procedure, that's the example of, you know, the orangutan sentences you.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Why would it not be sufficient to say miscarriage of justice on the assumption that everybody who's going to be applying that standard knows it's a high bar, has seen it before, has thought about it before? The idea of, you know, defining it into three discrete situations is not usually what we do when we speak of miscarriages of justice, and yet, you know, everybody gets that it's a high bar.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: The problem with setting the high bar is not that we're concerned that -- that judges won't know what constitutes a miscarriage of justice. The problem is that defendants won't know and they may well think that their case does present the miscarriage of justice.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, maybe that's right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: And then we have to litigate it, and that deprives us of the benefit of the bargain, which was to not have to litigate.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: You know, that -- that's right. But, if -- if that's the case, that kind of challenge can be easily dismissed. I mean, I guess I -- I wouldn't think that that would take very much of anybody's time.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: You know, we do end up having to brief the merits of these disputes because courts will sometimes just ask for more briefing. It -- the -- the circuits that have this more open-ended waiver -- pardon, open-ended exception, they do report a more serious burden to litigate it. So we do think that capturing the discrete kind of buckets of cases that do seem to give everyone concern, and I think those three do really capture the universe of what people are worried about, the, you know, categorically impermissible sentence or categorically impermissible condition, the sentenced by an orangutan, the race-based sentence --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- I think that is the universe, and so just limiting it to those three and making very clear what those exceptions are and then applying them to this case rather than signaling to lower courts and litigants that this is a borderline case, I -- I think would be far preferable.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Did you say ineffective assistance of counsel is one of them?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes, of course. I think we're all taking as given that ineffective assistance of counsel is one, and the Seventh Circuit does say that.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And -- and the sentence exceeding the statutory maximum?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So -- so I want to be careful about how I define that.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Because you used categorical rather than statutory, and I want to know what that --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes. So what I'm getting at with that is I think what everyone is worried about when they're talking about this sort of statutory maximum thing is the idea, like, you pleaded guilty to an offense that carries 10 years and you get sentenced to 15. So I'm trying to capture that. But what I'm trying to exclude are things that some courts have said are -- fall within the statutory maximum exception, which are things like whether your restitution was proximately caused by your conduct, whether certain prior offenses qualify as ACCA predicates. Courts have sometimes said that those fall within a statutory maximum exception on the idea that if they're correct about their claim, your sentence exceeds what Congress has lawfully authorized. And we think those types of claims are really what we have bargained to not have to be litigating. We have bargained that the final decisionmaker on those issues will be the district court.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: What about supervised release conditions? So I asked Ms. Blatt this.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But supervised release conditions can be challenged on appeal notwithstanding an appeal waiver if?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: They are categorically unlawful for the statutory offense of -- of conviction, same as the sentence terms. So that falls in my second bucket as well.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: What does categorically unlawful when you're applying it to supervised release conditions mean?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I know what it means when you're talking about the statutory --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- sentence.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I think that refers to the -- the type of condition that there's really never any justification for for this offense. I mean, like, the -- the -- a condition like you can never get pregnant during supervised release.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well, what -- is there a term that -- because we have to write an opinion --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- that's going to capture this.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: That's why we think categorically unlawful is sort of the best that we can do. We don't want to have to be dealing --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: That's kind of -- I don't think that captures it.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I mean, the issue is we don't want to have to be dealing with questions like, you know, was this sufficiently justified on the record, is there enough stuff in the record to support this, did the judge make enough fact findings? Those are exactly the kind of reasonableness issues that Petitioner says are out of bounds, and we don't want you to just be able to call it a due process claim and then all of a sudden we are doing those reasonable -- reasonableness inquiries when we have bargained not to. And, again, I want to be clear, when we're bargaining for this, this is to the defendant's advantage. I mean, there's a reason that the defense bar does not want to go the route that Justice Jackson proposed of getting rid of all of these altogether because this is something of great value to the government, and so it is a bargaining chip --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: No, I under --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- for the defendants.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But then the -- oh.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Sorry. Are you --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Go ahead.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: I -- I appreciate that, but I guess what I'm a little surprised about with the government's hard-line position is that I can't quite figure out whether you are sticking with the contracts idea or not. You've said many, many times that this is about the bargain and the government is bargaining not to litigate and that's what we really have to care about. But, as Ms. Blatt points out, every contracts regime that I'm aware of has some exception where the court is looking at the fairness of the bargain, where there's some consideration of the, you know, different degrees of ability to negotiate, the fact that you might have people who are being coerced into accepting this kind of deal even though it's not knowing and voluntary. The court is policing that. And the government's position here seems to be that we are not supposed to be caring about that; we just need to focus on the fact that the government has made this deal, that it's not going to want to litigate any more of these cases. And so it kind of brings me to Justice Gorsuch's original point. Like, that seems kind of unconstitutional in a way that the primary value here is to prevent the government from having to litigate appeals when we're talking about people's constitutional rights. And so I'm just trying to understand, is it your position that notwithstanding the contracts-like nature of this endeavor, we are not to be treating this the way the courts ordinarily treat contracts, which is to consider these kinds of exceptions?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So I'm really glad you asked this question because I think this is a really important point for us. Our position is not that contract defenses do not apply to plea agreements or to appeal waivers. It is that the contract defenses that Petitioner has raised here fail. They fail because a subsequent sentence that a defendant receives under just ordinary principles of contract law, the ones that Petitioner has relied on here, do not make the agreement against public policy or unconscionable --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Right, but wouldn't you --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- or frustrated purpose.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- have to do that at an individual level? Like, I don't know how you could categorically say we allow for these defenses, but they're never going to apply in this situation because something like the fairness of an agreement really takes into account what's going on with respect to that particular case.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: This is why Justice Kagan is -- is -- is, I think, resisting the granular statement of what counts as a miscarriage of justice, because we could look at a particular case and say: This bargain, this scenario is unfair because it relates to the kinds of things that my colleagues have pointed out. Right?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So -- so, if we're in contract world, and I'm going to bracket the miscarriage-of-justice world, which I think, if this Court's going down that road, it's not on the basis of contract doctrine; it's -- it's something else, some other kind of --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Wait. We can -- we can fold --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- policymaking. But -- but --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: No, no, no. Let's fold the miscarriage-of-justice concept into something like public policy because it's a -- you agree that public policy is an exception, right, in -- under the contracts world? And one would think that if what is happening here is a miscarriage of justice, we -- we would say that that's against public policy. So let's put it under that umbrella. Go forward.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Sure. I'm happy to talk about public policy exception. Under contract doctrine -- again, I'm assuming we're in contract world. Under contract doctrine, the question is not whether the sentence is against public policy. The question is whether the agreement is against public policy.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: And the -- the agreement to waive your right to appeal is not against public policy. It's not against --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Because?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- the public policy of the appeal rights statute --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Because?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- because the policy of the appeal rights statute is one of defendant choice always. And it's not against the policy of the underlying, you know, say, constitutional amendment you say is violated. Take -- take, for example --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Ms. Jacoby --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: What about -- what about the Sentencing Reform Act, which says that appeals are important, that they incentivize the court and the parties to actually follow the law, follow the guidelines, not issue these egregious sentences, right? We have a congressional policy that, in fact, revamps the entire sentencing system to allow for appeals. So to suggest that an appeal waiver is not against public policy, I think, runs up against all of that.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: But, again, our system still, even after the Sentencing Reform Act, leaves it as a matter of defendant choice whether to exercise that appeal. If Congress really thought that the appeal --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: That's the question. That's the question today. That's my question that everybody else has given up --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- but I'm still working, right?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: If -- if --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: My question is, should it be left as defendant choice given all of these problems? Given the fact that it doesn't seem to advance anything other than the government's interest in not wanting to litigate, you know, these kinds of issues, should it be left to defendant choice in this circumstance?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: It -- it definitely should given that Congress has left it to defendant choice. I don't see a basis for this Court to upend that. And then, as to the idea that all we're doing here is protecting the government's interest in finality, no. I mean, this is a bargaining chip for defendants. The -- the appeal waiver is valuable for us, so, here, a deal with an appeal waiver was worth dropping nine charges for Petitioner. I have no idea what a deal without an appeal waiver would be worth, but --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Ms. -- Ms. --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- basic economic logic suggests it would be less. Different charges --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Ms. Jacoby, two --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- two questions on that. One is your answers to Justice Jackson about the contract approach, as you're calling it, you argue you win under contract principles. You don't argue that they don't apply.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct. Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: So why doesn't this defendant get a remand --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Because we win --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- to argue contract?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- we win categorically. The subsequent sentence that the defendant receives --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah, but the -- if I --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- is never a basis to find that the contract is against public policy.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: If I -- if I might? The Fifth Circuit hasn't addressed that question. Nobody has addressed that question. This Court hasn't addressed that question. Why wouldn't we remand to allow the court of appeals to address that question?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I think what Petitioner has -- has asked this Court to do is to say that in some instances, an appeal waiver could be against public policy.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: No.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: And I'm asking the Court --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: No.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- to say it never could.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: No. No. What -- what -- what Petitioner is asking us to say is that the Fifth Circuit's rule that there are two and only two bases is not correct and that I should be allowed to try a contract defense. And you say you've got good contract defenses. God bless you. How about litigating them?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: To -- to make it a possibility that they try to raise a contract defense, I think Petitioner needs to show how any contract defense could in theory in the right case give relief here. And there is no public policy that an appeal waiver violates based on the subsequent sentence that --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: But, if we're not prepared to decide that in the first instance because no court has passed on that question, do you object to a remand to have a court --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: We very strongly object to a remand, particularly because of what it would signal about the facts of this case. You could say it may be possible in some case, but we would really urge you not to suggest that it would be this case because this is the type of appeal that even the circuits that have broad standards, I think, perhaps excepting the Ninth Circuit, would categorically not find this a miscarriage of justice.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And -- and then --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: And if you suggest otherwise, that -- that truly will open the floodgates and cause a big problem for the United States.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Because -- because an issue that hasn't been litigated should never be litigated. Okay. All right. And -- and then you -- you -- you tout the benefits of these deals. Let's take this case as an example. The defendant here pled guilty to one count of stealing $32,000. He was sentenced as if he was guilty of all the counts the government dropped and a half a million dollars' worth of -- of stolen money. How -- if I think about this as an unconstitutional conditions possible problem, we normally say that there has to be some nexus between what you're giving up and what you get and some proportionality. And if he's being sentenced as if he committed all the crimes that weren't charged, it's pretty hard for me to see what benefit he's getting from an appeal waiver here. Can you help me with that?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Absolutely. So, first of all, on uncondition -- on unconstitutional conditions, there is no constitutional right to an appeal. So --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: There's a statutory right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes, but --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And -- well, as a matter of --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- it's not an unconstitutional condition and it doesn't burden your constitutional rights.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: As a matter of due process, you're entitled to that statutory right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I mean, no, I think that you're just --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Really? You just --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- constitutionalizing the appeal right if you say that as a matter of due process you're entitled to the statutory right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Oh, okay. Okay. All right. So --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: But -- but setting that aside, I think your second question is about --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I -- I think maybe you better set that aside for my purposes at least.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Understood. Setting that aside, your second question, I think, is about if he got a good deal in the end here, if -- if, in fact, the sentence is -- is one that his bargain to drop nine charges proved to be a good deal. As -- as my friend has said, you know, he obviously thinks it ended up not being a good deal, but that is not a basis to undo a bargain and that's not a basis to find a bargain to be unconscionable. Unconscionability isn't about harsh results later when it proves you made a bad deal. Unconscionability is about a deal that you made that at the time you made it is so one-sided no rational --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: If --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- person would enter into it, and that was not this deal.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: If the government's position is a defendant can knowingly and voluntarily give up his appeal rights, I wonder what the government would say a defendant couldn't give up? Could a defendant give up, for example, his right to go to church after his conviction or to own a gun after his conviction --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- or his entitlement to federal unemployment benefits after his conviction?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- again, this comes back to my point that this is not -- an appeal waiver is not an agreement to be sentenced unlawfully. An agreement to be sentenced unlawfully would be against public policy --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Oh --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- because performance --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- okay. Okay. Now that's a --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- of the agreement would be against public policy. This is --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- that's an interesting test. Okay. So, if it's an unlawful sentence, he should be able to appeal?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Not at all.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: No?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: No, no, no, no, no. If the agreement is to receive an unlawful sentence, that is an agreement against public policy. But, here, the agreement is not to receive an unlawful sentence. The agreement still contemplates that the judge is oath-bound.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Right.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: It is an agreement that the final decisionmaker on your sentence is a --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Will --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- district court --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- will be --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- and that is not an unlawful agreement. No public policy forbids the district court from being the final decisionmaker on your -- on your -- on your case.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: All right. Go ahead.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: That was the status quo for a hundred years.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: What about -- what about --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Ms. Jacoby, can I -- can I ask you a question, Ms. Jacoby -- Ms. Jacoby? I'm having a hard time tracking exactly what the government's position is. So I asked Ms. Blatt, explain to me how these defenses that you're proposing fit within the contract analogy. And, I don't know, I -- I sense some going back and forth about whether the contract analogy is a perfect fit so that all these defenses are available. And, if so, I'm not really sure how the miscarriage-of-justice back-line position fits in, unless we try to shoehorn it through public policy. So explain to me what the government's theory is here.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Sure. So Petitioner has litigated this as a contract doctrines case, saying that all these contract defenses apply. Our -- our position is, if -- if we're going on contract defenses, no, none of them applies.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Would you go on contract -- well, let me -- let me ask you that just as a matter of first principles, is it the government's position that this should be litigated as a contract case?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I do think so. And I think that there's not really another source of law that Petitioner has identified to lodge this miscarriage-of-justice exception. It's not contract principles.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: No, no, no, no, the government. Like, do you think of this, do you think the Petitioner is right to litigate this? Because you've gone along with it --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes, yes.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- and you've said, if we're talking about contracts, it doesn't work. But do you think of this challenge as something to which the contract analogy should apply?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I do think that this type of argument is one to which the contract analogy should apply. There's no constitutional right to an appeal, so I don't think it makes sense to say that there is a constitutional right to an appeal in certain egregious cases, so the Constitution isn't really a home for this doctrine. And other than that, I think you would just be engaging in some kind of federal common law policymaking --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- where Congress hasn't --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So then --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: -- Ms. Jacoby --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So is the position -- oh, sorry. Can I just finish --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: No, go ahead.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- this one? So is your position that the contract analogy applies, but none of the contract defenses work in this context?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. So, when you're making this concession about, you know, potential miscarriage of justice, et cetera --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- you're just kind of pulling that from the ether?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: That -- so, there, we're assuming that you -- you are kind of going outside of contract doctrines and you are trying to find some sort of policy or maybe constitutional backstop, some safety valve. And we think, if you are going down that road, the safety valve I proposed to Justice Kagan is the right one, but, again, we do not think that that is the right way to go here.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Well, why isn't Justice Gorsuch right then? I mean, are we supposed to march through every single available contract defense for the Restatement and say this is why this couldn't apply here? This is why that couldn't apply here?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Petitioner has come up with four potential defenses. None of them applies. I -- I think that you can just categorically say --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: As to his case, but we're not --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: No, no, no, categorically, when a subsequent sentence -- sorry, a subsequent sentence does not make an appeal waiver against public policy. It doesn't make it unconscionable. It doesn't make it a breach of the implied duty of good faith. It doesn't frustrate the shared purpose that goes to the essence of the bargain. Just categorically those defenses all fail. If there are other defenses out there, it was on Petitioner to raise them, and he hasn't.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Is the --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Didn't argue that. Sorry.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice -- Justice Kagan?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Is -- is the premise of your answers to Justice Barrett that this Court has no power to establish rules intended to safeguard the integrity of the judiciary?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: That is not our position. But the rules need to be lodged, I think, in some source of law. There's no congressional source of law. There's no, really, constitutional source of law given that there is not a constitutional right to appeal. So I don't think it makes sense to say --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: No, I mean, that was my question. In other words, you're saying that we have to point to a statute, we have to point to a particular constitutional provision to set some boundary lines on what judges can do in a task that is supremely a judicial one.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I think that --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: That we can't just say, you know, there are some things that judges can do that would be a miscarriage of justice and we -- we -- we -- we don't need to point to a statute to be able to create a rule that polices the judiciary to that extent.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I think particularly because we are in the world of federal criminal law and federal criminal procedure, which is highly regulated by Congress and the Rules Committee, that's an especially, you know, dangerous place for this Court to be making policymaking, even though I understand that it's policymaking about what judges should do. It's policymaking about which court should be the last word on certain types of cases, and I think that really is the province of Congress and the Rules Committee. If you disagree with me and you are going down the road of -- of a miscarriage-of- justice exception, again, we strongly urge the Court to cabin it to the circumstances that really give everyone pause.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, whatever the miscarriage-of-justice exception says, whether it's less cabined, whether it's more cabined, you're saying that the only way that we can do that is by referring to contract law principles or by finding -- which I don't think exist because people would have found it -- some statute that allows us to do that?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Or constitutional principles or -- I -- I think you're maybe gesturing towards something to do with the supervisory powers of the courts or something like that. But this isn't really a good home for the supervisory powers because this isn't about supervising the conduct in the courtroom. This is really about making rules about when certain -- you know, when a decision should be final, whether that's at the district court stage or the court of appeals stage. That's kind of bread-and-butter federal criminal procedure stuff that Congress deals with and the Rules Committee deals with.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas, anything further? Justice Alito?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, can't we say, to continue your colloquy with Justice Kagan, can we not say that a plea bargain has some attributes of a contract, but it's not like an ordinary contract. I don't know. Even the -- even the amici supporting Mr. Hunter say -- this is the Cato/ACLU brief, point 1-b, "plea bargaining is no ordinary contract negotiations." So we can adopt a principle that is informed by contract law without taking a position that you now seem to be taking, which is this is just like any other contract and all of the contractual defenses that might be recognized are available here. I find your position really hard to understand. You -- on the one hand, you say you don't want to be burdened with having to litigate a lot of -- a lot of appeals that are taken by defendants who have entered into a -- entered into an appeal waiver. And then you're -- you're happy to have judges decide -- don't you think that anything that -- any objection that a defendant might have could be -- could be characterized as unconscionable?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: If I -- if I --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: I mean, we occasionally see issues of unconscionability in cases involving -- involving arbitration. And, boy, some state courts really go to town on -- with the -- with the unconscionability argument. But you're happy to -- you're happy to deal with all those?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I'm -- I'm definitely happy to say why categorically appeal waivers are not unconscionable if -- if that's the question. If the question is whether there should be some -- some other rule that informs the court, yes, I agree plea bargains are not perfectly like contracts, so the -- the analogy doesn't hold in all respects. But you would have to say that there's a constitutional dimension. I mean, there would have to be sort of some source of law that is informing what rule the court makes if it's not a contract rule. And there's not really a constitutional principle at -- at play here, and I'm not really sure another source of law. So, no, I don't -- I want to be clear, we've been litigating this case as a contract case because that's how Petitioner has brought this. If the Court wants to say that there are aspects that are not like a contract and other rules should apply, it would just need to ground those -- those rules, I think, in something. I'm happy to explain, though, why.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Okay. Thanks.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Sotomayor?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Counsel, on the second question presented, there is a way of reading that transcript in which one could say the judge basically said, I'm going to impose a condition, come back to me later if you disagree. And then he mentions the right to appeal, that there was permission to appeal at least this -- this -- this condition. Why can't we read that colloquy as such?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Because a district court doesn't have authority to modify the parties' agreement, so --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Well, then that goes to the silence that was the government's position there. All right. What does that do to the ripeness question that Justice Barrett had? Presumably, you would argue at any point in time that the waiver applies, correct?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: It -- that depends on the language of the agreement. Here, this agreement doesn't bar Petitioner from seeking modification of the condition of supervised release. So he could do that. The Fifth Circuit has said that an appeal from the denial of modification is covered by a waiver if it's the type of agreement that -- pardon -- the type of appeal that could have been brought from the beginning if -- if --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: That's -- isn't that the -- the vicious circle you're putting this defendant in, isn't it?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I -- I don't think we're putting the defendant in any circle.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: The Fifth Circuit is.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I think the defendant entered into an agreement, and this was the terms of the deal.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And so you're saying tough luck because the Fifth Circuit won't let you do it, so we should let you do it? We should let you say --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: It is possible --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- it's not right?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- I think, under the terms of the Fifth Circuit's doctrine that if the type of appeal that he brought were more as applied and not the type of thing he really could have brought from the beginning, given that this appeal waiver doesn't cover --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Let's go --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- appeals from a modification --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Now --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- it could be allowed.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- you admitted that it would be unconscionable to contract to have a racist judge decide the case, correct?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I -- I admitted it would be against public policy to say my -- my sentence will be decided on the basis of race.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But it's not, in fact, against public policy to have a racist judge sentence you?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes, the sentence would be against public policy. But the question is whether the agreement is against public policy. And, again, the agreement is not to have --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But the -- but that's what you're -- you're --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- a racist sentence. The agreement is to have no appeal and that the agreement to have no appeal is not against any public policy.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Even though it involves, so -- a breach of the duty of good faith dealing, which applies to third parties that you delegate contract rights to.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: But a judge is not a delegee under -- under the agreement.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Oh, you can't have it both ways. He is either a judge acting in conformity with the law, or he is a delegee subject to the good faith and fair dealing condition. You want to pick and choose defenses.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Not at all, Your Honor. He is a judge acting in good faith in the law, but a presumption of the entire appeal waiver is that the defendant might not think that the sentence he ultimately receives is unlawful. That is kind of the core --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Well --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- premise.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- but it's not a question of unlawful because it's a question of whether he's violated statutory rights, whether he has used impermissible constitutional factors, whether he's violated statutory limitations, imposing restitution when the statute doesn't provide for it and the agreement doesn't contemplate it. He's acted outside the bounds of expectation.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: The relevant expectation under contract doctrine -- again, I'm -- I'm assuming now we're in contract world. The relevant expectations are not the parties' expectations as to what sentencing outcome will occur. Contracts hold even when --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I -- I agree. I submit things --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- unforeseen and unexpected things happen. The relevant expectation is what -- how the parties expected their agreement would operate, whatever the outcome at sentencing.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So why isn't it -- and going back to Justice Kagan's question -- we all assume that judges will act lawfully, not that they can't make errors in calculations but that they'll act lawfully and not unconstitutionally?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: We -- we do assume that, but the premise of the agreement here is that both sides might not think that the judge has acted lawfully, and if the defendant thinks that the judge hasn't acted lawfully, he can't appeal. That's kind of the whole premise of this agreement here. That is the assumption.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. Then we're going around in the circle we started with.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kagan? Justice Gorsuch, anything further?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: You agree that some prospective waivers are just unenforceable, so, for example, you cannot prospectively waive your Title VII rights?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct. Yes. This is quite different, though. I mean, you can't prospectively waive your right to sue under Title VII, this Court has said, because the right to sue is basically integral to the substantive policy of Title VII. But the right to appeal is not integral to the substantive policy of any constitutional amendment or statutory amendment or anything like that.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Except for Congress --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: And we know that because it didn't --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- granted a right to appeal, just as it granted a right to pursue Title VII remedies.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Waiving the right to appeal also isn't against the policy of the right to appeal because that would just mean we could never have any statutory waivers.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, we didn't have appeal waivers until about three minutes ago in Missouri.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: We also didn't have appeals for a hundred years, respectfully.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah. And we also --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: We didn't have sentencing appeals at all.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And we also didn't have plea agreements before that if you really want to go back, counsel. So I'm not sure that works for you. And then, with respect to contract in what you call contract world, you agree that at least in principle, a defendant would have contract defenses, correct?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. Thank you.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kavanaugh?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Let's see. I appreciate your having alternative arguments and a party having alternative arguments. I think that's helpful because you don't know where the nine of us are going to go. But then it's important to keep -- for me, to keep clear on what the alternatives are. Your first one's the contract, no exceptions. Okay. The lower courts have not gone that way, have rejected it. Assume --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- I'm not going that way.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Sure.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay? Just me.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Sure.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay? So first alternative out for me. On the second alternative, I think you raise a good point, what source of law are we doing, but all the lower courts have been doing it, right? All the courts of appeals. And I -- could be federal common law, could be supervisory power, but it's there. And I think I'm just taking that as a given, and that is --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yeah, courts have done it. The way this has arisen is courts, you know, in the early 2000s, late '90s, often confronted with this would say, yes, these are okay, but, of course, we would never enforce it in X, Y, Z circumstances without really explaining why.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: It -- it -- but it's -- but there's a --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: But, yes, they have said that. They have said that.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: At this point, I -- I take your technical point and maybe it's more than technical, where does that come from, but it's -- it's everywhere in the courts of appeals. My old court, all -- every court, right? And it might be interpreting the federal criminal rule, it might be supervisory power, it might be federal common law, it might be going to what an appeal is in the statute, to Justice Gorsuch's point, but it's there. Then it's just what are the exceptions, right?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay. So, if we're on that, it's just what are the exceptions and whether to identify a general miscarriage of justice or to list three or four and then to say they're not exclusive, correct?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And there's a pretty good consensus of exceptions in most of the courts of appeals.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct. Correct. And the ones that we've articulated I think track the --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Like, in -- in other words, I think this is not so hard in the sense that there's a kind of defined list. What happened here is the list is shorter than what most of the courts of appeals have, correct?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: If this Court is going down that road, I think saying there's still a defined list; there's just, you know, two more bullets on the list --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Exactly. Exactly.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: -- we can live with that as long as the last bullet isn't catch-all, know it when you see it if it's sufficiently egregious, because that is a real problem for us. If the bullets are just -- if you just say the Fifth Circuit has one too few bullets, two too few bullets, that makes sense. But, again, we don't think there are any bullets that could capture Petitioner's argument.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well, in the D.C. Circuit, we did have a bullet that said results in a miscarriage of justice --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yeah.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- and I don't remember the place falling apart.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So I do think that if this Court were to announce a standard like that, we would see kind of a flood of that.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: And there has also at this point been kind of enough common law, I guess, you know, built up around it that courts have denied those miscarriages enough that defendants may raise them less. But, if this Court were to announce that standard, we think defendants would raise them a lot. And, again, I'm not suggesting courts would find miscarriages of justice constantly. The opposite. But that's the very problem.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But it's going to come up.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I mean, if we're looking for the needle in a haystack, but in every case, we're being deprived the benefit of our bargain, that's the problem.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And the ultimate benefit is the resource, right?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct. I mean, we enter into 45,000 plea agreements a year, so --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And, ultimately, it's a judge-protective thing too because the judges are -- yeah.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Correct.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I got -- got all that. The amicus brief of the Association of -- of -- let's see, which one -- the Association of Federal Defenders says, if we are too strict on this, there are going to be fewer plea bargains, so the resource problem is actually going to be worse. Do you want to respond to that very quickly? Because I'm using time.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I -- I don't agree with that. I mean, the most common alternative to entering into a guilty plea pursuant to an agreement is not a trial; it's entering into a guilty plea without an agreement, where the United States gives no concessions and the defendant retains his right to appeal his sentence. That's, I think, kind of the most common alternative that we have now and that's, I think, where things would get channeled. So I think we'll still have pleas, but those pleas will probably be less favorable to defendants because we're not giving the concessions.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Thank you.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Barrett?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Counsel, would the government be amenable to having defense counsel insert qualifications on the right to appeal and bargaining for the kinds of exceptions that some of the courts of appeals currently allow?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Yes. I'm -- I'm very glad you raised that point. Defendants are always free to do that. I mean, again, I -- I want to be clear it's a very important term to us, so in some cases, we won't budge, and in many cases, we won't budge. But it's case by case, it's district by district, and we do enter into plea agreements with carveouts for constitutional claims, carveouts that limit the appeal waiver to only certain guidelines ranges, all the rest. And we have in the appropriate cases entered into plea agreements with no sentencing appeal waiver at all.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: So it really is a matter of defendant choice here.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So you've emphasized that if we're going to do something other than the contract analogy, we have to find some source of law in which to ground it, and you've been pressed about supervisory power. I'm wondering whether, in addition to supervisory power, another rationale is that this isn't a pure contract agreement because it has to be accepted by a third party. The district judge has a role in the process. And, hence, because the district judge has a role in the process, there have to be some parameters to what the district court does in that process. And so our supervisory power over -- it's not just purely between the government and the defendant. So our supervisory power over the third party in that process is a source of law that can justify some of these exceptions.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I see that argument. I think that could make some sense. I -- I mean, I want to be clear, it's often the same judge that approves the plea deal as the one who sentences. I -- I want to be clear, we're -- we're -- we have gone sort of hard on the contract doctrine here because that's how Petitioner briefed this case, but I'm not trying to suggest that this Court lacks powers to --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: All right. And one other thing. You have repeatedly honed in on the nature of the appeal waiver. You say an appeal waiver is an agreement to let the court be the final arbiter at sentencing. Is that what the government's position is?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON

Could he contract with the government to prospectively waive his right to appeal any and all trial errors, errors, in other words, we're leaving it to the trial court to make all the calls with respect to evidence, et cetera, and I'm not going to as a matter of contract appeal any of those errors?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I'm -- I'm not prepared to commit on all trial errors, but, of course, you can prospectively waive right to, for example, certain evidentiary objections. That was Mezzanatto.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Why wouldn't you commit it's the same principle?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: That's --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: If -- if -- if the idea is that we can contract around making the trial judge be the final arbiter, which is what I understood you to have said --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: I see what you're saying. You're saying that there would just be no appeal, like, from the trial. Yes, I would think that would be okay.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And you would think that there would be no public policy interest of the court or the public in ensuring that people get a fair trial?

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Again, I just -- I -- I'm really wary to get out ahead when we're talking about these trial issues which are outside the scope of this case.

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: No, I'm not -- I'm not asking you to get out ahead. I'm testing your principle that --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
text: Well --

case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- there is no -- I'm testing your principle that there is no problem with an agreement to prospectively appeal errors in a proceeding that will ultimately impact whether it's the trial or the sentencing. case_name: Munson P. Hunter, Iii, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Zoe A. Jacoby
