Now I think there's a reasonable contrary argument that wouldn't apply here under the second head as Kokkonen puts it of -- of ancillary jurisdiction. There is an argument theoretically available that if the court compels arbitration but there's no arbitrator, appointing an arbitrator is a way of enforcing the order compelling arbitration. So I think a court could reach that conclusion, which wouldn't apply here because the arbitration is over. Like, the order compelling arbitration has been carried out. So I think the Court can reserve this question until the next time it has the opportunity to decide whether a particular type of arbitration --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Here, the court didn't order arbitration because it thought it didn't have the power to, so --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: That's correct. It stayed -- our argument --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So, under your theory, your answer to Justice Kagan is it doesn't have any power.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: No, but I think, arguably, even in a case where the court stays pending arbitration like this one, the premise of the stay order is that the arbitration will happen. Otherwise, the arbitration will last forever. And so a court -- this is not my -- this is not my bottom-line answer, but I think a court could say that the court is in a sense enforcing the order staying arbitration by appointing an arbitrator to make sure the arbitration happens. That's just a way a court might avoid that result. But, ultimately, I think that the FAA says what it says. The court -- you know, Congress included jurisdictional language where one --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. Thank you, counsel.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Yes.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Counsel, no one -- oh.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Go ahead.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: No one, I think, disputes the court's jurisdiction to enter a consent decree. So why isn't confirmation of an arbitral -- arbitral award analogous since both involve taking a private resolution and making it a judgment of the court?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Because consent decrees require a degree of judicial involvement that doesn't exist when the court confirms an arbitration award. There's a rich body of law from this Court about when a court can enter a consent decree, and the Court has made clear that the court has to undertake an independent assessment of considerations such as whether or not the terms of the consent decree advance the objectives underlying the law at issue in the complaint and whether there's a sufficient nexus between the terms of the decree and the complaint. Obviously, there's a lot of discretion to the parties, but still, precisely because it's a judgment of the court, the court has to undertake an independent assessment of the terms. That doesn't really happen under the FAA.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Is that just because it has been -- those kinds of assessments have been given to the arbitrator and sometimes even at the court's direction?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: I don't think so. When the court confirms an arbitration award, the court isn't independently assessing, for example, whether the arbitrator's award furthers the goals of Title VII or the ADA or whatever federal statutory claims are being advanced. The court isn't sort of taking a second look at -- at the merits. All the court is doing is assessing whether the arbitrator exceeded its authority under the arbitration agreement and engaged in certain specified types of misconduct. So I think that the degree of judicial involvement under the -- on Section 9 and 10 is much less than what this Court has said is necessary to justify the court transforming a -- a pure settlement into a consent decree. So that's why I don't think that analogy carries over.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: The Second Circuit and the district court both thought that our statement in Cortez Byrd kind of made this simple because, there, we said, "We have, however, previously held that the court with the power to stay the action under Section 3 has the further power to confirm any ensuing arbitration award." So I know you're going to say that was out of context and -- but that statement on its own would resolve this, wouldn't it?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: On its own, that statement is favorable to Respondents. And I'm going to say what you said I was going to say -- (Laughter.)

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: -- which is that if you read that whole paragraph, it's actually making a very different point which I think ultimately supports our position, which is that Congress wouldn't have intended a court's ability to -- to -- to decide a Section 9 or 10 application to turn on whether there was a preexisting suit on file, right? So the question in Cortez Byrd was one of venue, whether venue existed only in the jurisdiction in which the arbitration occurred or was broader than that. And the proponent of narrow venue conceded in that case that if there was a Section 3 stay, that court could exercise jurisdiction over the Section 9 and 10 application but argued for a different result if there was no Section 3 stay.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Different question. Section 10 in state court. Thoughts?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Yes. So, I mean, we view Sections 9 and 10 as -- as joined at the hip. Like, Section 9 refers to confirming the award unless there's a Section 10 vacatur.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: The standards set forth in Section 10.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Oh. The Court reserved that question in -- in Badgerow.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Yeah. What are your thoughts?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: My thoughts are that it doesn't have to be exactly identical to the federal standard, but if the Court --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Does it have to be close?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Pretty close. Like, if the court authorized de --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Pretty close?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Yeah. Basically, pretty close. I mean, the Court hasn't addressed this. Look, if the state court authorizes de novo review of an arbitration award --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Because the state court theoretically could have very different standards. Then the arbitration award's thrown out. But then the new suit, again, back to Justice Thomas's first question -- not the new suit -- the suit comes back to federal court then after the state court's thrown out the arbitration award.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: So, typically, that's not --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Isn't that a strange system?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: I don't think it would come back to federal court. Typically, what would happen is they would arbitrate the claim again. Like, the effect of, for instance --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well, it depends what the state court said in tossing the arbitration award, right?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Well, not really because, if the federal court -- if the case is arbitrable, then -- and the state court says there's some defect in the arbitration proceeding, but the case is still arbitrable, you'd presumably go back and rearbitrate. THEoretically, the parties, for example, might stipulate that if the award is vacated, they're just going to give up on arbitration, and then they could go back to federal court, either file a Rule 60 motion, or the federal court could opt to wait to dismiss the case until the state court's proceedings are done and it could be reactivated in federal court.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Do states have pretty close standards?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: They do. I don't think that's -- I'm not aware of any state that diverges significantly. Like, there's, like, minor wording differences sometimes. I think there would be an obvious preemption problem. As -- as I said, if the state authorized de novo review of an arbitration award, that would be contrary to Section 2's substantive standard that arbitration agreements should be enforced. But, if there's, like, very small distinctions or differences in things like the statutes of limitations, I don't think that those types of differences would necessarily --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: I have another question also just about practice here. Are -- are most of these 9 and 10 applications brought as freestanding applications, or are they connected to a -- to a federal suit in -- in the way that this one was?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: I mean, I've read a lot of cases. I'm -- I'm not sure of the empirics there. I think they're mostly brought independently because, usually, there's not that much dispute over whether parties have to arbitrate, but I've seen it on both sides. I -- I don't know a specific number.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: And is there a way in which your theory or Mr. Geyser's theory would push the practice in one direction or another in a way that either made sense or didn't make sense?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: So, yes. I appreciate the opportunity to say that. So one of the concerns about Respondents' position is that it'll create an incentive every -- in every case to file a freestanding motion to compel arbitration or do something else to get to federal court if you want to have that anchor. And this Court remarked on this in both Vaden and as well as Justice Breyer's dissent in Badgerow. Vaden said it would be a totally artificial distinction between -- to distinguish between Section 9 and 10 applications associated with preexisting suits and not so associated. And Justice Breyer's Badgerow dissent reiterated that language that the jurisdictional anchor would create that totally artificial distinction.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas, anything further?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, just out of curiosity, do you think we should ask Claude to decide this case? (Laughter.)

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: No. I -- I adhere to the wise judgment of -- of this Court.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Sotomayor?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You're suggesting to me that people who have stays in place typically don't move that court for motions to confirm the award, that they usually go to -- to -- somewhere else for that?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: No. I'm suggesting that usually, motions to confirm the award aren't necessary, especially when there was --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: No, no, no, I understand that. But, when there is a stay, what's the number of cases that go to another court?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Well, there's a circuit conflict on this issue. And it's true that most of the courts have gone with Respondents' position, but most of those opinions are sort of not -- not very -- there's not a lot of reasoning --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: It doesn't matter, but the -- the vast majority -- I'm not aware of a Section 3 stay case where the other side has come to a different court to confirm the award.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Well, I mean, there's a -- there's a circuit conflict on this issue. And --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So the -- where they're not permitted -- that's what drew us to take this case. Where they're not permitted to, they can't.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Right.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But the point is, when they are permitted, they stay in the court where the stay is granted, correct?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Right. It's likely that if the Court rules for Respondents, people don't want to pay a second filing fee --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: -- so they'll probably go --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You -- you talk about your fear of -- of people choosing litigation, choosing a venue, and not arbitrating in order to get a venue.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Yes.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You have to be Houdini and -- well, not Houdini. You have to have magical powers to know whether you're going to win or lose, right?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: No. You can just bring a freestanding Section 4 motion to compel arbitration, which this Court held you could do in Vaden.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Well, you didn't bring it.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: No.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You had to have the foresight -- you went to New York, a jurisdiction that had no connection to the dispute where -- where the dispute happened, and only because you lost in New York are you wanting to get out of New York.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Your Honor, the facts of this specific case don't present the practical concern you've elaborated --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Well, but they present the practical concern that your fear requires a lot of predictions that parties are unlikely to engage in because, right now, most of them don't fight where they're going. They just do arbitration.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And most of them don't fight awards. They accept them.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Right, but the point is, look, if I'm -- if I am advising a client and the client says we're about to arbitrate and we might need down the road to file an application to confirm or vacate the award, and the client says, I'd rather be in federal court, in every case, I would say let's go to federal court.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You know, I practiced a lot of arbitration law. I don't know a client who ever said that to me. I want to file -- file it in this court in case my -- I win the award, I want to be in federal court. Thank you, counsel.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kagan? Justice Barrett?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Just as a practical matter, under your theory, the stay is in place. You have the award. You want to confirm it. Do you have to go get a -- do you file a motion to dismiss first in the district court before you go to the state court to try -- state court to try to get the arbitral award confirmed or vacated?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: No, I don't think you necessarily have to do that. I don't think there's a specific order of operations because we view this as a non- -- like, the arbitration award as a non-jurisdictional defense, akin to res judicata or release. I think the federal court could opt, if it knows that there's an ongoing vacate or confirm proceeding, it could opt to just wait to dismiss the federal suit until those proceedings wrap up. I don't think there's necessarily an order of operations that's required.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. Thanks.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Jackson?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Can I just take you back to the original questions that I think Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan asked about treatment of this as a motion --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Yes.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- and Section 6. And I know that you referenced Badgerow's statement that the applications will get streamlined treatment as a motion, but Badgerow cited a case called Hall Street Associates for that proposition. It quoted from Hall Street. And that entire quote says, "will get streamlined treatment as a motion obviating the separate contract action that would usually be necessary to enforce or tinker with an arbitral award in court." So it appears at least as of Hall Street, the -- the Court understood the way that this worked, that the reason why you're treating this as a motion is that it would mean that you wouldn't need another contract action in another court in order to enforce the award. Why -- why doesn't this undermine the argument that you're making now?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Because I -- I interpret that language in Hall and Badgerow differently. Section 6 does not distinguish between applications in a freestanding case and applications that are associated with a preexisting case. It's just a single rule that covers all FAA applications that says that they'll be treated like a motion. And what the Court said in Badgerow was what that means is not that it is a motion in a case in which there is jurisdiction. It'll just be treated like one.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: I understand, but in Hall, it says the reason why it's treated as a motion is because it will obviate the separate contract action. And what I'm confused about is how that could be consistent with your vision, which would require a separate contract.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Well, I think there has to be jurisdiction over the contract action. If there isn't jurisdiction, the court couldn't hear it. And if there is jurisdiction, then, yes, you could -- the court could hear it as a motion and it would save a lot of time and effort. And Section 9 and 10 have these very specific service-of-process provisions. And if the defendant is within the district, it's sort of easier to serve process than it is normally. And I think Section 6 is similar with that streamlined procedure, but that doesn't mean there is jurisdiction. It simply talks about what happens if there is jurisdiction.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Thank you.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Mr. Geyser.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Consistent with decades of established doctrine, federal courts with preexisting jurisdiction may resolve related claims in the same pending case, and nothing in the FAA or Badgerow overrides the ordinary jurisdictional rules in this setting. A federal court already vested with original jurisdiction has obvious power to hear FAA motions in that pending action. There's no need to ask if there is a redundant basis for original jurisdiction because jurisdiction already exists, and any FAA motion falls squarely within a court's supplemental jurisdiction. This follows under the plain text of Title 28. It adheres to ordinary jurisdictional principles, and it promotes the FAA's purpose and objectives, including facilitating the judiciary's supervisory role in enforcing awards. Petitioner's contrary approach contravenes Section 1367. It is at odds with Badgerow, and it invites unworkable and untenable results. Respondents are simply asking to go back to the same court to enter judgment and dismiss Petitioner's case, without having to bifurcate these proceedings, file new state law litigation, and endure a parallel federal appeal and chase down Petitioner to finally bring this case to a close. I welcome the Court's questions.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: How exactly does 1367 apply to a Section 9 application where there are no apparent claims?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Where the --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: Where the claims in a section -- in an application under Section 9?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, I think it applies exactly under Section 1367. You have an existing federal case which vests original jurisdiction. The Section 9 claim, if you look at it as a state law analog, as a contractual resolution of the claim, as Badgerow did, then it -- there would be supplemental jurisdiction over that -- that state law claim. Now --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: But it's not a state claim.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: It -- it isn't, which I think is all the more reason that there clearly is jurisdiction under 1367. 1367 isn't limited to state law actions. It's any claim that's so related to the original claim that it forms part of the same case or controversy.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, but it's the same nucleus of operative fact. That's the -- that's the test. How is this the same nucleus of operative fact? It seems to me completely two different sets of facts.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, I don't think so, Your Honor. It's the -- it's the contractual resolution of the pending claim in the same case.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, but, Mr. Geyser, I mean, what -- what the -- I think Mr. Unikowsky said this -- what the -- the -- the second case is going to be about is something like did the arbitrator commit fraud. It's going to have nothing to do with the actual claims in the case. You're not allowed to relitigate those.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: You -- you -- you're not, but I don't think that matters. I don't think the test is are the elements coterminous. It's do they -- are the claims so related they form part of the same case or controversy. The arbitration award is an affirmative defense in the case. It's hard to see how something can be an affirmative defense to the claim in the case without being related to that case.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Yeah. I think that that's just not 1367's focus. 1367 says we're -- we're not going to look sort of as an abstract matter as to whether two claims were brought by the same parties or have certain features or are connected witheach other in a certain way, other than one particular way, which is are the facts the same in these two claims. And the facts are not going to be the same in these two claims.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well -- well, not all the facts, but -- but you're still asking -- this is a contractual resolution of the claim that is pending. It's like saying that the judgment in a case is somehow unrelated to the original claim that produced the judgment. I -- I think it doesn't have to be the same. We -- we absolutely -- I agree with my friend that these claims will not overlap. Often, they have nothing to do witheach other, except --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Yeah, common nucleus of operative fact. And often they have nothing to do witheach other. I would say almost always they have nothing to do witheach other.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: How could that possibly be a common nucleus of operative fact?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, it doesn't -- it's not that every fact has to share the same, you know, original atom. It's the, is there a common nucleus of operative fact?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: It's the great-great-grandchild of the original claim kind of tenuated on? I mean, what -- is it a claim? I mean, you -- you characterize it as an affirmative defense. Not a counterclaim. Not a subsidiary claim. It doesn't seem like it's a claim.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, it's -- it's resolving -- I think it is resolving the claim in the sense that it is -- it is contractually, you know, disposing of the claim that has been brought. Now I will say that there's an entirely different way to look at this. And part of the problem is that the FAA, as this Court has acknowledged, is unique. We have an unusual situation where we have a federal right under a federal statute that doesn't give rise to federal jurisdiction. And one analog is to say that the arbitration award is like a contractual settlement. So then confirming the award under the FAA, even though it's a federal statute, is like resolving a state law contract dispute, sort of like Kokkonen. Another analog, though, is just to say this is the federal directive on how a court decides what to do when the claim that's pending before it is now settled. So, in the same way that Congress can provide rules of decision in Rule 23 to say, if you're going to settle a class action, do you accept the settlement or not, or attach conditions to Rule 41, or do exactly what the Court contemplated could have happened in Kokkonen --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: And if that's the way you're looking at it, are you drawing on original jurisdiction then?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Yes. It's --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: I mean, that's not -- that's not a supplemental jurisdiction idea.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: The -- then we don't need supplemental jurisdiction --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Right.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: -- which is why we offered two competing paths in our brief that lead to effectively the same result.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: And it's not ancillary jurisdiction, just to clarify. You're saying that the original jurisdiction, the 1331 hook is carrying you all the way through?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: I think that is one way, I think, and a sensible way to look at it. I think it's actually the way that -- that Cortez Byrd was contemplating, saying, of course, once you have an original case and you've stayed it under Section 3, then, of course, you have jurisdiction to resolve what's a motion in the pending case, just as Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson pointed out, to decide what to do with that contractual resolution of the single pending claim.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: You heard his response on Cortez Byrd. Do you want to -- your friend. You want to react to that?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Sure. So I think -- I -- I think my friend is correct that Cortez Byrd was citing Marine Transit, which is a Section 8 case, but Cortez Byrd was not a Section 8 case. So the way I read Cortez Byrd and I think the way the courts have read Cortez Byrd is the Court was importing this common-sense intuitive proposition that happened to arise in the Section 8 context and putting it into the Section 9 through 11 context. And Cortez Byrd, by the way, was a 2002 decision. It's been decades on the books. Courts have construed it exactly the same way. It was only until the Fourth Circuit --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Most of the courts have gone that way, right --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, I think --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- most of the courts of appeals?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: I -- I think every court has gone that way. The only one that hasn't was the Fourth Circuit, which, with -- with all due respect to the Fourth Circuit, I think just profoundly misread Badgerow.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: That's why I said "most."

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Yeah. And -- and that -- that is -- and, in fact, when we say "most," that -- that is effectively as far as we're aware the only court that has gone the other way. I'm not aware of a single court before Badgerow that's gone the other way.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Mr. Geyser, you've laid out two paths for us, one, the supplemental jurisdiction path, reliant on a statute that could never be accused of being overly precise. The other would be the original jurisdiction path. I know what your answer's going to be, and it's going to be they're both great, Your Honor, but which one do you think, if forced to choose, is -- is the safer route and why?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: I mean, I -- I really do think that they're both great and I do think that they both work.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I knew -- I -- (Laughter.)

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: So the --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Any -- any -- any lawyer who -- who -- who doesn't say that isn't worth his salt where you wish to win, and I understand that. But --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: I -- I think that -- and it really is that it's -- it's half -- you know, half in one hand, half in the other. It's -- I would say that you could say it's part of the original jurisdiction. That's just a very easy way to resolve it. We're in the same pending case. We're trying to dispose of the original claims.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Your brief -- if I read your brief, your brief is a supplemental jurisdiction brief.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, we -- we did make both arguments, and we did supplemental jurisdiction --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: I mean, you made one in a couple of paragraphs, and you made the other in 50 pages.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, we thought one --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: That might be a slight exaggeration.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, no. We thought one was so obvious that we were trying to help the Court if it decided to go the other way. But I -- I do think, though, that the reason that we were fronting 1367 is -- is because of the analogy that the Court drew in Badgerow, is that if you do think of this as a contractual resolution of the claim and then you think of it as a dispute over the -- that contractual settlement, then it -- it does look like it's a little bit different. And I do think that they clearly arise out of the same ultimate, you know, common nucleus of operative fact. It's clearly the same case or controversy because, again, it is -- it is literally resolving the single controversy before the case, which is why, if you looked at how courts typically dispose of these actions, if they do retain jurisdiction, as every court outside the Fourth Circuit does, is that they say we're going to -- if we confirm the arbitration award, you enter judgment on the arbitration award and judgment on the underlying claim. You do it in one fell swoop because it is effectively the same action.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Can you respond to your friend's comments, picking up on Justice Breyer's dissent in Badgerow about incentives?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: The -- I think that it's really hard to see how there's an incentive to file an anchor suit for any number of reasons, including that courts -- just parties aren't doing that. Again, Cortez Byrd's language, you know, my friend can quibble whether it was overstated or improper, but Cortez Byrd's language was unequivocal. If you imported that -- that sentence into this decision, you could write a one-page opinion with a holding that says we resolved this in Cortez Byrd. That was in 2002, and there hasn't been a single identified case of someone filing an anchor suit, and I think it's for similar reasons that Justice Sotomayor pointed out. It's a very odd litigant who's choosing an original venue not to litigate the case and not to compel -- not to compel arbitration, which is sometimes heavily contested, and that's what you'd be worried about, but thinking months or years down the road, what is this going to look like once we get that award? Do I want to confirm it or vacate it? And I'd rather be in federal court, so I'm going to file this preemptive federal action. And for some parties, it's not even an option. If you're a plaintiff and you file the original lawsuit to litigate, then the -- it's not even clear. You might have -- first, under Morgan versus Sundance, you might have forfeited your arbitration rights because you're trying to litigate. And if the defendant doesn't move to compel arbitration, you're then out of luck. I mean, you -- you showed up there. It's -- it's your lawsuit. So I -- I don't think that those incentives actually play out. And if you're concerned about the practical consequences, I would look at the practical consequences of where my friend's position would lead courts and litigants. It would create this -- this odd situation where a party finishes in federal court after the stay. Now -- now, apparently, they have to -- the federal court will either dismiss the case without knowing whether those claims are actually resolved or not, or they stay the case to wait, as my friend said, potentially several years for the post-arbitration motions to play out in state court. Now, if the court -- if the federal court does dismiss the case, now we have an even worse situation. Now we have parallel proceedings, you have a federal appeal potentially contesting the pre-arbitration motion to compel arbitration because you can't take that until you have a final judgment in federal court. And then you have the same litigants going to state court to challenge what happened in the arbitration itself. So, instead of having one proceeding up and running where parties have already paid a filing fee, they've found the defendant, they've effectuated service, they've maybe thought about venue, they thought about personal jurisdiction, everything is up and running where you can resolve it in one proceeding, take one appeal -- it's nice, neat, and tidy -- instead, you have now competing litigation in separate tracks in different court systems. I -- I think -- I don't think that's what Congress intended. I think that would create what Cortez Byrd described as, you know, attributing to Congress a taste for the bizarre, and I do think that would be a bizarre situation.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: I agree with you that it seems more practical and tidy to do it the way that you just described. I'm wondering if you fronted the 1367 argument because, in some ways, it provides -- I mean, I still struggle with the common nucleus of operative fact and exactly where is the claim issues, but it provides a theoretical grounding. When I'm trying to think about 1331 just by itself, I'm trying to figure out what in 1331, if I'm blinded, I'm taking 1367 out of it, justifies the adjudication of a separate contract dispute.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: I think it would be exactly the same way that when a court invokes, say, Rule 23(e), it doesn't say do I have separate jurisdiction to decide whether to accept this settlement or not, or whether, in the Rule 41 context, do I have jurisdiction to decide whether to retain, you know, jurisdiction over the settlement to police it or to put it in the decree. I think -- I think it is part of the -- the original power to dispose of the claim.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: And so, under that formulation, we're thinking of it more as a motion than a claim, which would be inconsistent with the 1367 THEory, right?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Debatably. I think -- 1367, I think, has -- has been described as -- as quite broad. I think it's pretty capacious. I think it can cover lots of things. But, luckily for us, Section 6 under the FAA says treat these as motions. So, if -- if you want to treat the -- the -- this as a motion covered by original jurisdiction, you have a very easy path to do it. It's consistent with Cortez Byrd. It's consistent with the fact that Section 6 says treat this as a motion. I think it's even consistent with Kokkonen. And, again -- and, again --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Well --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: -- just to be clear, Kokkonen was dealing with a far more aggressive assertion of ancillary jurisdiction. That was a dismissed case, and the parties were trying to get the court to reinvoke jurisdiction to decide something.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. Let's talk about Kokkonen. What about Kokkonen's kind of Bucket 2, where Kokkonen says, well, it would be different if the court had reserved in the dismissal the authority to enforce the terms of the settlement? You didn't push that particularly hard. Why?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, I -- we did, and I'm sorry if it wasn't clear that we did. Here, it's even better. You don't -- you don't have a dismissal. You have existing pending claims in a pending case. So Kokkonen, again, is a much harder case. There, the Court's saying, I'm going to dismiss this action and I'm going to retain jurisdiction just in case something happens down the road. Here, we have pending federal claims. And if you -- and you don't even know what to do with these claims. So I think, with all due respect to my friend, I think he's incorrect. To dismiss the case without knowing whether the arbitration award will ultimately stand doesn't make any sense. If the award is ultimately vacated, the parties could very well say, you know what, that was a waste of time, let's just litigate in court.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: So is ancillary jurisdiction of the sort -- ancillary enforcement jurisdiction of the sort that Kokkonen talks about applicable here? Is that a coherent way to think about this?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: I -- I think you could. Now I -- I do think that this raises a slight complexity about -- to the extent 1367 has displaced or captured ancillary jurisdiction, but I think the very fact that Kokkonen contemplated that a court could retain jurisdiction to decide those subsequent settlement disputes suggests that this would be covered then by 1367.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Well, that's why I said enforcement jurisdiction. I think that's different because nobody really disputes that a court could exercise enforcement -- ancillary enforcement jurisdiction over, say, a contempt proceeding. So that would be different. It wouldn't be subsumed by 1367 the same way.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: We -- we think that works perfectly well, and I think it's -- it's a sensible way to look at this. I do want to address just very quickly the Section 8 argument about does the text of Section 8 somehow preclude jurisdiction under 1331 or 1332 or 1367, and I think it quite clearly doesn't. Section 8 is a maritime provision, and it starts off by saying, notwithstanding anything else going on, so this is Congress's attempt to say we're creating a self-contained unit to deal specifically with admiralty and we're going to provide specific rules for that context. In order for that to preclude the assertion of jurisdiction elsewhere -- because, again, we're not relying on the FAA for jurisdiction; we're relying on Title 28 -- it would have to show that Congress in Section 8 was thinking, I'm going to foreclose jurisdiction for every non-maritime case, the overwhelming swath of cases that arise under the FAA, simply by creating a specific rule of decision for that narrow context.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Mr. Geyser, just going back to this, oh, it's just a motion in a case, if you have jurisdiction in a case, of course, you have jurisdiction over this too, I mean, this is a very unusual kind of motion, right? It's a motion which could have been brought as a freestanding suit, which is -- which is essentially a freestanding suit and a freestanding suit in which there would have been no jurisdiction. So notwithstanding that there's this sort of, like, unusual posture in which it appears as, like, a motion in another suit, we all know that it's a different suit and a different suit in which there is no jurisdiction. So why do you -- why does that carry you home?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Well, I -- I think it's -- it's not quite just an entirely different suit because, again, it's -- it's a motion with a different nature of claim to resolve the original pending claim. So I -- I do think, again, just like Rule 23(e) is not a different suit, the -- the parties settle class-wide --

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: I think what I mean of it as a different suit is it's a bunch of contract claims. Let's say it's about, like, the arbitrator committed fraud and so my -- the contract is invalid. That's what this suit is. That's what this motion is. Call it whatever you want. That's what this thing is. And that has nothing to do with the employment action that's kicked off this whole thing.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Except for the fact that it is resolving the employment action that kicked off this whole thing. So, again, that's why I think you'd be -- it's really hard to say that resolving a claim is unrelated to the claim, even if the reason you resolved it, maybe you settled because they give you -- they offered you a lot of money or they -- they gave you something that you wanted. That has nothing to do with the underlying factual allegations. It's still resolving the claim. And that -- I think that shows why it's part of the same case or controversy. I mean, it is literally resolving the case or controversy. And -- and, again, I think a contrary view on that would say that an affirmative defense to a claim in a case doesn't arise or relate to that same case, which -- which it -- it's hard to even articulate the concept because it just doesn't make much sense. But, again, I think that's why they're -- we tried to offer two different paths in the brief because depending on which way you look at it, we're dealing with this odd hybrid that the FAA set up. Again, no -- no one has ever applauded Congress for creating, you know, the world's cleanest statute. It's five pages of the U.S. Code. I think this Court is burdened with two or three cases a year, it seems, under this statute going back I don't know how many years. But looking at it here, I think what Cortez Byrd acknowledged, you know, two decades ago still holds. Of course, if you have jurisdiction to stay the case under Section 3, you have jurisdiction to process it at the end of the day.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas, anything further? Justice Kagan? Justice Barrett, anything further? Thank you, counsel.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Daniel L. Geyser
text: Thank you.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Rebuttal, Mr. Unikowsky?

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Adam G. Unikowsky
text: Thank you, Your Honor. I'd like to first begin with the discussion of Section 1331, which didn't occupy much of the briefing but did occupy much of the discussion this morning. I don't think that confirming the arbitration award can be justified under Section 1331 because that judgment is not the resolution of the original claim. The original claim was a federal employment claim, and the resolution of that claim is that the claim cannot proceed in federal court because the parties agreed to arbitrate that claim. So just as a court dismisses a claim based on res judicata or release when it turns out that the parties have adjudicated the case in a different forum, the appropriate resolution of a federal claim is to dismiss it because the federal court can't hear it when it's being decided elsewhere. But confirming the arbitration award is different. It's transforming the arbitration award into a judgment, and the practical difference there is that it allows Respondents to execute a money judgment against Petitioner. So what happened here is that the parties agreed to arbitrate, and then this arbitrator entered the sanctions award, which is a money judgment against Petitioner, and then confirming the award transforms that contractual resolution of the claim into a federal judgment. And that's not a federal judgment. The money judgment against Petitioner, which is the real practical effect of confirming this award, is not resolution of the original claim. It's transforming the parties' agreement to adjudicate this in a contractual method into a federal judgment. That's why I think extra jurisdiction is needed. Section 1331 doesn't do the trick. And so then you get to Section 1367, and as some of the questions from the bench today made clear, there is no common nucleus effect. I think Kokkonen is directly on point on this issue. I understand, in Kokkonen, there is a dismissal rather than a stay, but as to the first head, as Kokkonen called it, of ancillary jurisdiction, the Court said it "permits 'disposition by a single court of claims that are in varying respects and degrees factually interdependent,'" which was very similar to the 1367 analysis. And then the Court held that the facts underlying respondent's dismissed claim for a breach of agency agreement and those underlying its claim for breach of settlement agreement have nothing to do witheach other. It would neither be necessary nor even particularly efficient that they'd be adjudicated together. And that reasoning is right on point here because, at core, the arbitration award is similar to a breach-of-settlement-agreement claim. It's a -- it's a contractual way of resolving a dispute. And the Court insight from Kokkonen is parties that agree to resolve a dispute via contract who later dispute that contractual resolution are adjudicating a different dispute from the underlying federal dispute. I'd like to say a few words about Cortez Byrd. You know, the Court has said that -- the Court has cautioned against, you know, giving too much credit to drive-by jurisdictional rulings. And I think this is just the canonical case of a drive-by jurisdictional ruling. So, first of all, jurisdiction was conceded in that case under diversity jurisdiction. Also, there was no Section 3 stay at all. So the jurisdictional anchor issue was doubly not presented. Meanwhile, the Court was talking about what it had previously held in this case, Marine Transit, that everyone agrees is irrelevant. The Court was also talking about a venue issue which was also conceded by one side in that discussion. And all of this in service of making an argument that's ultimately the argument we're making in this very case, which is that Congress would not have intended for a court's authority to hear a Section 9 or 10 stay application to depend on whether or not there is a preexisting suit on file. So I do understand that lots of lower courts have followed that statement from Cortez Byrd, which makes sense. I think, when a lower court sees a sentence like that in the U.S. reports, much like in the Royal Canin case, which presented a very similar scenario, the courts will often go along with it. That's essentially what happened here. But I think that, you know, this Court has, you know, the authority to check, as it did in Royal Canin, whether one sentence really establishes a holding. And I think it just doesn't when you look at the posture of that case as compared to this one. Finally, in terms of the practical effects that Respondents identify, I don't think that they're that -- that significant. I mean, what happens is, after there's an arbitration award, you go to the federal court and if a party says, look, we're planning to go to state court to confirm the award or vacate it, the federal court can say, look, okay, I'll wait to see whether or not the case ever comes back and I'll just delay the dismissal a little bit longer and they'll go to state court and -- and litigate there. I mean, you know, parallel federal and state litigation happens every day in our system of -- of -- in our -- in our federal system, and I don't think that the practical concerns here are any greater than they would be in any other case when you have parallel litigation across the federal and state systems. If there's no further questions, we'd ask the Court to reverse the judgment below.

case_name: Adrian Jules, Petitioner, V. Andre Balazs Properties, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: We will hear argument first this morning in Case 25-5146, Abouammo versus United States. Mr. Loss-Eaton.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: The question here is whether Mr. Abouammo committed his Section 1519 offense in San Francisco. In Section 1519, Congress created a broad document integrity offense distinct from obstruction that requires no communication, no obstructive effects, and no investigation. Under that broad law, Mr. Abouammo's offense started and ended in a 30-minute window during which he never left his home in Seattle. He was guilty and his offense was complete the moment he finished creating the false invoice with the requisite intent. Whether he sent it to investigators, whether it affected them in some way, or whether an investigation even existed at all, none of that is relevant to liability under the statute, so the government didn't have to charge any of that in the indictment or prove any of it at trial. But the government now wants to have it both ways. It says the uncharged, unproven effect of Mr. Abouammo's offense means that he committed it in San Francisco. That is wrong. From the common law, through the founding era, and up through this Court's decisions in Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue has always turned on the location of the offense's essential conduct. That is the question that this Court's venue cases all ask, even if not always in so many words. Here, Section 1519 has one essential conduct element, falsification, and Mr. Abouammo did that entirely in Seattle. Sending the document to investigators may have been evidence of his intent, but it was not essential for conviction, so it cannot support venue. In arguing to the contrary, the government relies on general, out-of-context language from cases addressing very different offenses, and it all but ignores Johnson, Cabrales, and the ratification-era understanding of where similar offenses were committed. With no grounding in statutory elements or text, the government's rule is unclear and unworkable, and accepting that rule for the government's own convenience would swallow the test this Court has always applied. I welcome the Court's questions.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: So are you saying that if he simply saved the draft to his computer that the crime would have been complete?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: Yes. Exactly, Your Honor. The only --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: So how is that?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: The -- the crime is knowingly falsifying a document with the intent to impede an investigation. The moment he saved the document on his computer, he had done all three of those things. Even if he had never sent it to anyone, if he had thought better of it, if he had deleted it, at that point, all of the elements were satisfied and the offense was completed and it was over. And that is vital for purposes of venue because that's the scope of the inquiry that the Court applies. It asks where did the defendant engage in the essential conduct elements of the offense, to use Rodriguez-Moreno's phrasing. In other words --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: How do you prove intent?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: So, certainly --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: If he didn't send it and never intended to send it, you're defeating your own argument.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: So, if he hadn't sent it, then, certainly, the government would have a much harder time proving intent, but just as a matter of statutory text and elements, if he had created the document intending to send it to investigators with the hope of impeding the investigation, and then, if he had thought better of it in that moment, say, and he thought this was a terrible idea, what am I doing, and he had deleted the document, he would still have violated the statute and his offense would be over at that point. the text of this -- of this provision is clear as to this. And I -- I don't take the government actually to dispute any of that, by the way. Congress knows how to write an obstruction statute that actually requires some sort of obstructive effect, some sort of nexus with the investigation or the proceeding. And Congress very deliberately didn't do that in Section 1519 because it wanted to capture a broader scope of conduct. Responding to the Enron and Arthur Andersen document-shredding and cooking the books, Congress said we want to be sure that we are sweeping in conduct taken in contemplation of an investigation even if one does not actually exist yet. And so, to that extent, the government actually benefits from the statute's scope because it doesn't have to prove actual communication to investigators or obstructive effects, and those are, THErefore, not elements of the statute that are required for a conviction.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Counsel, can I --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Is there --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- ask you a question --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Is there any other -- it just seems very bizarre to me. Is -- is there any other body or -- or statutes that are like that? I mean, the guy does whatever it is to create the document, and he says, oh, that's a crazy idea, and tears it up. You're going to prosecute him?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: So, practically speaking, of course, it would be relatively difficult for the government to learn about that in the first place. But I think the -- the specific scenario that Congress had in mind when it wrote the statute is illuminating, and that is the -- the Enron scandal. And, there, not only were Enron and Arthur Andersen shredding documents, which, of course, doesn't involve any communication with anybody by definition, but they also were keeping a second set of records, not because they had any specific intention of investigators ever seeing them -- I'm -- I'm quite sure they hoped that that was never going to happen -- but, essentially, it was just in case. And so Congress quite deliberately severed the nexus between an actual proceeding, because the statute doesn't even require that there be an investigation or a proceeding, and the conduct.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, but, I mean, that's a huge conspiracy, you know, affecting all sorts of different people and operations. You're -- you're suggesting the -- the same rule would apply in the case that I gave, somebody who, you know, drafts up a falsification, thinks better of it, tears it up. He's -- I mean, how much time is he facing for that?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: I don't remember offhand what the maximum is, Your Honor, but just as a matter of statutory elements, that's what the text says. And, again, I do --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Have courts actually applied it in that way?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: I don't know --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: I mean, what -- if you look around the universe of 1519 prosecutions, what are the -- you know, what might be considered the fringe cases?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: I don't know offhand of a case in which a court has ever considered a scenario where someone just created a document with the intent of impeding the investigation and then never did anything further than that, presumably, because, practically speaking, it's going to be quite difficult for the government to find out about that. But just -- again, if you just turn back to the text, knowingly falsifies a document with the intent to impede, that's -- those are the three elements. That's all you have to do. And that is what Mr. Abouammo did.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. But, if -- if that's -- let -- let's just imagine that it did require -- just -- just work with me here. Let's assume that it did require some kind of communication. The agency -- the agents were in his house, right? They were downstairs. Let's imagine, instead of e-mailing it, he handed it to them. You would still say that all the offense conduct happened in his home in Washington?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: Absolutely, yes.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. How does it change matters, again, just assuming that some kind of communication of the document is required, that he e-mailed it to them? So he could just say, for convenience, I'm just going to go ahead and e-mail you the document as an attachment rather than physically handing it over. In your view, would that change -- how -- how might that change matters, if at all?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: I don't know that -- that those scenarios are any different. Assuming that there is some sort of communicative element in the statute, handing a piece of paper to someone versus e-mailing it to them, I think, is communicating to the same extent. And so, in either of those cases --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So we don't have to worry anything about a server? This is -- you know, it's -- it's -- it's going to their San Francisco server and -- and their computer there and living on it in some way, right?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: No, you do not have to worry about that, both because, as a legal matter, the conduct would be the same, and also because there is no evidence in the record about where the government's servers actually are or were.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. So --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: The government, I think, is -- is hoping that you'll assume that the servers are in San Francisco, but that was never asserted at trial, there's no evidence of it.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. So you don't understand -- and, obviously, we can ask Mr. Yang this when he stands up -- but you don't understand the government to be contesting your interpretation of the statute and that only the creation of the document is required even if you put it in a drawer and never communicate it to anyone?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: I -- I do not understand the government to contest that, no.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And is that because -- and -- and I'll ask the government this -- but is that because both of you are focused on the statutory elements, not so much what the facts were in this particular case about how he transmitted the document but what the statute requires, and that's what we should be focused on in determining venue?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: That is exactly right, Your Honor. This Court's venue cases have always asked where did you commit the elements of the statutory offense necessary for guilt, in other words, where did you commit the actus reus of the offense.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: So these questions about, boy, that's a weird offense and a strange actus reus real -- really, it seems to me, isn't dispositive of our consideration here. We have to look at the statute and determine what its actus reus is. And so you say it is, what, falsifying a record?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: Yes.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: With the intention that it impede an investigation?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: Yes.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: But both of those things, the falsifying the record and, presumably, the intention, occurred in Seattle in this case, and so that's why I think you're saying Seattle is the appropriate venue?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: That is exactly right, Your Honor. And cases like Cabrales are a perfect illustration of this. In Cabrales, the Court emphasized that we're not asking in a broad sense what did you do in a sort of related factual way. We're looking at the specific statutory proscription that Congress enacted, and then we're asking how did the defendant violate it and where did they do so. So, in Cabrales, it was irrelevant to venue that she also had engaged in a drug distribution conspiracy in Missouri for which she was also going to be prosecuted no matter what and that she had been physically present in Missouri for various parts of that scheme or even that she had to know for the substantive money-laundering counts that the money was the proceeds of a specific other offense, which was the criminal conspiracy in Missouri. The Court asked simply, where did she actually commit the acts that constitute the money-laundering offense.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: The acts or the elements? Is it all elements, or is it some subset of elements?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: So the way the Court has framed it is essential conduct elements, which I take essentially to mean the actus reus. None of the Court's cases seem to treat intent as part of the venue analysis for these purposes. But I don't know that that would make a difference even if you looked at the intent element, as Justice Jackson said.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Do you think that there's a reason to treat those two things differently?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: I think, historically, commission has been about acts. If you go all the way back to the common law cases or the ratification-era cases, the Court is generally looking at acts or actions, conduct, in the -- in the sense of the actus reus. But -- and I don't know of any example that does look to an intent element, but even if you do, I don't think it changes anything here because, if the intent element was committed anywhere, it was committed where he was. It was committed in Seattle.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Counsel, we have the government's late-breaking argument that there's a separate metadata document that was created in San Francisco. I -- I know you argue that that's forfeited. I -- I wonder whether you would actually be better off having the Court address that, though, because one can imagine that we say it's forfeited in this case while, in every 1519 case to follow, the government's going to say, oh, we have a separate new document with different metadata in our offices and that changes everything, so we'll be right back here. Thoughts?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: So forfeiture aside, Your Honor, I think that argument has got real problems both legally and factually. Factually, you don't just have to create or falsify a document to commit the actus reus. You have to do so knowingly. And there is absolutely no evidence in the record here at all that Mr. Abouammo knowingly created a copy of a document anywhere, much less in San Francisco, because, as Justice Barrett and I were discussing, there's no evidence about where the server even was. But, if you get past all of that, then you get to the legal question. I'm not aware of any support for the government's position that just e-mailing a copy of an existing false record to someone is a separate act of falsification that can violate the statute. The best analog that we found is the Sixth Circuit case that's cited in our reply which says that at least for Section 1001 purposes, faxing and mailing two copies of a false statement are not two separate violations because there's no additional falsehoods or false content. And I think that's consistent with the ordinary meaning of "falsifies," which means essentially to make deceptive. It's the act of introducing falsity.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: He falsified the original -- the duplicates are duplicates. He didn't falsify anything in the duplicates?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: Exactly.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: If there's any falsification in the duplicate, it might be the government's metadata?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: Yes, I think that's fair, Your Honor. And -- and -- and -- and this is not to say, by the way, that he couldn't potentially violate some other statute by actually communicating the document directly.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Oh, goodness, I'm sure there are many out there.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: I think there probably are. But, for purposes of Section 1519, the only act of falsification was the creation of this document on his own computer in his own home. And that was the government's consistent position at trial in its opening arguments, in the Rule 29 argument. The government quite consistently said that the falsification was when he went upstairs and he modified the PDF on his computer, and at that point, the offense was over.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: What if he had --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: The situation --

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Go ahead.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: The -- the situation in which someone creates a false document but then never sends it, changes his mind, that person is going to be prosecuted under this statute, that's really fanciful. What is real -- what is going to happen in the real world is that the person creates the document and then sends it. But your -- your argument is that even if this had been e-mailed to San Francisco, e-mailed to a specific address of a person in San Francisco, there would be no crime?

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: Tobias S. Loss-Eaton
text: That is correct, Your Honor. And I think Johnson is the perfect illustration of why that is. In Johnson, the offense required using the mails for the purpose of sending or bringing into any state contraband. So there was similarly an intent requirement, much like there is here. It was even more closely tied to the interstate communication. And the Court said that does not change the venue analysis. We construe that statute to proscribe only the act of sending, meaning depositing in the mail. And once you've done that, the offense is complete. And so we are -- we don't care, really, that you did that for the purpose of sending something into another state or even that you actually succeeded in doing so, THEreby causing precisely the effect that Congress enacted the statute to proscribe.

case_name: Ahmad Abouammo, Petitioner, V. United States, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
