speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Respondents' position is that when Congress said "arrives in the United States," it meant stopped outside the United States. That theory is wrong for the simple reason that it defies the statutory text. You can't arrive in the United States while you're still standing in Mexico. That should be the end of this case. But, even if you see some ambiguity in the text, the Court's decision in Sale should clinch the case for us. In Sale, this Court determined that the protections of the refugee convention and the withholding-of-deportation statute do not extend to aliens outside the United States and, further, that it is entirely lawful for the executive branch to prevent aliens from reaching U.S. soil and claiming those protections. If Congress meant to depart from that territorial approach when it adopted the statute here, just three years after Sale, it would have said so. It didn't. This Court should, therefore, uphold the metering policy and reverse the Ninth Circuit's judgment.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: Are there treaty obligations that are implicated by either the metering policy or the issues here?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: No, there are not, Justice Thomas. Respondents rely primarily here on the refugee convention and the protocol, but there are two reasons for which those don't apply in this case and those aren't violated by metering. The first is, as this Court held in Sale, those provisions simply don't apply extraterritorially. They apply to the return of someone from the United States, not to, in Sale, the return of Haitian refugees who are interdicted in international waters. And, secondly, even where that convention does apply, what it prohibits is returning someone to a foreign country. Metering doesn't return anyone to Haiti or Guatemala or wherever the person might be coming from. It just says you can't set foot in the United States.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I'm not sure that I understand how you can say that we're not violating our treaty obligations with your reading and why Sale -- you think Sale protects you. Sale very clearly says that U.S. asylum and withholding protections apply to those who reside in or have arrived at the border of the United States. It also explained that refoulement means a defensive act of resistance or exclusion at the -- at the border, not merely returning a person to a country. Now the Refugee Act was passed in response to the MS St. Louis situation, which was a ship in 1939 carrying over 900 Jewish refugees that landed in Cuba, the refugees weren't permitted to unload themselves. It then came to the coast of Saint -- of Florida, and the U.S. wouldn't let it dock at all, all right, and turned it back. And it did the same in -- it did the same in Canada. Canada wouldn't let it dock. So the Refugee Act was passed to ensure that people who arrived at a border and knocked on the door -- because that's what you're saying. These are people who come to the line, there's an agent standing at the line that's open to everybody else except refugees, correct? They're letting in workers with permits to come into work, they're letting everybody else in, but they're not permitting the people who come to the line, to the door, and knock on it who want to claim refugee status. You're saying we're not going to inspect you. How does that not violate the Refugee Treaty Act or the spirit of the St. Louis U.N. convention?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: To start with the statute, the statute doesn't say "arrive at the door," "arrive at the border" --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: No, but it says "arriving in the U.S." in various provisions. The inspection provision says, "all aliens who are applicants for admission or otherwise seeking admission or readmission or" -- "to or transit through the U.S. shall be inspected by immigration officers." So various provisions of 1125 also speak about aliens arriving. Someone on a plane arriving to land in LaGuardia may not have put their foot on U.S. land, but they've arrived in the United States. They're arriving. They're knocking on the door.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Again, the statute that is specifically at issue here says "arrives in the United States."

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So, if I believe that your reading violates the U.N. convention, then what you're telling me is that Congress, when it passed this language in 1996, intended to reject its treaty obligations?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: No, I'm telling you --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Without conversation about it, and a House report that basically said there is no evidence that Congress -- Congress, in fact, told us it intended to make that provision. The House report stated that the new version of 1158 applies "to any" -- "any alien who is physically present in the United States or at the border of the United States." That was the language of the House report.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Not the language of the statute. The statute says "in the United States" and not --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But don't we read statutes in their context?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: You read statutes according to their text. And there's no ambiguity --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: No.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: But --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You start with the text and context, correct?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- Mr. -- Mr. Suri, the text has to make sense. And what is a little concerning to me about your reading of the statute is the practical implications insofar as it suggests that a Congress that was authorizing asylum would be requiring people to break the law in order to obtain it. So imagine a polite asylum seeker who wants to do everything by the book, he approaches the border but does not cross precisely because the law says you are not supposed to enter the United States without authority. Why on earth would Congress have intended or meant for his asylum request to be discarded, not taken seriously, not entertained, but someone who manages to enter the United States unlawfully, when the law says you're not supposed to do it, and requests asylum gets their application entertained? That doesn't seem to me to make any sense, that if we're trying to think about what "arriving in" means, surely, Congress was contemplating that a person was -- would be coming to the United States, would be doing so with an intent to comply with the law that says you're not supposed to enter and thereby asking for entry.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: There are two reasons for which that makes sense. The first is that we have a separate refugee admission statute, Section 1157, that protects aliens outside the United States. So it makes perfect sense for Congress to say: If you're in the United States, you go to the asylum route, and if you're outside the United States, you go to the refugee route.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Yes. But I'm trying to understand your -- the rationality of your interpretation of "arriving in." You're suggesting that "arriving in" means the person who is literally standing on the U.S. side of the border as opposed to the person who approaches the U.S. side of the border. And I don't understand why Congress would make that distinction.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: The second reason that Congress would have made that distinction, apart from the fact that the person in Mexico already has this other statute, the refugee statute that he could turn to, is that the problem of the world's refugees is not solely the United States' burden to bear. It's a shared responsibility of nations throughout the world and it makes --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: No, I understand. But think about the statute at issue. It says "arriving in." It -- it, first of all, distinguishes physically inside, right, and it says "arriving in." And it gives those people the ability to ask for asylum. And the way that your reading plays out, a person who is coming to, arriving in, approaching the United States, can't make that ask, but they have to somehow violate the law by entering the United States in order to make that ask.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: If I might complete the answer, Congress could reasonably determine that if a refugee is in Mexico, then the Mexican government is primarily responsible for processing his claim. Once the refugee is in the United States, whether legally or illegally, then the United States has greater responsibility toward that person.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: I guess I don't --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Counsel --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Mr. Suri --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- understand how that's responsive -- can I just finish? I don't understand how that's responsive to my point, which is the person who is arriving in the United States asking for permission to enter is not necessarily "in Mexico" in a way that implicates all the concerns that you're talking about. Yes, he's physically standing in Mexico. But imagine a person who has a placard on their body as they approach the border that says, you know, I would like entry, I'm being persecuted in Mexico. Your suggestion that the United States would say: Unless you can figure out a way to illegally cross, we're not going to entertain that claim, seems very peculiar.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: It seems to me that the premise of the question is that there is something improper about blocking someone from completing the arrival, arriving into the States.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: The premise of the question is that "arriving in" has to mean something.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: And to suggest that it means that you have to actually illegally cross doesn't make sense.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: There are other penalties that apply to people who illegally cross. It's a crime to illegally cross into the United States. And the fact that someone has illegally crossed into the United States can be taken into account when the person is making the asylum application.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Precisely.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Mr. Suri, I --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Sorry, please. Counsel, the statutory language, is it "arriving in" or is it "arrives in"?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: It's "arrives in."

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Okay. Thank you.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Mr. Suri, if --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Mr. Suri --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kagan?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: I don't think you had much of a chance to answer the part of Justice Sotomayor's question, which I am interested in, about the treaty obligations and particularly how the treaty obligations should or should not be interpreted in light of the St. Louis incident that gave rise to the treaty.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: The treaty was a compromise between the interest in protecting refugees and the interest in protecting national sovereignty. And the compromise that was reached was we're not going to require nations to admit anyone into the country, but we're going to forbid sending people back to other countries if -- once they have already entered that country. And, here, the treaty doesn't apply for two reasons. One, the individuals at issue haven't entered the United States, and, two, they're not being sent back to any foreign country. They're just being denied admission to the United States. I would also note that even on any interpretation of the statute, the St. Louis situation wouldn't be covered because there's a parenthetical in the statute that talks about people interdicted in United States or international waters, and they're covered by the statute only if they're brought to the United States. So, in the St. Louis example, those individuals were not brought to the United States. Therefore, they'd be outside the scope of the statute, I think, even on Respondents' reading.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I think Justice Jackson's question got at the fact that your interpretation privileges someone who illegally enters over someone who legally comes close to the border. And why would Congress privilege someone who illegally enters the United States? Can you answer that directly?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: I -- I think it's a bit unfair to say that we're privileging people who illegally enter because people who legally enter are being treated better than people who illegally enter.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I got that distinction. The distinction is between the illegal entrant and the person who lawfully gets very close and wants to follow the rules, that person is disadvantaged as compared -- on asylum as compared to the person who illegally enters. And the question as I understood it is why would Congress do that, so what's the answer?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Two answers to that. The first is we would deny that the person is being privileged because metering is not saying to the person, the polite asylum seeker in Justice Jackson's words, you can never enter the United States and your only option is to enter illegally. It's saying our port is at capacity today, try again some other day, and that time when that person comes in, that person could come in legally. The second answer is that Congress could reasonably determine that the United States has greater responsibilities to aliens in the United States than to aliens in Mexico. That's how sovereignty is divided among nations in the world. And whether you got here illegally or illegally, Congress could say we have greater responsibilities once you're within our borders.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: More generally or separately, I guess, what is the problem -- what was the problem that was trying to be solved here when this policy was put in place?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: The policy was put in place in 2016 when ports which might have a capacity of something like 50 or a hundred people, a holding capacity of 50 to a hundred people, were facing lines of aliens far larger than that. And those individuals were demanding entry at that particular time, and ports were overwhelmed. Sometimes they didn't have enough food to feed the people arriving at -- in the United States. Sometimes they didn't have beds in which they could sleep. They didn't have places where they could hold them. So it was necessary for the ports to say, sorry, we're at capacity, try again some other time. And I think Respondents' position is that that is categorically illegal in any circumstances because it always violates the asylum statute and the inspection statute to say we're full right now.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: That's not quite what they're saying. It's certainly not what the circuit court said. What the circuit court said was we have a law that permits the United States to have people reside in Mexico or stay in Mexico while the application is being considered. So there is already that remedy for the government, correct?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: There is a contiguous territory return provision, but --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Exactly. And that only -- and what the circuit said is, it's okay for you to say stay somewhere else while we process this. What you can't do is do what the statute doesn't permit you to do, which is not to inspect me at all. The circuit said you can make a list of people and have a rational basis to tell them to come back in a particular time. But, instead, what you were doing was saying you, alien, we're not going to even consider your application, we're not going to take your number, we're not going to do anything. We're just going to turn you back. We're going to be the ship on the MS Louis and ship you back to be killed wherever you end up. And that's what the statute doesn't permit. Now you mentioned --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Might I answer that?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: That's an argument that Sale was wrongly decided because that's exactly what the United States was doing in Sale, sipping -- shipping people back to Haiti.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: No, because Sale made very clear that the U.N. obligation is, if you're a refugee who's arriving at the port of entry, if you're knocking on the door and I'm staring you in the face, you have an obligation to at least listen to my application.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: And the --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And you can tell me to wait, you can put me in a safer place to wait, you can do a bunch of different things. What you can't do is just turn me back from the border.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: And the second answer is we're not shipping people back to Haiti or whichever country the person might be coming from.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: No. You're just telling them walk back.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: No, we're not telling them anything.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So they can just -- the people on the St. Louis could have swam back. They happened to be on a boat. But that's what we did. They were off the coast of Florida, and we didn't let them dock. We didn't let them dock and take -- and interview them at all. We didn't consider whether they were being persecuted. And the majority of those people were shipped back or had to go back from where they came and were killed. That's what we're doing here, isn't it?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Like the Court in Sale, I do not deny the moral weight of claims made by refugees. But that is not the question before the Court. The question before the Court --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So tell me why --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Could I -- would you complete your answer?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: The question before the Court is, what obligations did Congress impose in the asylum and inspection statutes? And those refer only to aliens who arrive in the United States.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: May I ask you a question about the statute and about that answer? You know, I totally get that if you just look at the language "who arrives in the United States," it sort of suggests, well, you have to be in the United States. So totally get that. It does seem to me that this statute -- you don't have to be a superfluity hawk to think that this statute has a massive superfluity argument -- problem, because the way you're understanding that second phrase, the statute ends up saying, essentially, any alien who is in the United States or who is in the United States. So what led to that kind of superfluity in this statute, and how are we to understand it? It really -- if you just sort of -- you -- it can't mean that. So the "in the United States" must mean something else.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: I agree that the "arrives" category is a subset of the "present" category, but there are a few different reasons why Congress might have mentioned that subset the same way it mentions subsets in other statutes that refer, for example, to money or property. One reason is that the "arrives" category is subject to special rules that other applicants of -- for admission are not subject to. For example, they're automatically subject to expedited removal if they are inadmissible. So, when the statute, 1225, is talking about the "arrives" category repeatedly in later provisions, it makes sense to mention them separately in the definitional provision. The second reason is that immigration law has historically drawn a distinction between deportation proceedings for people in the interior of the United States and exclusion proceedings for people who have just arrived in the country. This provision -- in this provision, Congress might simply have been trying to make clear that both of those are covered. The third reason is that under the entry fiction, this Court had previously interpreted terms that are close synonyms for "present" in the United States, like "found in" or "within" the United States, to exclude recent arrivals. And Congress might have wanted to make clear that it's covering recent arrivals as well. So, for all those reasons, the "arrives" category serves important clarifying function.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: You know, it also serves a sort of confusing function. When Congress did this, it must have realized or you would think it would have realized that it was just going to confuse matters to essentially say the same thing twice about an alien who was in the United States. I don't think, on the entry -- what is it called, the entry fiction?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Fiction.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: I mean, I don't think you would have needed this second provision to do that because you have "physically present." That should have tipped people off that we're not talking about the entry fiction. And we also have the language about "irrespective of the alien's status," which also should have tipped people off that we weren't talking about the entry fiction. So, if -- if -- I took that to be your primary argument in the brief, and I don't think it really sort of does it.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Well, if you're positing that there are already two parts of the asylum statute that are meant to address the entry fiction, then it isn't much of a stretch to say that there's a third piece as well. Secondly, the two pieces you've mentioned are not included in Section 12 --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: It's like belt and suspenders and, you know, whatever, a new pair of pants.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: And the second point is those two pieces are not in Section 1225. They're only in Section 1158. So, if Congress had included the phrase "arrives" in 1225 but omitted it from 1158, then people might draw a negative inference from the inclusion in one provision and the exclusion in the other.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Can I just ask --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Mr. Suri, can I ask you, does the administration -- the metering policy has been rescinded. Does the administration intend to reinstate the metering policy if it's successful in this case?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: The administration would like to be able to reinstate metering if and when border conditions justify. I cannot predict in advance what border conditions will look like or what specific policy responses the administration would take in response to that.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Thank you.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: So, Mr. Suri, why -- why then aren't we just issuing an advisory opinion in this case? I mean, your back-and-forth with Justice Sotomayor raised another line of questions that I had along the same lines as what Justice Barrett just indicated. At the time in which the district court in this case issued its opinion, the metering policy had been rescinded, and, as you've now represented, the government has no concrete plans to reinstate it. So I don't understand what we are doing other than advising the government in sort of the abstract as to whether or not this kind of thing is lawful. We don't have an actual policy. We don't know who's right as between you and Justice Sotomayor about what metering actually contains because the government doesn't have a policy in effect and hasn't shown us that it wants to have a particular policy. None is on the table. So how do we even have jurisdiction, really, to be addressing this?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: The question of mootness turns on whether the Court can grant any effectual relief whatsoever to the prevailing party. You can grant us effectual relief and the case isn't moot because there are three types of prospective orders that the district court issued that are still in place against us, the most important of which is a class-wide declaration saying we can never engage in metering at the southern border. If you agree with us, you would lift that declaration and we'd be able to resume metering. Therefore, the case is not --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: But you don't -- but you don't have a -- you don't have a plan to resume -- I mean, are you suggesting that -- I -- I'm -- I'm a little worried about the judiciability in the following sense. At the time the case was initially brought, there was a policy in place, the government was engaging in metering, and, obviously, we had a live controversy about it. But, before the district court issued its opinion, that policy was rescinded. There was no more metering. And yet, I think, in the record, it demonstrates that the parties just sort of said to the district court: Well, it would be helpful if you would go ahead and enter your ruling. That's ordinarily not the case, that you don't just have the district court opining on policies that are no longer in effect. So I appreciate that the district court did and so you would like to get rid of the order. But why wouldn't the right remedy be to just vacate the order rather than having us speak to the merits of it in this way?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: If you'd like to look at the issue through the lens of voluntary cessation, you get to the same result. Yes, we voluntarily ceased metering at one point --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: There are no findings about voluntary -- the district court did not make findings about voluntary cessation, so I don't know how we could get -- go there.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: But the test under voluntary cessation is, is it absolutely clear that the conduct can't reasonably be expected to recur? And that can't possibly be satisfied here because we're telling you we want to do this policy again if border conditions justify it.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: The --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas? Justice Alito?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: During the period when metering was suspended, what would happen in the hypothetical situation or not so hypothetical situation you were talking about where a port was capable of handling, let's say, 50 aliens and, instead, 300 wanted to -- wanted to enter? What was done?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: What was done during the previous administration differed from what was done during the Obama administration. During the previous administration, the aliens were generally paroled into the United States. And the current administration has serious concerns about that approach as a policy matter because that means that individuals who may not necessarily be entitled to asylum are allowed to enter the United States without showing that they have a valid claim, and it may be years before the person can be found and deported if that is appropriate.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Do you happen to know how many people were paroled?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: I don't have an exact number on that, but it would not surprise me if it was in the millions.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Thank you.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Sotomayor?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Counsel, the Office of the Inspector General issued a report that said that some of the metering that was done was not done because of lack of space. It reported on the fact that there were empty beds in at least two ports, okay? So Justice Alito assumes the moment in which there were not enough space, but there is a claim that at least one president was using this as a subterfuge for ignoring any inspection whatsoever. Do you have a response to that?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Yes, I have two. The first is that we dispute those facts, and this is at the summary judgment stage, so you can't resolve those disputes in Respondents' favor.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But we do have an Office of the Inspector General report that says that, correct?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: True. The second answer is that Respondents brought two different types of challenges to metering in the lower courts, first, a facial challenge saying metering is never okay, even if done for a legitimate reason. That's the only one before you today. And they also brought an arbitrary and capricious challenge saying, even if metering is acceptable when the port is actually overcrowded, you can't use it as a subterfuge. That's not before you today.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. The language at issue here was passed in 1996. In 1998, the government modified its regulations to define an "arriving alien" as an applicant for admission coming or attempting to come into the United States at a port of entry, which is consistent with the policy that had been followed since 1980 -- '80 I think it is, when the Refugee Act was passed, correct?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Not correct. The Court said in Cardoza-Fonseca when it was talking about the 1980 Refugee Act that the asylum statute applies only to aliens in the United States.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But the port -- the regulations have always been treating aliens who knock on the door at the port of -- a legitimate port of entry, have up until the metering policy, were at least letting -- giving them the opportunity to claim asylum, correct?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: I'm sorry, that's not correct either. The regulation refers to an applicant for admission, and an applicant for admission is --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. We're back in the same circle.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kagan?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: I'm going to take you back to the statute, Mr. Suri, and the superfluity problem. You said to me the second phrase should be viewed as a subset of the first, and I want to understand what you mean by that. What does the first include that the second does not?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: It includes individuals who may have arrived in the United States a long time ago, but the process of arrival has been completed. The person would be present in the United States, but the person doesn't arrive in the United States.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Is that really what you're saying? Is that your best -- because it strikes me that that's actually a better argument than the ones you've given so far, that the first phrase is people who have been here for some time and the second phrase is meant to refer to people who sort of may arrive right now after this statute has gone into effect?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: If you're intent on giving these provisions non-superfluous meanings, then we think that's the --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, that's --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN

I mean, these phrases are, like, right next to each other, and they must have meant -- you know, if you're right about what "arrives in" mean, I'm -- I'm looking for a theory as to how that just doesn't repeat what the first phrase does.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: It -- it's a subset, but that's different from saying that it has a completely different meaning and --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Okay.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

text: -- includes people who --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Correct.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Thank you.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: We believe that it is lawful, but we're not asking the Court to go that far today. case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

text: I -- I recognize that --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: -- you dissented in the case we're relying on.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I -- yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: But --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

text: I -- I think commas grammatically are a little --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

speaker: ROBERTS

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: I think it's far too late to do any of that now because we also have the class-wide declaration that independently keeps this case live.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Right. Let me talk about the class-wide declaration. You're -- you're asking us to reach the merits of whether or not metering is lawful and reverse the district court's judgment on that basis. Why isn't vacatur a permissible remedy here? I mean, I understand you -- you'd like us to say today metering can be done, give you the okay to do it, but another way to address this, I would think, given that the district court declared a policy unlawful even though the policy was no longer in place, and the government today is saying it has no concrete plans to reinstate it, and the district court issued this order without making any findings about whether or not a live case or controversy existed, I think one could argue that the district court at least abused its discretion by nevertheless entering this broad declaration, so it would solve your problem, I think, if the Court on those grounds just vacated it.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: The Ninth Circuit reached the issue of mootness and issued a ruling on that issue. I think it's the first footnote in its opinion. This case isn't moot because we'd like to reinstate metering and we're being prevented from doing so.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: But you don't have a concrete plan, I just want to make clear?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Concrete plans are necessary for standing --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
