case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: -- not for mootness.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: All right. Let me just ask you one question about your response to Justice Kagan. You were talking about the various reasons why Congress had "arriving in" in this statute and that one of them, you said, was the fact that there was previously a distinction between deportation and exclusion and that Congress was trying to ensure that that was also covered or that the principles related to deportation and exclusion were covered by this new regime. My understanding is that exclusion applied to people who were "at alien border," at a port, but your reconceptualization of what "arriving in" is doing does not allow for at a land border or at a port. And so can you help me to understand how Congress could both be attempting to ensure that those principles were included, but we still agree with your reading of the statute?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: The phrase "at a land border" in this context refers to people on the U.S. side of the border rather than the Mexican side of the border, and we know that in two ways. The first is the Court's entry fiction cases like Kaplan against Tod and Leng May Ma repeatedly refer to aliens on the U.S. side of the border who have just arrived as the --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: In the entry fiction context, but we don't have a case or a scenario in which Congress makes clear that it's responding to the entry fiction when it uses the words "arriving at," right?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: And the second answer is that in Cardoza-Fonseca, when the statute said "at a land border," the Court interpreted -- understood that to refer to aliens in the United States.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Thank you.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Ms. Corkran.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: In the 1980 Refugee Act, Congress established a statutory process for noncitizens fleeing persecution to seek protection in the United States. Congress designed the scheme to track the United States' treaty obligation not to refoule refugees to territories where their life or freedom would be threatened. Because refoulement includes, to quote Sale, "defensive acts of resistance or exclusion at the border," the Act requires immigration officers to process claims not only for noncitizens already present in the country but also for those arriving at ports and elsewhere along the border. For decades, port officers followed the statutory procedures designated by Congress for inspecting and processing arriving asylum seekers. It was not until 2016 that the government asserted for the first time that it can wholly avoid these mandatory duties simply by blocking asylum seekers just as they are about to step over the port threshold. Petitioners' theory of the statutory text isolates the word "in" at the expense of making the rest of the statute nonsensical. By Petitioners' account, the phrase "arrives in the United States" has no meaning not already covered by "present in the United States," "arrives" means "already arrived," and amendments that Congress intended to encourage noncitizens to lawfully seek admission, in fact, did the opposite, permitting border officers to effectively eliminate access to asylum at ports. Petitioners' position is also at odds with the original public meaning of the provisions reflected in the government's longstanding inspection practices -- practices at the time of IIRIRA's enactment and in the government's own regulations, which have recognized for nearly 30 years that the Act's inspection and processing duties apply to noncitizens "coming or attempting to come" into the United States at a port of entry. As this Court observed in Thuraissigiam, Congress carefully crafted our asylum system to ensure that the United States lives up to its ideals and its treaty obligations towards noncitizens fleeing persecution. The turn-back policy flouted both. And the nine -- Ninth Circuit was correct to deem it a withholding of the government's statutory mandates. I welcome the Court's questions.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: How would you distinguish this case from Sale?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah. This case is distinguishable from Sale in a number of ways. One, Sale involved the withholding provision alone. It didn't involve the statutory mandates that are at issue here in 1225, the inspection and processing mandates. So, here, we have a 706(1) claim about whether the government has withheld compliance with those mandates. Sale is also different from an extraterritoriality and a treaty perspective because it involved interdiction on the high seas, which, as Sale explained, is outside of the jurisdiction of the United States. So it raises a host of questions that aren't raised here. I'd be happy to address some of the points my friend made. I'll --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Could you address 1157?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. So 1157 is the refugee program. My friend takes the position that our -- that we have collapsed the distinction between the two. Our position reflects the way that 1157 and 1158 operated from 1980 to 2016. So, for 36 years, no one was concerned about the distinction being collapsed, and that's because they served two entirely different functions. Section 1157's refugee program is entirely elective. The president chooses whether to admit refugees. It's not something that refugees in other countries can apply for. It's decided between the countries. There are a host of benefits you get if you were admitted through that program. But 1157 is not the provision that implements the Article 33 obligations. That happens through the asylum processing that's under 1225 and 1158. And that asylum processing is also how you determine whether someone is entitled to withholding.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Mr. Suri gave some responses to Justice Kagan in saying that there's a subset of people who are arriving in the U.S. who are -- as opposed to longstanding people. The problem with that is those people who are arriving, he says, are present in the U.S. So I'm not sure how his answer gets you around --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- the surplus problem.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes, I agree. My friend made a -- a number of new arguments about surplusage that weren't in the briefing, and I think that is one of them. But I would note exactly what you said. Making it a subsection doesn't mean that it's not redundant. It's still entirely redundant --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, that's true, Ms. Corkran, that it's a subset and so there's still redundancy, but I suppose, if Congress in IIRIRA had just created this big deal about expedited removal and said that expedited removal was what arriving people got, you know, it -- it might be that they just wanted to emphasize that just because you were in the -- that you were subject to the expedited removal procedures did not mean that you still couldn't apply for asylum. So the -- the -- the -- the -- the -- the fear, if you might say, is that if they just had that one "physically present" provision and struck out what had previously been in the statute, the "arrive at the port" provision, somebody might have thought, like, all these people that are now being subject to expedited removal do not have the right to apply for asylum, and this provision is supposed to make clear that they do.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: There is no reason for the inspection mandate to need to make that clear because 1225(b), the asylum processing section -- it's in (b)(1) to (A) -- has a whole process in place for how you assess asylum claims by arriving aliens. So that credible fear interview provision says, if an immigration officer determines that an alien who is arriving in the United States has expressed a fear of future persecution, then the immigration officer shall refer them for a credible fear interview. And then there are a host of provisions that explain how that credible fear assessment plays into expedited removal. So there would be no way that someone could read the entirety of 1225 and be concerned about how it applied to arriving asylum seekers.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Can I ask you a question? I feel like there's some slippage between "arriving" and "arrives." And as the Chief Justice pointed out, the language is "arrives in." I mean, "arriving" sounds more in the process of. "Arrives in" sounds more like you've reached your destination. How do you know under your theory when the person is close enough that we could say they've -- they have "arrives in" or "arrived" in the destination? I mean, what if there's a queue and they're far back, or what if they arrive not at a port of entry? How close do you have to be to the border? Could you say that someone arrives in the United States if they're at a portion of the border that does not have a port of entry? Like, what is it -- if it's not crossing the physical border, what is the magic thing or the dispositive thing that we're looking for where we say, ah, now that person we can say arrives in the United States?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: So I'm going to try and keep that in order in my head, and I'm going to start with --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: -- the first point, which is, actually, it's the -- "arrives in" is the tense that triggers the inspection under 1225(8), but "is arriving in" is the language that triggers the credible fear interview. So that's the provision under 1225(b) that mandates asylum processing within the context of expedited -- expedited removal. And as the government acknowledges and I think Your Honor just said, "is arriving in" does suggest a process. And, in fact, that's exactly -- that determination is what's happening under the turn-back practices. So they have immigration officers standing at the border asking arriving noncitizens, what's the basis for your admission? They get right up to the borderline. And if they say, I'm here seeking asylum, then the border officer turns them away, when, in fact, 1225(b) says that if the immigration officer determines that the person is seeking asylum, he shall refer that person to a credible fear interview. So that argument stands separate from the inspection mandate. And what used to happen is that you have inspection and that's how you'd find out someone had a fear, and then that would trigger the credible fear interview. But both of those provisions are at play here. I'm sorry.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: And can you answer the question about what is the dispositive thing that has to happen to say that someone arrives in?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. So a person arrives in the United States at a port of entry when they are at the threshold of the port's entrance about to step over. So they are arriving there. I think that's consistent with ordinary meaning. "I arrive at my house" or "I arrive in my yard" when I'm going through the gate. Now that process of arriving is interrupted by the border officer physically blocking them from completing the arrival such that the person never arrived, but the process of arriving is beginning at that moment.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: And is that just for the person? I mean, if there's a -- if there's a line, you know, and you're far back and you hear, oh, no, no, no, we can't cross the border today, have they arrived in and been turned away, or is it only the person initially told, and how could it be something different if you arrive at a port of entry versus if you cross the border or you arrive on the other side of the border, the Mexican side of the border, but, say, cross into Texas or try to cross into Texas, where there's not a port of entry?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah. So, to start with the hypothetical where you have a line --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: -- I'm going -- I think that the -- I mean, our position is not that "arrives in the United States" is doing no work at all. The question is what "arrives in the United States at a port of entry" means. And I think that means you have to be at the threshold. If I'm in a line waiting to get into my house for some reason into my yard and I'm half a block back, I haven't actually started the process of arriving in because I'm in a line waiting to get there. So I think, you know, if -- if the word was being passed down a line that's going over the bridge and people are turning away without actually getting to the threshold, they wouldn't fall under the -- under the statutory inspection mandate or processing mandate. The second question I think has to do with how arrival looks between ports. As a practical matter, the borderline isn't generally delineated in a way between ports that would allow for this kind of discernment about have you reached the threshold of the port.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: But doesn't the statute say whether or not at a port of entry?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes, yes. So I was going to get to that part next. So we -- we take out "at the port of entry" when we're talking between ports and the question is, what does it mean to arrive in the United States? I think you would have to be at a place where you could, in fact, cross. So, if you got up to, let's -- let's assume it's a place on the border where there is an actual line, identifiable line. I would say the same analysis applies, right? Have you made it to the threshold and you're about to step over?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: So anybody at the water's edge of the Rio Grande on the Mexican side has arrived in?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: No, the border is halfway through the water.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. All right. So half -- they've got -- they've got one step short of halfway through. They've -- they've arrived, but somebody who's on the water's edge has not arrived?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: I think that's right. So you're looking at being at the threshold of when you're going to cross the border.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And so somebody who's at the fence has arrived in, but somebody a step away from the fence has not arrived in?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Well, so the fence, if we're talking about the border wall --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: -- that is -- the border wall is entirely on the interior, so, in fact, anyone who gets to the border wall --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: They're already in?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: -- is also physically present in the United States.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: So -- so anybody who's arrived at the fence is in?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: They're -- yes. But that's just a matter of geography that they're -- they're already present.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: To take the hypothetical, though, what if there was a border wall --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Fence along the line, yeah.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Exactly, on the -- on the borderline.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: There, the analogy that I think of is a stadium. So I'm arriving at a stadium when I'm at the entrance going through the turnstile. I probably wouldn't describe myself as arriving in the stadium if I'm still in the perimeter making my way to a place where I can enter. So I don't think someone who's at a --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: So, at the top -- top of the wall, they're in, but if they're at the bottom of the wall, they're -- they're out?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Oh, so now they're -- they've climbed?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah. No, I'm just trying to understand what it means.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah. So I suppose --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: We're going to get these case -- you know --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- we're going to get case -- as soon as we decide what it means, we're going to get cases.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Well, so, as a practical matter, that's not going to be a concern because the wall is, in fact, within the perimeter.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I -- I understand. Okay.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: A hypothetical wall that was on the line and a person had kind of gotten to the top and was --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: -- about to fall over, I guess, would potentially be arriving. It would depend on the situation.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah, be in. How come somebody who's in the line isn't in? I mean, if the whole point is to make sure that people who are attempting to get into the country have -- have the opportunity to file asylum claims and they've made it all the way, why -- why does it matter he's second in line?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: I think that's just a function of arriving in or is arriving.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: So the whole debate boils down to the one person who's at the port, the one person who's at the front of the line?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah, and I think that's because I think it's important to remember --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: So the rest of the case you agree with the government on?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: No.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And everybody else in the line -- everybody else who's being metered doesn't have an asylum claim, just the person who's --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: They have an asylum claim. They have to get up to the border to present it. Now I think maybe the question is if the government was stopping people from getting physically to the line because, if you're waiting in line and you just decide to abandon waiting and you don't actually make it to the threshold --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: No, no, no, no. These -- these people want to make these claims. They're there.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah. Right. So, if they --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And they're being metered and they're told no, not today. And you're saying the person who's made it up to the -- to the inspection officer gets to make that claim and everybody else who's been waiting there maybe for hours or days doesn't.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Well, they just then, once they get up there, can -- can make the claim. That's when they tell --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: But they have to get up there, yeah. Okay.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah, but I -- there's no reason to think they wouldn't be able to do that. And I think it's important to remember that from 1917 to 2016, 99 years, there weren't -- there was not a single example of a turn-back. So what was happening is people would come through the port. At that point when they were in the port, they would be inspected and processing would happen. So it's an unusual scenario we have here where we have the officer standing there and turning people back.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, I --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And now we have these expedited removal processes at the border.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So many of them are not getting in at all. But they're coming to the line and they're at least being questioned and permitted to make the claim?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Under the expedited -- if they -- if they were being applied the way that they're supposed --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I think your point that you're making is the statute is very clear that anyone in the U.S., now the other side says a foot. I don't know why the foot is magical. I could put my hand through or my nose through. I don't know. Why does a foot count as opposed to a piece of your body count? So, if you're up on the top of this wall, that's not on the U.S. side? But my point is, in asking or clarifying this question, is "arriving at the border" means you're knocking on the door, correct?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. That is what it has meant for -- for 99 years before this --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Mr. Suri suggested that's not what it meant, that that's not what the federal regulation said, that that's not what practice was. Was he simply wrong about that? I --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- in reading the papers, I understood that up until 2016, anyone who knocked on the door had the opportunity to make the claim, and they weren't guaranteed success, but they could make the claim.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: That's right. So the government purports to cite a few earlier cases which it says support its position. That's Leng May Ma, Kwong Hai Chew, Mezei, the Ellis island case. All of the cases that the government is citing it cites are playing fast and loose with entry. So each one of those noncitizens was present in the United States, arrives in the United States, at which point they were subject to exclusion proceedings. That's the statutory process that you got if you arrived and then you weren't actually admitted or physically present in the country. That is all that -- we're just looking for the statutory process to be applied to our class members or we were when this policy was in effect.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Ms. Corkran --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: I just want to make sure I understand exactly. There's a line of 50 people trying to get in. The first one knocks on the door, so maybe he or she is processed. I don't know how many people are there processing. But, if there's one person there, maybe Person 3 to 50, they don't have a claim, right?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. So -- so --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: No, no, wait. Yes or no? They -- do they have a claim or not?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: They are going to have a -- it's -- it's going to depend on whether it's a reasonable delay.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, what do you think a reasonable delay is?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Well, so that's under 706(1). I think Justice Sotomayor made the point earlier that the Ninth Circuit made a determination that this was complete withholding because there was no ability to wait. case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: So, if you -- so it's not knocking on the door. It's getting your name on a list?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah. So it's a -- yeah, it's a turnstile if you're at a land port and it's a -- there's a plaque halfway across the bridge, so not a physical door, but yes. So, when you go through the line, if it's working the way it should, you should make your way up to the borderline, at which point you come across and you're processed.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, but -- but -- maybe I just don't understand it. I mean, it depends kind of on how long the line is, right?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. There were no -- there were non-examples prior to the turn-back policy and even during the turn-back policy of there being kind of lines of people waiting to be processed who were outside of the United States because, under the prior practice, you came through the turnstile and then you were inspected and processed. Now there could have been long waits within the port. That certainly happened. And that would have been subject to kind of a reasonable delay analysis. But this idea of kind of lines and people piling up on the Mexican side of the border didn't happen until the turn-back policy was put in place and you've got this bottleneck of people waiting on that side.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, I -- I understand that, but I -- I'm still struggling with the Chief's question. And we do have situations where there are lines. And I had thought you had said to me and -- and Justice Sotomayor and others that the first person at the turnstile with -- with the inspection officer has arrived, but people further back in the line haven't. And now I -- I -- I thought I heard a different answer to the Chief Justice, and I'm just wondering, I really do -- whatever you think it is, I want to know what it is.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: I think I was skipping ahead when I answered the Chief's question to kind of the nature of the 706(1) claim and the difference between withholding --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I'm just curious --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- what "arrives in" means.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: "Arrives in" means they reached their threshold. I didn't mean to create confusion about that when I was answering the --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. So it's the person at --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- the turnstile, it's the person halfway through the Rio Grande, not somebody two people back, not one person back, not one person who can't reach across the halfway point of the Rio Grande? None of them?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: You have to reach the threshold in order to be subject to the 1225 mandates --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: -- for inspection purposes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: So how does that fit, Ms. Corkran, with 1225(b)(1)(A)(i), which says, if an immigration officer determines that an alien who's arriving in the United States is inadmissible, the officer shall order the alien removed from the United States? Now, to me, that suggests not -- you remove somebody from the United States when they are all -- when they already have crossed the threshold.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. That --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Not when they are knocking at the door. So that suggests to me that "arriving in" suggests that they've already crossed.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: So it's a process of arrival. So the person is arriving in when they are about to step over the threshold. And, again, I may go to the plain meaning, and I think about kind of being in a house or a yard. If my husband called and said, are you arriving at the house as I'm walking through the door and I said no, that would be a strange answer to give him. The ordinary meaning is, yes, I am crossing through --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, but if you're -- it's arriving in, the officer shall order the alien removed from the United States, that seems to suggest that your view of plain meaning, whether it is plain or not, is not the statutory meaning because, if you're removing somebody from the United States, that person has clearly made it over to the United States. You don't remove somebody from the United States when they're just knocking at the door.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Well, so I think that provision makes sense if you remember that removal is a legal term. It refers to removal proceedings. So what that provision is assuming is the completion of arriving because, in 1996, when Congress was drafting the language, it had no reason to think that 20 years later, the government was going to change its position and start blocking people while they were in the process of arrival. So you see in the regulations and I think also in Sale kind of the understanding that the process of arrival starts when the person is at the threshold and it continues as they step over the -- the threshold and are being inspected.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: And --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: So I don't think there's an inconsistency there.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- so, to -- so, to clarify, when the person is arriving at the threshold, the process of inspection, you say, kicks in based on their arrival, and that process could take place on U.S. soil, presumably without metering. The inspectors are on the U.S. side, and so they're asking and they're investigating, and the person is in the U.S. at that point. But the obligation to do that kind of inspection, I think you're saying, kicks in based on the person's arrival.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes, that's exactly right, and it makes sense when you remember that that is how it had worked from 1917 to 1996, when Congress was -- was amending the provisions in IIRIRA.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Can you speak of --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: It will be interesting -- it'll be interesting to read the actual transcript of the oral argument because I -- I believe that both you and Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson on several occasions have used the phrase "arriving at." I think you said you arrived at your house. But that's not the term that is in the statute. Do you think there is no difference between arriving at a location and arriving in the location?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. Thank you for the opportunity to clarify. So we have "in the United States" "at a port of entry." I can explain the amendment history on how we ended up with the prepositional phrases in that order, but I think my first-order answer is "in" is just how you describe being in a region. You wouldn't say "at the United States." You would say "in the United States." I'm arriving in Baltimore when I'm on the train as it's coming in. I am at Penn Station when I'm in New York. So that's the deference -- difference in prepositional phrases, which, even if it doesn't completely answer the question, does give you some pause to say, well, maybe "in" isn't doing the work that the government is suggesting here because it has to do with kind of the natural way that we talk. But the way we ended up with that order of the prepositional phrases is that the pre- --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, I'm not quite sure I understand that. So there's been talk about knocking at the door. Do you think someone who comes to the front door of a house and knocks at the door has arrived "in" the house? The person may have arrived "at" the house.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: No, but that's past tense. Are they arriving in the house?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Has -- does a person arrive in the house when the person is not in the house and is knocking at the door asking to be admitted to the house?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes, I think, here, the door is open. The officer is standing on the other side of the threshold. The person gets there and is ready to -- to take the step over, right? The officers and the asylum seekers here were toe to toe. This was happening right at the line, and they're about to step over. They are arriving, present tense. Once they're inside, they've arrived, past tense, but we know that Congress used the present tense here.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, it does make -- I gather you think it makes a difference whether there -- there's a door or a turnstile, you have to be there. If you're at the end of a long line, you're not there. You haven't arrived at the turnstile.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Okay. So then does it matter how many people are processing the arrivals? I mean, how quickly the line's going to move? I mean, it strikes me as a very significant factual question. In other words, it's not -- if you're at the end of the line, you're -- you're not covered by the requirement to process, is that right?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. So, once you get to the -- you have to arrive, and that's just the nature of the -- the language that Congress used. However, if -- if the government was complying with the inspection and processing mandate, people would be going right through the turnstile. There is no stopping or processing that happens at the turnstile under the prior practice. A person goes through, and at that point, they are in --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: So you don't even have to knock?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: No, there was no knocking. You went through. There was no immigration officer who was stopping you. You're going straight through the open door. You are now in the inspection area. You're in the port. And at that point, there would be perhaps a delay of processing for the reason you say. That delay would be subject to 706(1), unreasonable delay. Here, we had a complete withholding. But I think -- I think maybe where we're getting stuck is kind of the idea that processing is happening at the border. That only happens under the turn-back policy. That's the only situation in which you're going to have immigration officers interacting with asylum seekers on the other side of the border.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: So, historically, if you were at the end of the line, you still went through?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: There -- there was no line. People just -- it was a constant --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Right, there was no line.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. That --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: This only became an issue, is what you're saying, and so the "arrives in" wouldn't have had the significance in 1996, is what -- based on the historical practice. And now we're trying to figure out what it means when there's a new practice not envisioned by Congress?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes, that's right. And if I could go back to something you said earlier, which is the logic or the logical problem the government has with treating this -- kind of the change in language as if it suddenly substantially narrowed access to asylum at the ports. Not only is that illogical, but it defies the express purpose that the text was seeking to achieve, to quote Justice Scalia. We know that the reason that Congress amended 1225(a)(1) was to expand the category of applicants to include people who were already present in the United States and people who -- who entered between ports because it needed to put them on equal footing. So to read that language as then re-disadvantaging people who attempt to enter lawfully makes no sense at all.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Can I ask you, this -- this is a new practice. Justice Kavanaugh just said a new practice not envisioned by Congress. The Chief Justice says we have a significant factual question here about how this actually works. Why wouldn't we wait until we had an actual policy with real facts in the record regarding what's going on? I mean, even if this is not technically non-justiciable, even if there is jurisdiction in the literal sense, we do have some control over whether or not we reach and discuss issues. And it just seems to me that we have a lot of hypotheticals regarding how this policy may have worked in the past, how it's possibly going to work in the future, but we don't have a policy in effect right now --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- that we can actually rule upon. So how should we take that into account as we think about this?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honor. So, as we explained in pages 15, I think, to 21 of our brief in opposition, this case has no virtually ongoing significance, certainly not for the plaintiffs. Now the government has sought this Court's review because it wants to preserve its degrees of freedom in the future. Right now, the border is closed under other authorities, but maybe that's not true in the future and conditions change. That is not a reason for this Court to -- to grant plenary review, and the government suggests that --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: I mean, if the government were to just bring its own action, I think Mr. Suri has conceded that they wouldn't have standing because they don't have an actual plan in place that they're trying to implement.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: What they're doing is saying: We have this, you know, essentially extant district court order out there, and at some point in the future, we might want to have a policy like this, so, Supreme Court, tell us now whether or not that's going to be unlawful.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes. That's -- that's what they're seeking. That doesn't -- you know, in order -- as the Court said in Camreta v. Greene, both parties have to have a live interest in the case in order for the court to proceed. And that explanation doesn't go to how plaintiffs continue to have an interest in the declaratory judgment against a policy that was rescinded five years ago. And so I think it's odd to -- to raise the voluntary sensation -- cessation exception here, where it's the defendants who want to continue to do the policy.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Absolutely. Usually, voluntary cessation is the defendant --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Right.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- wanting to avoid --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Right.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- the court's orders.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: And the --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: They -- they -- they remove the policy so that the court doesn't order.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Right.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Here, we have them pointing to the voluntary cessation as a reason for the Court to weigh in on this policy.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Right. And it's the government that's saying, you know -- you know, the government has control over the extent to which it's most likely --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Correct.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Counsel, do you think the Ninth Circuit was wrong to say that it was not moot then?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: So the --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: You didn't challenge that in your brief.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: No. So what the -- the Ninth Circuit said that the declaratory judgment was moot, and the dissenting judge agreed. The reason that the Ninth Circuit reached its holding was because of the transit rule injunction, that smaller class, which, at that point, that injunction was still in place and it imposed a number of obligations on --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Right.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: -- other parties. So the -- the Ninth Circuit was not wrong about that. But, on remand, the parties agreed to essentially dissolve the injunction because the burdens that it was placing on the parties no longer had any benefit to the class members. The class members had been identified.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: So you're taking the position it's formally moot?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: I do think it's moot for the reasons that --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Why didn't you make that point in your brief?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: We -- we wrote six pages of all the reasons that we thought --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: In the BIO?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yes, in the Brief In Opposition. It wasn't until the reply in support of cert that the government suggested Munsingwear vacatur. I'll say we don't object to that. We didn't address it in our Brief In Opposition because that would be an odd thing for a respondent to suggest. And once the Court granted review, we focused on the merits. But, to Justice Jackson's point about Munsingwear vacatur, we don't have an objection, and I think that resolves all of the government's concerns in this case.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas? Justice Alito, anything further?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: On that last point, the Court said declaratory judgment, it was vacating that. And then, when -- and it's also vacated the preliminary injunction?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: No. So the declaratory judgment was -- is still in place but I think is moot for the reasons that the -- that the Ninth Circuit said. The Ninth Circuit went on to reach kind of the -- the statutory interpretation question, not with respect to the declaratory judgment but with respect to the transit rule injunction, which would only be in place if the, you know, underlying statutory question was resolved in the plaintiffs' favor. But then that injunction was dissolved, so we really have nothing that's before the Court at this point.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Thank you.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kagan?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Is your position that when a person gets to the border, she has a right to apply for asylum only or that she also has a right to enter?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: So enter in the -- so right to cross, I'll say cross to avoid --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: A right to cross.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: -- the entry. So I think the right to cross is -- is tied up in the inspection and processing mandates that are on the government. So we have a 706(1) claim here. It's based on ministerial duties that attach to the government under these circumstances.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: And if the United States figured out a way to do its various things that it has to do without having the person cross, would that be sufficient? You know, like, you could have a Zoom interview or something like that.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: Yeah, I suppose that 1225 assumes that all this is happening on U.S. soil and I think for good reason because that's how it already worked. The government's extraterritoriality concerns might weigh against doing some sort of process, but I don't know that I have a stake in -- in pushing back on that way of -- of approaching things.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Okay.

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Gorsuch, anything further?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Just briefly. You mentioned the -- the court of appeals revised opinion. It said it didn't think the case was moot because of the equitable relief still present, which I -- I -- I took to mean both the declaratory judgment and -- and the injunction. Am I mistaken?

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Kelsi B. Corkran
text: So, yes, they were both left in place. The reason that the Ninth Circuit reached the underlying statutory interpretation question was because --

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Kristi Noem, Secretary Of Homeland Security, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Al Otro Lado, A California Corporation, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Vivek Suri
text: Just a few quick points, Mr. Chief Justice. First, this Court should decide this case. The case is not moot because there is still effectual relief that the Court could award, namely, lifting the class-wide declaration and the individual injunction to which the government is still subject. There's also a strong practical reason for the Court to decide this case. Administrations of both parties since 2016 have consistently said that this is an important tool in the government's toolbox for dealing with border surges when they occur. I can't predict when the next border surge occurs, but I can say that when it does occur, this is a tool that DHS would want in its toolbox. It's not something the Court should leave to future uncertainty. We've been faulted here for not having a specific policy in place, but that's not really fair to us. There's a class-wide declaratory judgment saying that this practice is unlawful. And I think the government should not be faulted for conforming its current conduct to what a court has declared to be the law. Once that declaratory judgment is lifted, we'll take appropriate steps at that time. Second, the text of the statute should control the Court's decision, and that text is "arrives in the United States." We've heard attempts to substitute other language that might be more ambiguous or more susceptible to Respondents' interpretation than the language Congress actually used. For example, we heard many references to "arriving in the United States." But the specific language at issue here is "arrives," not "arriving." Further, as Justice Kagan correctly pointed out, there's a separate provision of Section 1225 that says that "arriving" aliens can be removed from the United States in certain circumstances, and that suggests that even the "arriving" category is limited to aliens who have already crossed the border. Even if you think that there is some ambiguity in the term "arriving," though, the correct approach is to use the clarity of "arrives" to resolve the ambiguity in "arriving." You shouldn't use the ambiguity, potentially, in "arriving" as an excuse to ignore the clear word, "arrives." Similarly, we've heard attempts to replace "arrives in the United States" with "arrives at a land border" or "arrives at the threshold" or "knocks on the door." None of those terms are the terms Congress actually used in the statute. Moreover, even when a previous version of the statute said "arrives at a land border," this Court still interpreted that to refer to aliens in the United States. We've relatedly heard a suggestion that the alien arrives "at" the port of entry because the port goes right up to the border. We don't think that's accurate. The entrance to the port might be something like a quarter mile from the border. So, even if you think the question is whether the person arrives "at" the port, the person hasn't arrived at the port. More importantly, the real question is whether the person arrives in the United States. Finally, Respondents' position raises serious line-drawing problems. It's not clear from their position whether you have to be at the front of the line, the back of the line, or the middle of the line. It's not clear whether they're distinguishing between someone who is stopped by a border officer versus someone who is stopped by the Rio Grande versus someone who is stopped by the border wall versus someone who's stopped by Mexican authorities working in concert with the United States, which is something that could happen in response to Justice Kavanaugh's question. I don't think we ourselves go into Mexico, but we could cooperate with the Mexican authorities to stop people from reaching the border of the United States. Our position avoids all of those line-drawing problems because Congress drew a clear line here. It said that if you're outside the United States, you -- you can apply for refugee admission under Section 1157. If you're in the United States, whether you've been here for a long time or you've just arrived, you can apply for asylum. The Court should respect the line that Congress drew.
