text: Well, I think it's  --I think it's actually okay under my friend's view, Your Honor.  We're not -- we're not making that ask.  I mean, as far as my friend's view are concerned, so long as somebody's designated a ballot receiver, they can be fine.  Party boss, party bag man, relative, any of those, so long  as the state says you are a ballot receiver, that's fine.  The only thing that apparently is not fine is a U.S. Postal Service common carrier.  And I think that is, I think, very -- a very odd way to read those statutes --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, the Postal Service is not part of the state, and a common carrier isn't part of any government.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: It's  --that's right, Your Honor.  But, I mean, certainly, we all  know the status of the U.S. Postal Service is a highly regulated government entity with certain obligations.  Common carriers in a very similar way, high  --highly regulated with similar obligations. And they give -- in both cases, they're imbued with a duty to deliver what they receive.  And, in fact, a duty that's, I  --I think, a good example -- maybe a good example is the fact that the IRS accepts tax returns, which are obviously highly consequential documents with key timeliness requirements, the  IRS accepts tax returns both through the mail and through common carriers.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, you will -- you will accept ballots that are received within five days after Election Day, that what -- what  is, you know, the whatever -- the -- the date that's -- that's set as Election Day, right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's right, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: And you have a variety of line-drawing problems.  So we've been exploring one, to whom and by what means is this thing to be -- the ballot to be delivered to the state.  But how -- what -- what about the length of time that a state could choose? case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: There are a couple that at the outlier it's kind of canvassing and it  can go that far.  I think more common is about --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

text: Well, is that okay? Is that all right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: So there's no limit? Except I suppose the day when the presidential electors have to be appointed or the day when the  --the next Congress begins, starts its session, that's the only limit on counting -- on counting mail -in ballots?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think, for congressional races, potentially, yes, Your Honor.  I think there -- there are other Title  III kind of things that push action earlier in the presidential context, but, again, I mean, there's nothing  -- the key question is these are one  -- three one-sentence provisions,  and we want to be, I think, very careful not to read them for more than they're worth.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON

I'm  -- I'm talking about UOCAVA, for example, and some  other federal statutes that indicate that Congress not only knew this was going on, but then it interpreted and incorporated the state's own post -ballot -- post-Election Day ballot deadlines into federal law.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Sure, Your Honor.  So I  -- I -- I think that's exactly right.  So UOCAVA is  --is maybe the best example where Congress was told that about a dozen or so states have post -Election Day ballot receipt laws.  It respected those explicitly as to a deadline for  -- for ballots in  -- in --in that law.  I think the United States has agreed with us on -- on that very point.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: And Congress wasn't worried, I think, about the states picking dates that were, you know, we might think are too long or whatnot.  That  --that was not in the statute.  Congress just said whatever the state has decided with regard to ballot receipt  deadlines is going to apply here, correct?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Right.  And that's been the case for 180 years, Your Honor.  And I think one feature that I  --you know, obviously, we're -- we're -- we're searching for what did the statutes mean at the time, but I think it's very hard for my -- my friends to explain a hundred  -- the past hundred years of history and this lawmaking.  The Soldier Voting Act in the 1940s was  --was another example where Congress recognized and respected state deadlines.  And it just  -- it gets very hard to explain those things if you don't adopt the view that the federal Election Day statutes just do not set a ballot receipt deadline.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay.  And  --and on this question, I just want to make sure I understand what you're saying.  When you said,  yes, my friends on the other side say it's okay for private parties to deliver just like you do, are you saying that's just a manner of receipt, and whether your -- whether the ballot is received before or after the election, on all sides, everybody agrees that absentee  ballots can be turned in by having, you know, the neighbor, the party operative, or whatever scoop them up and bring them to the -- the ballot box?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Your Honor, I mean, maybe -- you know, I'm not sure if I answered the earlier thing as crisply as I could.  I'm not comfortable with the neighbor piece.  I do have serious concerns about that.  I  -- I --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: But is that tied to the ballot receipt problem, or is that just tied to, hey, maybe this is an unlawful way of executing absentee balloting regardless of when the ballots make it to the official?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think it's the finality of the choice that has to be done by Election Day.  And  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: -- my --my concern is that if you're not sending it by mail or common carrier  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You're getting caught up, counsel, again.  Could you go back  to the question?  Justice Barrett is not arguing with you.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Fair, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: What she's saying and what you said earlier is -- and you believe that under your adversary's  -- the opposing counsel's theory, you can give it to the RNC operative, you can give it to anybody, and so  long as it's received on Election Day by the state, that's okay.  That's what you're saying your opposing counsel's saying.  And you're saying the only question before us is, if they  can designate an appropriate vehicle to transmit the votes, then that's okay.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think I was saying the lat  --the latter part, yes, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I actually think, under my friend's view, it's okay for -- like, a state can deem the ballot -- deem received when the party operative himself or herself receives it because all that person has to do is be a ballot receiver designated by the state.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Right.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: And we're trying to hew more closely not just to the text but also the historical hundred-year-long you can submit it by mail.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Okay.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So  --but the bottom line is that states can choose when the final vote has to be counted?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: States have discretion over counting.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Exactly.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel.  Justice Thomas, anything further?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: Just as a point of clarification, without looking at the  subsequent history, what do you think the federal law required as far as the Election Day?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That the voters make a final choice by that day.  The  -- the way I'd boil it down, Justice Thomas, is choice is  critical and unchanging; method of making that choice is malleable.  And that does also explain all the subsequent history.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: And you don't have to formalize that choice?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: You do by submit -- by parting with your ballot and submitting it to the state.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Have we had any  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice  -- Justice  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I'm sorry.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: -- Alito?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Your position does require some difficult line-drawing problems, and maybe that's inevitable, but one is the degree of confidence that one must have in the  entity or person who transmits the ballot to the state.  We've talked about that.  One is  how long after the Election Day vote -- votes must be  -- votes can be received.  A third is whether it has to be postmarked.  Are there  -- aren't there quite a -- aren't there eight states that do not require a postmark for late ballots?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: There are a number of states that don't require that, Your Honor.  I think postmarking is  --is good evidence that something has been timely submitted.  That's  kind of borne out in the tax context.  I -- I think, you know, if -- if somebody were challenging a law like that, it would potentially be a very different kind of a challenge.  They'd have to make sort of factual showings to challenge that ballots were not cast by Election Day but surely not this case.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, maybe these -- maybe it's inevitable that some sort of line-drawing decisions like these have to be made, unless the rule is anything goes, you know, states can do anything they want in this area.  We don't have a whole lot to go on here.  We have the phrase "Election Day" and we  have history.  If we looked just at the phrase "Election Day," what would we take from that?  I think you're  --you've been saying we're -- and we're moving in this direction.  We don't have Election Day anymore.  We have election month or we have election months.  I mean, the  --the early voting can start a month before the election.  The ballots can be  received a month after the election.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Well, I  -- I think the best way to read it, Your Honor, is that by setting Election Day, the Congress set the final choice day.  And that's the key thing, final choice day.  What Congress was concerned  about at the time was some states making final choices, say, a month before other states were making final choices and the distortions, the fraud, the risks that -- that that had. And when everybody's making a final choice on the same day, even if some individual choices are made before then, you're honoring the statutes, and I think -- you know, I think, Justice Alito, you made this observation, you know, not a lot to go on because the statutes  are just not very -- there's not a lot of prolixity there.  I think that's a point in favor of deference to the states.  You know, if Congress  has not spoken to something, especially in this context, where states are expressly empowered to regulate these things, that's a big point in favor of letting states continue to do so as they  --they have for a century.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Do you think it's legitimate for us to take into account Congress's desire  -- Congress's passage of the Election Day statutes for the purpose of  combatting fraud or the appearance of fraud and will and some of the briefs have argued that confidence in election outcomes can be seriously undermined if the apparent outcome of the election at  --on the day after the polls close is radically flipped by the acceptance later of a big stash of  --of ballots that flip the election or  -- yeah.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: You've got ballots that are delivered by somebody -- by -- you  know, by a neighbor and they're received a month after the election and they don't have postmarks.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I -- I think the best way to do it is to honor the statute's purpose by  --but doing so by respecting the statute's text and animating context.  And what these statutes were getting at was not just any kind of fraud writ large in all elections, which, you know, no statute could do, but a situation where, okay, you know, State 1 votes  -- you know, has their election on one day, ends it, and State 2  neighboring has its election three weeks later because the concern would be let's say State 1 goes for one party and then State 3 goes for the other party with a huge turnout for that other party. You could have potential fraud. People went across state lines and voted, or you could have the appearance of that sort of fraud even if it didn't actually happen, like  people just said, oh, my gosh, they voted for that person, I -- you know, big turnout. So I think that's the kind of thing that animated those statutes, whereas fraud writ large was not  --was not a good example. I do think it's  --it's notable that my  --my friends with the United States, you know  --you know, obviously, they  -- they -- they've sounded the antifraud theme.  They  haven't cited a single example of fraud from post-Election Day ballot receipt in this century.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: All right.  Okay. Thank you.  I'll let my colleagues have a chance.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Sotomayor?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Has there been any history of voter recall in the mails in -- in Mississippi?  You say the law doesn't permit it, but has there been any history of it?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: None that I've ever heard of, Your Honor.  I mean, this isn't something that was raised until the appellate reply briefs.  And nobody cited a single example in history of it.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right.  And I understand Justice Alito's questions about the  policy questions of what will create discomfort or not.  But the Constitution vests the issue  of elections in the states unless superseded by Congress, correct?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's right, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So, if there is a policy question to be had, the entities to decide that are the states and Congress, not the courts, correct?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's right, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And absent a law in federal law that suggests that absentee  ballots must be received by a certain time, there's no explicit requirement of that, correct?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Right, Your Honor, or even implicit.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And -- and the implicit, we have the military acts that since World War II at least and the Civil War -- I should go back that far  -- have permitted absentee ballots to be received long past Election Day, correct?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: We have a very long history of that, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Exactly.  So the people who should decide this issue are not the courts but Congress, correct?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Right, Your Honor. And I -- I think what --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: The states and Congress.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's right, Your Honor.  And as I -- as I was mentioning in my colloquy with, I believe, Justice Alito  earlier, that's kind of the structure of our system.  States go first.  If Congress doesn't  like it, it overrides.  And, as I think Justice Scalia said for the Court in Arizona Inter Tribal, we respect what Congress said as far as it went but no farther.  And that's kind of the history  of voting and election law in the country to begin with.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: One last question. With respect to history, history is informative  of what's been permitted by Congress because what we're looking for is what understanding  Congress had with respect to elections, correct?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's right, Your Honor, yeah.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right.  And it doesn't talk about the receipt of absentee ballots after elections at all, so we look to the history of whether Congress has accepted it, correct?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think that does help here, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right.  But the attempt by some of the amici here to Bruenize this inquiry and say that history  tells us how elections must be held and on what date and when receipt can happen or not happen,  why is that not an acceptable way to look at this?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Well, I  -- I think the difference between Bruen and here, Your Honor, is that Bruen  --in Bruen, the Court -- the -- the question at issue, you know, whether a restriction on firearms is consistent with our historical tradition of firearm regulation,  there's a rich history addressing precisely that issue, sometimes through analogy, but very  much, I mean, Bruen itself, I believe, I want  to say 40 pages of history just analyzing those things.  We don't have anything like that, a rich history suggesting that Congress was even thinking about locking in Election Day ballot receipt or anything like it.  It was addressing different things.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right.  Thank you, counsel.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Thank you, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kagan?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: I guess, Mr. Stewart, your answers to Justice Sotomayor's questions leave me unsure about what you think about these appeals to history. I mean, you've said that there's not a lot of text here.  I agree with that.  I think that the way this case has been argued all around suggests that that's so.  So  -- so then we're left with history.  Or are we left with history?  You seem to appeal to history sometimes  --Justice Barrett said this -- but then repudiate the appeals to history at other times.  And I guess I want to know what we're supposed to be doing when we're looking at this  statute and deciding this question with respect to all this historical evidence, scant or not scant as it may be.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Sure, Your Honor.  So I  -- I -- I think the best way I can break it down is this, is that history's informative here, and the way it's most informative is that since Congress set  -- I mean, throughout our history and, certainly, since Congress set the federal Election Day, election administration  in our country has been very, very dynamic.  As I tried to highlight in my opener, it was one thing, in-person, on-the-spot qualification checks by fellow voters, ballots were naturally received on Election Day, all those features.  As soon as Congress had a  reason to alter the methods by which a choice was made, it did so.  But the one constant is that the voters, in a popular government, it's most critically the voters, the constant is that the  voters make a final choice of officers by Election Day.  So I think history shows that election administration is dynamic.  States have wide  leeway.  They just have to make sure that the voters make a choice by Election Day.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Thank you, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Gorsuch?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Almost done, Mr. Stewart.  You -- you emphasized to Justice Kagan and many others that the  --the final choice at least has to be done on Election Day and so recall would be a problem for you if  --if it could happen.  But you say that  --that that doesn't happen in Mississippi, that that's -- that's your position, right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Right.  It's not permitted.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: If recall could happen, that would be a problem for your position?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think there  -- potentially.  I think there's a  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Because then it wouldn't be a final decision on Election Day, right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's right, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think there would still be a factual question, though, of whether  -- I still have not been cited anything to say that recall is actually a thing that can happen in the rule.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: No, I understand. But, if it could happen, that would be a  problem for your theory because the final choice wouldn't have happened on Election Day, right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Fair, yeah.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay.  So you -- you say Mississippi prohibits it.  We -- we've -- we've been through whether that's the case or not.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Very good.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: But let  -- let's say it did.  Let's say there was a law prohibiting recall.  How would it ever be enforced?  Because how is a state to know and how is even a common carrier carrying an envelope to know whether that is a ballot that needs to be recalled?  And who are you going to prosecute?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Well, I think  -- I think it could be enforced similar to -- to other vote  --voter things.  I mean, in our state, there are notarization and affidavit requirements, signing things.  I think one -- if  -- if -- if it were critical to -- for the voter to say that there will be no recall, the voter could say, I hereby commit that I will  not attempt to or recall this package in any way, shape, or form.  They could just add that, sign it.  I take the point about proof problems, but, I mean, gosh, Justice Gorsuch, I mean, violating state election laws in a state that  really is antifraud and really takes wide measures to enforce its laws, that would be quite a thing for a voter to do.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, in my hypothetical, which, you know, you say is unlikely to swing an election and all of that on recall, but as soon -- you know, if --if history teaches anything, scant or not scant,  it's that as soon as something's allowed, it will happen eventually, right?  And, you know, so -- so somebody --my hypothetical happens and everybody recalls their ballots.  I'm just not sure what recourse  the state would have against people who violated its anti-recall law.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I mean, if people are, say, recalling things through a common carrier,  there's going to be some record that they recalled those things.  A state could  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: How's a state ever going to find out about it?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I mean, I think the same  --the same way it would find --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: It's going to go -- you're going to go prosecute individuals?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I mean, Your Honor, I'd say, like, if somebody is lying in an affidavit that they're not going to recall something, I mean, if  --if people are doing that with impunity, we have quite a problem, but it is a problem that the state can address and enforce  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I just don't know how they'd ever find out about it.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I mean, I think you -- obviously, you know, some crimes are harder to  find out and prosecute than others, Your Honor, but I think it's still -- I mean, people can do things, try to, like, tamper with ballots, all that sort of thing.  I think it's just still a  matter of respecting the statute.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Thank you, Justice Gorsuch.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kavanaugh?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: When did Mississippi switch to this method?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: 2020.  In 2024, it added common carriers.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And why?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: It was first because of the pandemic.  I have -- I don't know that  there's necessarily an answer about why as to the 2024 one in a clear -- in a clear way.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And the other side makes a point when we're looking at history, to the extent historical practice is relevant,  that it only became widespread to allow it to be mailed by Election Day in more recent years and that the predominant approach was to require receipt by Election Day throughout the historical practice you cite, until very recently.  How are we supposed to think about that?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I mean, I think it's the same way to think about, I -- I think, the broader history of election law, is, when  -- when states have kind of seen a problem, they've adapted and adjusted in  --often in -- in the direction of allow -- making sure more votes can be counted.  I mean, that was obviously a big thing when absentee voting started to become a prominent thing.  You know,  certainly, we cared for much about our history of people showing up in person, but we realized that was very difficult for people away from home and that we wanted to, you know, kind of widen the tent and make it -- make it so that people could vote.  And I think perhaps another realization, even though we've had UOCAVA for  40 years, Justice Kavanaugh, is that for military voters in particular, this is a perennial challenge about making sure that they  can actually get their ballots in on time.  I mean, that's perhaps why UOCAVA voters in particular are a very popular group for post-Election Day ballot receipt.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Would you say that the states that require receipt by Election Day are disenfranchising voters?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: No, you're not  -- they're not, Your Honor.  I mean, a reasonable ballot deadline does not do that.  I would  asterisk just there are the practical barriers for those overseas military voters.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think  -- I certainly respect the perception.  I think one thing notable in this case and I think helpful is that there -- there -- there has not been much  --much of a showing about actual fraud from post-Election Day ballot receipt itself. I mean, that was --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well, I think Justice Alito referred to and I think this quote refers to the appearance of fraud.  And is that a real concern?  Is that something we  should be thinking about, confidence in the election process?  Just  --just curious how we factor that in here.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Right, and I think it would go back to the same answer I had for  Justice Alito about scant -- you know, there -- simple text, straightforward text, and respecting the limits of that text, and looking  at the animated history, I think it really was  -- it was the double-voting fraud concern. I don't know that people have that particular concern.  I think, you know, obviously, people can be, you know, unhappy when a -- a result flips.  I think Congress may be able to take measures to address that.  But I think there's  no good evidence that Congress was doing that beyond preventing double-voting in this context.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But, if you have to have a deadline, which you acknowledged, and if having a deadline of November 3rd rather  than November 10th doesn't -- for receipt, doesn't disenfranchise anyone, why wouldn't it make more sense to  -- to take account in some respect of that concern as we think about how  the text and history fit together?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Well, I think, I mean, something that Congress was clearly, I think,  trying to do was adopting a simple rule in this text.  And I think a very simple rule is everybody must cast their ballot by Election Day.  I mean, that's quite administrable.  I  mean, if you have an Election Day ballot receipt deadline, there are certainly things to commend that.  I think you're alluding to some  of those, Justice Kavanaugh.  But there's also a question of, when do I vote?  You know, I'm not sure.  You know, do I need to do it 7, you know, whatever it is? Whereas, you know, if somebody wants to get all the information possible, they like voting on  Election Day, you have a pretty nice, clear, simple rule, and that seems to dovetail quite well with the  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well, the simple rule, but, if it arrives on November 11th, you're out.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Right, but I think that's kind of baked into the risks you always get when you're doing -- there are always some  risks, you know, regrettably with mail-in voting.  You can eliminate some of those risks by voting in person, but --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: The risks would seem the same no matter whether it's November 3rd or November 10th, in other words, that it could take longer than a week for the mail to get there.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well, I take your point, but it really goes to just thinking about what Election Day or day of election means.  But I -- I take your point.  Thank you.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Yeah, I  -- I -- I'm having a  -- I guess I'm having a hard time conceiving kind of a dual-track rule in -- in  -- in that circumstance.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

text: And I'm not sure, Your Honor.  I mean, I think  -- I --I guess I just keep coming back to you can't recall or change your vote or  -- or make any effort like that --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

speaker: BARRETT

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents

speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Jackson?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: So let me just clarify.  This case is not about a Mississippi  practice or policy related to recalling ballots, is that right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's right, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: So I  --I guess I'm a little confused about those kinds of policy questions, and I guess -- I think that the Constitution's allocation of responsibility  here actually makes this case about who decides.  I mean, there are a lot of policy questions.  Justice Alito ran through several of them, who gets to receive the ballot, how long after can they be submitted, does it have to be postmarked.  I suppose we can add is recall allowed, et cetera, et cetera.  But the question, I think, is whether Congress has precluded the states from making those calls, drawing those lines, and your position as I understand it is no.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's correct, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: That the  -- that the scantness of Election Day in the federal  statutes actually is a point in your favor because it indicates that Congress was leaving  it to the states to draw the various lines that might arise in this circumstance.  Is that right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's right, Your Honor.  And that's reinforced, for example, by  -- by the 1866 statute, which shows that when Congress wanted to be really prescriptive in this area, it was very prescriptive.  It  described this is what the states have to do and so forth.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: So, if we were focused, really focused on what we're asked to answer here, which is, is the -- are the states preempted by federal law from having post-Election Day ballot deadlines, you would say no?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Let me ask you about the history with respect to Bruen.  I -- I -- I guess I'm not sure I understood your answer to Justice Sotomayor because it seems to me that Bruen is not even the right methodology by which to be thinking about this.  Bruen applied to the Second Amendment because the Second Amendment incorporated a preexisting right.  And the point of the history and tradition test was to try to evaluate the contours of that right.  We -- we don't have that dynamic here. We're trying, I thought, to figure out what  Congress meant when it included Election Day in its federal statutes.  So it seems odd to me  that the suggestion that the limitation on our understanding of Congress's intent is somehow tied to the state's practices.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think that's right, Your Honor.  I think the other thing -- I think the point I'd emphasize is that the idea of embodying a preexisting right confirms that there's something very much unchanging.  And  the thing that we know about election administration, it has very much been changing throughout the course of our country.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: It's been changing throughout the course in a way that undermines the notion that there was one consistent  practice, first of all, or that Congress's law, the meaning of Election Day in the federal statutes, somehow was tied to what the states' practices were about that.  I mean, I think this was your original point, that there were lots of different practices.  And so, to the extent we're saying,  oh, you could only look at Election Day in the federal statute to mean exactly what the states were doing back at that time, this imperils a  lot of different things, not just post-Election Day ballot deadlines, right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: That's right, Your Honor.  And, I mean, the only way to explain all of these changes is to read them in line with plain text and the limits of history, which is to say election is a final choice.  I mean, otherwise, you have to do what my  -- my friends have to do, which is, hey, look, we're going to pick out the one practice from these eight -- 19th century codes that we like, ballot receipts, say that's what an  election is, and just ignore in-person voting, qualification check on the spot by fellow voters, and that's just not sound history.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Can I ask you one final thing about the amicus brief from the Society For the Rule of Law Institute, because I found it very interesting, and I didn't really know what your view of it was.  That amicus brief focused on the Electoral College and Congress's setting it up,  you know, back in 1787 with the understanding that the casting of votes can happen on a particular day and the receipt of those votes by election officials can happen on a different day.  And, in fact, the way the Electoral College is set up, I think, at the time, Congress permitted in nine -- in 1792 about a month to elapse between the casting of votes,  which, by the way, it called Election Day, and the receipt of the votes by the -- the electors submitted them to the president of the Senate up to a month after.  So I -- I think that to the extent we're worried or thinking about historical evidence, that seems to me to be pretty  significant and compelling historical evidence  of Congress's understanding of what was required by Election Day versus the receipt of those ballots at some subsequent point, correct?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Yeah.  I think that's  -- that's well stated, Your Honor.  The  -- the other thing I'd tie it to in the same amicus brief, and I think the -- the brief, the amicus brief does a nice job of tying it to this, is  that the key thing is -- is choice, choosing. The Constitution refers to choosing, choice, you know, those  -- those --those kind of verbs.  And that's why that sort of thing is allowed, that the key thing is --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: And the choice is made when you cast your vote under the electoral process system, when the electors cast their vote, right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Right.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: And that is distinguished  --I'm just trying to make clear that the casting of the vote and the receiving of the votes historically have been conceived  of as two different things that can actually happen at different times, right?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: I think so, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Scott G. Stewart
text: Thank you, Your Honor.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel.  Mr. Clement.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  All agree that elections for federal office have to end on the day of the election  specified by Congress, and all agree that you can't have an election unless you receive ballots, and there must be some deadline for ballot receipt.  Nonetheless, Mississippi  insists that ballots can trickle in days or even weeks after Election Day.  That position is wrong as a matter of text, precedent, history, and common sense.  Mississippi all but concedes that the original public meaning of election included both offering to vote and the receipt of that vote or ballot by election officials.  And, of course, the key distinction between voting and an election is an election involves the combined action of voters and  election officials, as this Court underscored in its decision against Foster against Love.  And, of course, Mississippi insists that at the time these statutes were passed, ballot receipt and the -- the casting of the ballot were so inextricably intertwined no one would have thought of one without the other.  That seems to me to be a damning admission, but it also ignores the advent of field and proxy voting in the Civil War and the  enormous efforts that states went to to ensure that all of the ballots, whether by proxy or by field vote, were received by Election Day.  In the state's view, all of those herculean efforts were for naught or were entirely gratuitous.  Now the state's position actually works even worse as a matter of common sense.  If somebody in Gulfport the day after the election asks is the election over, the common sense answer is no, it's not.  The ballots are  still coming in.  And if somebody asks who won,  the truthful answer is we don't know why yet. The ballots are still coming in, and they may trickle in for weeks or months.  And, in fact,  they may trickle in for weeks or months with or without a postmark in differing ways in differing states.  That reality gives the lie to the idea that we have a uniform national Election Day.  I welcome the Court's questions.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: How would you define the day of election?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: I would say that the day of the election is the day when -- it's the last day in which all the ballots are cast and they are received into official custody.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: So how would you treat early voting as compared to late reception of votes?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: So I would say, I mean, you know, I think the best place to look for a treatment of early voting is the Kreisling -- the Keisling decision by Judge Kleinfeld in the Ninth Circuit because, after Foster against Love, there was a suggestion in Foster against  Love that maybe early voting is a problem.  He rejected that claim based on two things.  One is the distinct history of early voting, and the second is the idea that was  explicit in this Court's decision in Foster against Love that Election Day is the date of consummation.  So I would say, under our theory, early voting is permissible largely because it has a different history and because of this  idea that the Election Day is the date where the election is consummated.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: Would you spend a few more minutes on or at least a little bit more time on the voting during Civil War?  There was some suggestion that that's an example of late reception of votes.  And I think, in your intro, and this was my thinking, that it was not, that proxy voting was a way to make sure that the vote occurred on Election Day as opposed to afterwards.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: Well, not surprisingly, Justice Thomas, you are exactly right.  So proxy voting is the thing that happened in the  Civil War that is most analogous to absentee  voting.  And the thing that is most striking is  -- I think five states had proxy voting -- every one of those five states required the votes, the ballots, to be received by election s back home by Election Day.  Now that's an incredibly inconvenient thing that was done in the Civil War to ensure the ballots were received by Election Day.  And  under the state's view, they didn't need to do that.  Now it's really no different in the context of field voting because there were, like, maybe a dozen states -- if you're not going to count the Confederate states, there  were about a dozen states that did field voting.  Again, every one of those ensured that  the ballots were received into official custody by Election Day.  And, of course, most of the states went to enormous efforts to replicate the machinery of the ballot box and everything else in the field and  -- but --and some variation in that.  But the one thing that didn't vary at  all was that the ballots had to be received into official custody by Election Day.  And just one last thought on this Civil War practice.  My friend's only real  answer to the idea that, at 1845, there was an understanding that everybody would have had that, of course, the election involves both the  offer to vote and receiving the vote, the ballot, into official custody, his only answer to that is, well, like, nobody -- the issue hadn't ripened, that nobody had even thought that you could divide the two.  But the issue ripened in the Civil War, and the issue ripened in such a way that every state required the ballot to be received into official custody by Election Day.  And  then that certainly informs what Congress is thinking in 1872 when they extend the presidential Election Day deadline to the congressional realm.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Mr. Clement, what do I do with the two states during the Civil War, Rhode Island and Nevada?  You say five favor you.  At least two don't.  Nevada simply designated three of the highest officers in command, didn't swear them  in, just said three officers in the command can create a ballot box or suitable receptacle for votes and collect the votes of the soldiers with little further formality.  Those military  officers then would mail those ballots in and they would be counted, whether they arrived on Election Day or after.  What do we do with Rhode Island, that simply directed soldiers to deliver a written or printed ballot with the name of the person voted for to the officer commanding the regiment to which he belonged?  That officer wasn't sworn in as a state official either, and receipt could happen thereafter.  So it's not  --yes, many states believed, as they did at the time, that voting had to be in person, that voting had to be not  -- it had to be by voice instead of by paper.  Lots of states had lots of beliefs  about what a proper election should look on. But how do we deal with the outliers?  Or you  just want to ignore them?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: No, I don't want to ignore the outliers.  I actually think Rhode Island and Nevada help me and my side of this  case, and I think that's because they did designate somebody  -- they might not have given them an oath, but they designated somebody as an official to receive the boats -- the votes. And they had to come in --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So there  --here, what's the difference between the post office and a common carrier?  It's the official.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: No.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You want an individual person, is that it?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: Well, I  -- I want somebody who's cloaked with government authority, so that's one difference.  But there's a critical second difference.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But it's not state authority, meaning you're now expanding what  you're saying as government authority.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: So what I would say is it was government authority, and I would say that my understanding of the history is that all those federal officers voluntarily accepted the responsibility, whether they took an oath or not.  And I think that's quite --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So could a neighbor and so could anybody else.  I'm not moved.  The point is that it permitted someone  else to deliver the item, a final cast vote, to deliver it and be received after.  Under your theory of this case -- and I think you and the government disagree on this  --you believe that absentee voting by the military and overseas voters, the various laws,  that federal laws under which states have proceeded with respect to those votes are illegal?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: No, I don't  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Or  --or  --or they're not saying what everybody has understood them to say, that states can accept absentee ballots after the election?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: So I  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Military and overseas ballots?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: I don't think any vote is unlawful.  Let me  --let me try to address how I think you would reconcile UOCAVA with the Election Day statutes.  And, to start, I think it's important to recognize that UOCAVA is not limited to the federal general election.  So UOCAVA applies to primary elections, to run-off elections and special elections, and federal general elections.  The  Election Day statutes only apply to the general federal election.  So the way I would reconcile the two is to say that all the references in UOCAVA to state deadlines are perfectly fine, not  preempted at all, not displaced at all, not even anomalous, with respect to the primaries, the run-offs, and the special elections.  Then the Court has a job to do in the federal general election as to say, like, kind of which is the specific, which is the general.  I think the more logical way to do it would be to say that  --with the understanding in this Court, if you decide in our favor, that for the federal general election, the ballots have to be in by Election Day, I would say --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Well, maybe we should have another president now because wasn't it in Florida that they were counting military votes after receipt?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: So, with all due respect, that is the reddest of red herrings  because what happened in the 2000 election in Florida is that pursuant to a consent decree  that was entered by a federal court because Florida was violating the principal provision of UOCAVA, which says you have to give the ballot -- absentee ballots to the overseas  voters 45 days in advance, because Florida was violating that, there had to be a consent  decree to create a remedy that was not provided under --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: There, what happened was that the judge made up the deadline, not the state.  But I wanted to  -- how do you deal with the Soldier Voting Act in 1942 that permitted ballots -- for the extension of absentee ballots?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: So the 1942 Act, at least as I understand it, again, is not addressed solely to general elections.  And then, with respect to general elections, it says that the  --the military special SVA or whatever it was, the special military ballot, had to come in on the -- by the time the polls closed on Election Day.  So I actually think the 1942 Act is fully supportive of our position here.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So the DOJ has been acting illegally when it has sued states  for not following the Act, the UOCAVA?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: No.  Again, remember that the UOCAVA's principal protection is the provision  --this is in 302 of the Act, not 303 and 304, but the 302 Act provision that says that you have to get the ballots to overseas voters 45 days in advance of the election.  And, interestingly, in the single most important provision in UOCAVA, it ties the deadline to the date of the election.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So what do we do with Congress saying process in the manner provided by law for absentee ballots in the states involved, that's UOCAVA, and that at the time the hearings were being held on it, 21 -- 12 states were identified as counting absentee ballots after Election Day?  So it just ignored it and decided it was going to exempt out a little part of it but not everything.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: With respect, Justice Sotomayor, that's why you have to remember that  UOCAVA is not focused only on the federal general election, which is the only thing where Congress has specified a federal deadline.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: But, Mr.  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: So it makes perfect sense --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: But does that help you or hurt you, the fact that it is broader? I mean, it's broader in the way that you describe.  It applies to all of these different elections.  But it doesn't make the distinction that you are making.  It says, with respect to all of them, state absentee ballot deadlines should apply.  You're -- you're  --you're encouraging us to treat the general election differently because you interpret Election Day with respect to the general election statute to have a defined time as of Election Day, but that is not what this statute appears to be doing.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: So I think it helps us, and I think it helps us because, to the extent you're concerned with those references to state election deadlines, they're inevitable.  If  Congress is going to address anything other than the general federal election, it has to refer to the state deadlines for receiving ballots because there are no federal deadlines  for any election other than the federal general election.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Yeah, but, if that's true  --if that's true, Mr. Clement, you would think that Congress would say, you know, with respect to the deadlines that there's no  separate federal requirement X rule and with respect to the deadlines that there is a federal requirement Y rule.  But it doesn't do anything like that. It treats them all of a piece.  And we know  that for many of these elections, states were setting their own deadlines and Congress -- and  -- and Congress, in passing these statutes, didn't suggest any kind of distinction between those elections and these elections.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: So, Justice Kagan, as with almost every statutory question that comes to this Court, Congress could have made it easier.  They could have done all that.  And they didn't.  And I think you just have to --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Well, but you're  --so what do we take from that?  I mean, it seems  what they took from that is that they thought that this state function of setting ballot receipt deadlines was something that was a state function.  And that's what they took from it, and so they wrote the statutes this way, where, with respect to all elections, the states were setting their own receipt deadlines.

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: So I don't think -- I don't see that in the text.  That doesn't seem  even logical to me.  I wouldn't think the one place we were going to especially defer to the states with respect to the federal general election deadline is with overseas and military  voters, where the interests of the federal government are probably paramount.  But I just want to be clear about this.  If you read the statutes different and want to recognize  -- reconcile them the way that the SG does, we have no objection to that. We just think the better way to read these two statutes is to -- to reconcile them then the way that we do.  And that would have one benefit, which is don't forget that in at least  20 states, they take the Election Day ballot receipt deadline seriously.  So, if you simply say in this case that that Election Day ballot receipt deadline is true of all 50 states, then every oversea  voters, every military voter is going to be treated the same, and they'll still have 45 days to get their ballot in.  And one other thing just about Mississippi in particular.  Mississippi has  provisions in its election code that specifically accommodate overseas military voters and overseas voters.  And it's not the  ballot extension deadline that we have challenged here.  There's a specific provision  that says for UOCAVA voters and UOCAVA voters only, they can e -mail their ballots in. So, like, the idea that anybody is going to be disenfranchised here when the  oversea voters and only the overseas voters have the option of e-mailing in the absentee ballot that they get from Mississippi seems to me to completely miss -- be misplaced, and the concern should really be the heartland cases,  and, remember as Justice Alito alluded to, you have eight states that don't even require a postmark.  And there is nothing in Mississippi's theory that turns on the existence or the non-existence of a postmark.  And that's probably a good thing because the Postal  Service has made clear that they don't even postmark all of the mail.  And postmarks have their own problems. I mean, the main mailbox, post box in -- post office, rather, in Chicago stays open 24/7.  So, when all the other polls close in Illinois or every other state at 8 p.m., the post box -- the  -- the -- the post office is still open until midnight.  Now I'm not here to say that there could ever be voting fraud in Chicago  -- (Laughter.)

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: -- but -- but the possibility that there's a four-hour window where people could go get their ballots -- absentee ballots postmarked after all of the returns are in and they know that, oh, this -- this is the election where these things could turn the result, that does not seem entirely --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: So is your argument that we  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Counsel, can I ask a  -- can I ask you a question about the offer to vote and the vote?  So, historically, it seems like the offer to vote was then you had  to adjudicate the voter's qualifications, and then, if the qualifications were met, then the  -- the official received the vote and then it was put into the ballot box.  And as I understand it, Mississippi still has sort of a similar system because they  have to adjudicate voter qualifications as well as accept the vote.  So you sometimes say, I know you and the United States, when the ballot box closes and you sometimes say receipt.  Are those two different things and do the voters' qualifications have to be adjudicated by Election Day as well?

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: I don't  -- I don't think they're exactly the same thing.  I mean, in  some sense, I think the ballot box closing is a nice kind of common-sense capture for the idea that the election ends on Election Day.  Now I think, with respect to the voter -- the -- you know, the candidate -- the qualifications challenge, rather, most of that  is solved in the current system by registration requirements which they didn't have historically.  So we think the critical thing is there are two things that have always been absolutely indispensable in elections, and  that's the casting but also the receipt into custody.  And one thing I want to make clear about this is Mississippi still takes receipt  into official custody very seriously, and it is indispensable.  They just have a different deadline.  They have a five-day deadline. And we've had a lot of discussion about the possibility of recall, and I think that is a problem for Mississippi, but they have an even bigger problem in my mind, which is the November 11 problem, which is to say, as Justice Kavanaugh pointed out, if the ballot arrives six business days late, Mississippi doesn't count it, it's a nullity, and under the state statute, they destroy it.  So  --

case_name: Michael Watson, Mississippi Secretary Of State, Petitioner, V. Republican National Committee, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
