case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  During an overnight recess, the defendant and his counsel have a lot that they need to talk about. They need to go over the testimony that took place that day. They need to prepare for the testimony that's going to be given the next day. These are basic discussions that any competent lawyer would have with a client. This is the assistance of counsel that the Sixth Amendment guarantees. But the defendant and counsel can't have these conversations if they're not allowed to discuss the defendant's testimony. For example, if the defendant's testimony has gone poorly, counsel may need to advise the defendant to accept a plea agreement, but counsel can't do that without discussing the defendant's testimony. The defendant needs  advice about how to testify without violating the trial court's evidentiary rulings, but  counsel can't give this necessary advice without discussing the defendant's testimony. Counsel has an obligation to prevent the defendant from committing perjury, but that would be impossible without discussing the  defendant's testimony. Our brief has many more examples, but the point is that the defendant and counsel often must discuss the defendant's testimony during an overnight recess. Now the court below tried to distinguish between discussions of trial strategy, which it allowed, and discussions of testimony, which it prohibited. But that's no line at all. It's often impossible to discuss trial strategy without discussing testimony, and responsible defense lawyers, worried about being held in contempt for crossing this invisible line, will be chilled from offering the assistance that the defendant needs and that the Sixth Amendment guarantees. The only conceivable rationale for restricting overnight discussion between defendant and counsel is to prevent impermissible coaching. But, as the Court  explained in Geders, there are other ways to prevent coaching. There's no need to prohibit the defendant and counsel from discussing the  defendant's testimony. I invite the Court's questions.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: In the judge's instructions, he says:  I don't want you discussing what you couldn't discuss with him if he was on the stand in front of the jury. What's wrong with that?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Because, if he was on the stand in front of the jury, he wouldn't be -- they wouldn't be allowed to discuss  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: No, he's saying  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: -- in-court testimony.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: -- I don't want you discussing anything that you couldn't discuss involving his testimony before it, the jury. That's the standard for the  -- what's permitted and not permitted at  --that evening.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Okay. Well, the -- the  -- the trial court, if you read -- if you read the entirety of the trial -- the colloquy between the trial court and defense counsel, it's  --it's clear enough that the -- the trial court prohibited all discussion of testimon y, the defendant's testimony, during the overnight recess, and that is how the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals interpreted it. So the  -- the Court of Criminal Appeals  -- the Court of Criminal Appeals interpreted the -- the -- let me get the word  --exact wording exactly right from the  -- from the court's opinion. The court  -- the Court of Criminal Appeals said -- they described the question presented as:  Does a trial judge's sua sponte order that defense counsel could confer with defendant on everything except his ongoing testimony violate the defendant's Sixth Amendment right to counsel?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: So would it violate the defendant's Sixth Amendment  right to counsel if the -- during trial he was precluded from being coached or managed by the  -- his attorney?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: You mean during an overnight recess to talk?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: No. During trial.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Oh, during trial. No. During trial --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: What's the difference?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Under  --under Perry -- well, Perry drew a sharp line between overnight recesses and brief daytime recesses. The -- the  -- and the Court said that during a brief daytime recess, like  --like I think you're talking about here  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: No, what I'm talking about is why is the standard different between what a lawyer can coach or manage with respect to testimony while he's on the stand, which is basically a concern, and what he can coach or manage during the recess.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: No, no. It's  -- it's the same. The  -- the -- the  --the distinction -- let's be clear about the distinction between impermissible coaching and legitimate, necessary counseling, right, because that's a sharp line. And in answer to your question, that line is the same at all times during the proceeding; that is, whatever is impermissible  before trial begins is also impermissible during an overnight recess. It's impermissible  at any time. And let's talk about what that difference is, right?  So the -- the impermissible coaching is where a  -- the --the lawyer tries to get a witness, the defendant or any other witness, to testify  -- to -- where the lawyer tries to change the substance of the witness's testimony to try to get the witness to testify to something other than that which the witness believes to be true. The court  -- but contrast that with conventional counseling, which is talking about the  -- the testimony in all other contexts, so, for example, advising how to comply with evidentiary rulings. Even  -- even -- even rehearsing the questions and the answers ahead of time.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: But did any of that happen here?  Do we have evidence that any of that happened?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: But it couldn't have happened, it didn't happen, because the trial court barred the defense counsel from discussing Mr. Villarreal's testimony with him during the overnight recess.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Can I follow up on  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Counsel, if you  -- one of the things you say could protect against any problems with your approach --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yes.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: -- I'm looking at page 14 of your brief  --you say that the prosecutor could cross -examine the defendant after -- after the --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: -- when the trial picks up again the next day as to the extent of any coaching. Isn't that a real problem with respect to the attorney-client privilege?  What is the prosecutor going to say?  Okay, you had a break, you spent the evening with counsel, what did you talk about?  Objection, Your Honor, attorney-client -- you see how -- I don't see how that could a reasonable counterweight to the problems.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: I understand what you're saying. The -- the -- the -- the attorney-client privilege has never been understood to insulate a defendant or any witness from being cross-examined about the extent of impermissible coaching. So the -- the  -- the -- the dialogue would go:  Well, didn't your lawyer tell you to say that?  No, he didn't, or yes, he did --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, what did  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: -- or something like that.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, what -- what did he tell you to say?  You say, didn't your lawyer tell you to say that or whatever? And he says no. He said, well, what did he tell you to  say or what did he tell you to change?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: The -- the Court in Geders said  -- and we're -- we're merely following that -- that the way -- the way to deter impermissible coaching is for the prosecutor to cross-examine the defendant about it. Now you're right -- you're right that  --to say that functionally it seems like it might raise the same -- same sorts of privilege problems as having the court ask it, but that's what the Court said in Geders and  not just Geders, subsequent cases as well, that the appropriate -- two appropriate ways to deter impermissible coaching. One is  cross-examination by -- by opposing counsel, and the other is just for the trial court to manage the -- the -- the schedule appropriately, do some -- you know, give some foresight to how long the -- the defendant's testimony is going to last, and if the -- if the court is worried about impermissible coaching, just delay the overnight recess some.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: But, counsel, I guess I don't understand why you're so focused on impermissible coaching as you have defined it. You say here and you say in your briefs that impermissible coaching is where the lawyer is trying to get the witness to change his testimony or whatnot and that was impermissible both before and after and during --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: All that's fine.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: That is not what I understood to be the concern here. Going back  to Justice Thomas's point, the management of testimony, the talking with the witness about his answers and what some people would call coaching, prepping your witness, can occur  beforehand, right?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Right. That's right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: But it can't occur while the witness is on the stand. So  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: It --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- Justice Thomas, I think, is pointing to a critical point, which is, to the extent that the lawyer couldn't manage, coach, prep, practice with the lawyer -- with the witness while he's on the stand, why should he be allowed to do so during an overnight recess?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: This  -- this is straight out of Perry, straight out of Perry. So the Court -- the Court in Perry said that during a  -- a brief daytime recess, the -- the -- the court -- the  --the trial court can prevent all contact between the defendant and counsel.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: I understand.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: I'm focusing on the content of the crime.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yeah. No, I understand. I understand.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: But the -- but the -- I'm  -- I'm --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: So Perry doesn't help us with that because --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: No. Yes, it does because I'm get  -- I'm getting to that, right?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: So the -- the Court said that  --after explaining all of that for a brief daytime recess, the Court then, in the  -- in the next section, in Section -- Section 3 of  --of Perry, the Court says:  Well, overnight recesses are completely different. The Court says:  Admittedly, the line between the facts of Geders  -- that's an overnight recess -- and the facts of this case is a thin one. It is, however, a line of constitutional dimension. The Court goes on to say:  During an overnight recess, it is the defendant's right to  unrestricted -- unrestricted access to his lawyer for advice on a variety of trial -related matters that's controlling. And then here's the key sentence:  The fact that such discussions will inevitably  include some consideration of the defendant's ongoing testimony does not compromise that basic right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Right. So that's  -- that's precisely what I'm getting at.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: I think there might be  -- and I want you to help me with this --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- a difference between discussions that take into account the testimony, maybe even the fact of the testimony, and something that one could call managing  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- or prepping --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- or, you know, the kind of thing that you have even admitted a lawyer does  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- legitimately to help his client before he takes the stand.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And what I  understood the trial court here to be doing was just eliminating that very narrow category of conduct that a lawyer engages in to actually prepare his witness with respect to particular questions and answers on something.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: And that  -- and that's the line the Court of Criminal Appeals tried to draw, right, between discussion of  -- what you're calling prepping the testimony and discussion of testimony in other contexts.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And why are they wrong about that?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Because that line just  -- I mean, to even call it a line is wrong. It's not a line. It's a Rorschach blot, right?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: But that's the line that Perry drew. I mean, if you go up a few sentences from the sentence that you read, the Court says, you know, an overnight witness -- an overnight recess is different. Why is it different?  Because an overnight recess will go to matters that go beyond the content of the  defendant's own testimony, matters that the defendant does have a constitutional right to  discuss with his lawyer, suggesting that as to only the defendant's own testimony, the defendant does not have a constitutional right to discuss with his lawyer. Now then it talks about how, of course, when you talk about the protected matters, there might be some incidental discussion of the testimony itself. So it concedes that perfectly willingly. But it draws a pretty sharp line between matters going to trial strategy and matters going to trial testimony of the defendant itself and says that that's the reason why the recess -- the overnight recess versus 15 -minute recess makes a difference.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: And, like I said, that's no line at all. And the way you can  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: But that's Perry's line. I mean --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: But, no, I don't -- no, I  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: -- it might -- it might be that Perry was wrong, but that's Perry's line.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: No, I  --I -- I disagree. Perry -- Perry  --again, Perry -- Perry goes on to say that a defendant has an unrestricted right of access to his lawyer during an overnight recess, including for consideration of the defendant's testimony. So let me  --let me g et -- so you're -- you're drawing -- you're trying to draw the same line that the Court of Criminal Appeals drew.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Yeah, I'm not trying to draw it. I'm suggesting that Perry --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: -- says it right here  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Okay.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: -- on page 284. (Laughter.)

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: That's  --that that's the key language from Perry. Now Perry goes on to say, as I think your friend in Texas goes on to say, that there can be all kinds of places where the testim ony has to be talked about as incidental to what is protected, which is the discussion of trial strategy, but not in and of itself.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Okay. First of all, I  -- I dis- -- disagree respectfully with -- with your view of what  -- of what Perry held, but if Perry held that, I think it's -- I think it's just incorrect, right?  So let's -- let's work through some examples. So -- so the  -- before --before the overnight recess, in his  --in his testimony, the defendant has come very  -- an unsophisticated defendant has come very close to mentioning excluded evidence that would be  -- that would be absolutely devastating. During the  -- the -- the -- the overnight recess, defense counsel needs to say to the defendant:  Look, you nearly mentioned this  --this  --this evidence. Look, when we resume again tomorrow, you better remember not to mention that because we're -- we're going to be in big trouble if you  --if you -- if you -- if you mention that tomorrow. Okay. Is that  --is that  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: See, I --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: --consideration or is that discussion?  You have to factor into that  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Mr. -- Mr. Banner, I  -- I -- I think maybe I'm missing something, but I would think that would be permissible because it doesn't refer to the testimony itself. It can simply be a reminder:  Hey, don't -- don't go here, that might implicate --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: No, but it -- but it does  --it does refer  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: If I might finish. If I might finish.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Oh, sorry. I'm sorry.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I -- I -- I think what my colleagues are getting at and -- and what I kind of thought you even conceded in your brief is that coaching  -- and maybe we're defining coaching differently, perhaps that's it  -- but that there are some things that a district court can constitutionally prohibit counsel from doing and -- while a witness is on the stand, even if there's a recess. You -- you agree with that, right? You think there are some things that can be prevented?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Absolutely. Coaching, in the sense of suborning perjury, altering the substance of the witness's --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, I'm not talking about suborning perjury. I'm talking about coaching.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Well, but  --but -- but we  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: All right. If you don't like that word, let's use management, okay, which is the word Texas used.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: I like that word even less.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Why  -- why -- what  --what in the Constitution, what in history suggests that you have a right to manage a witness's testimony during a break --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Okay.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- as opposed to derivative or collateral matters that you do  need to advise him on?  There's a plea agreement, and the way things have gone today, maybe we ought to take that plea. There's some excluded evidence, be careful not to step into that. I -- I can see all of those kinds of comments, but I'm  -- I'm having a hard time understanding historically, traditionally, what have you got that says that there's a right of a witness to  --to be coached or, if you don't like that word, managed by his attorney while he's not on the stand?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Okay.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Whatever the length of time.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yeah. So let's  --let's talk about the -- the --the history. So the  -- the precise question presented in this case could not have arisen at the founding because defendants weren't allowed to testify until the late --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Obviously.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: --19th century. Right. And so the question is, what's the appropriate inference to be drawn from historical practice, right?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And  -- and -- and historical practice is that once you become a witness, you  --you are generally subject to the rule that you can't talk about your testimony, and that's generally understood to mean coaching and  managing but not advice about other legal matters. That  -- that's -- that's my understanding of the traditional rule.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Okay. I've got  --I've got three points I'd like to make about the history.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Please.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Okay. First of all, it's crystal-clear at the  --at the founding and all  -- all the way until now that while the defendant -- there are times when a defendant can certainly be denied access to counsel. When he does have access to counsel, he has a right to whatever assistance, including discussion of testimony, will be -- will be -- will be useful to him, right?  So the  -- there's -- there's  -- there's  -- while there's certainly historical warrant, as the government points out, both -- both governments point out, there's certainly historical warrant for saying that there are times when a defendant lacks access to counsel. So, you know, in a prison in the middle of the night or something like that, sure. But there's no historical warrant for saying that when a defendant does have access to counsel, the trial court can say:  Well, yo u can talk about Topic A, but you can't talk about Topic B.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Would your rule apply to witnesses who have counsel?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: No. No, no, no, because non-party witnesses, they don't have a Sixth Amendment right that a -- that a defendant has.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: This is a rule specific to the defendant.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, they have -- they have a right to counsel and they brought counsel. I  mean, would -- would --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: During a criminal -- a right to counsel during  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Would it apply as well in civil proceedings too --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: No. No, no, no, no.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- to the defendant there?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: No, no, no, no, no. The trial court can sequester non-party witnesses. This case isn't about that. This case is about -- about the defendant as a witness.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: In civil  -- in civil proceedings, where there's a right to counsel, presumably?  Yeah, it would apply there, I think, your rule.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: I  --I don't know. I mean, the -- the -- the --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: It's just that there's a long historical tradition of witnesses going on the stand being told something like what the trial court said here.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Non -- non-defendant witnesses.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So, Mr. Banner, can I just clarify?  You're entirely rejecting the line that Justice Kagan drew to your attention, and you're saying that even during the day, let's say it was an hour  -- you're saying this is all about time -- so, even if the recess was for an hour for lunch, you are saying that the district judge cannot restrict what the counsel and the client, the defendant, can discuss? That's not what you're saying?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: No, no, no, no. No, no, no. So, again, this is  -- this is Perry. Perry says that during a  --a -- a -- a daytime, brief daytime recess, the court can cut off all contact.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: But what if he doesn't cut off all contact?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Well, and then there's a footnote in  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So, if -- so you're saying that once the district court allows contact, no restrictions?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: No, no, no, because  -- there's a footnote in Perry, maybe is what you're leading up to, that -- that -- that basically the greater includes the lesser; that is, if -- if  --where the trial court can cut off access to counsel, the trial court could allow selective access to counsel. But that  -- that logic doesn't apply during an overnight recess, when the court has  held there's an unrestricted right of access to counsel.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: So it's all about time?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Mr. --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: It's all about time.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: If it were three hours, if it were four hours, and it was daytime  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Well, look, the  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- how do you -- how do you decide when it's too long?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: So -- so, in theory, there could be some hard cases between 15 minutes in Perry and overnight in -- in Geders. I have to say, in practice, the lower courts have had no trouble drawing this line. Daytime recesses are usually pretty short. Overnight recesses are much, much longer. It's very easy to tell  --to  --to  -- to draw that line. Now, in theory, you know, if a court were to say, look, we're going to have a recess from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and we're all going to  --we're going to be like  a vampire court and just do it at night, you know, maybe  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. So  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: --you get some hard drawn lines.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- your rule then is that anytime during the day when there is a recess, the district court could, subject to maybe some extreme case where it goes on for too long and you have a vampire court, the court could say you can talk to your lawyer about everything, except the lawyer cannot manage your testimony during the day?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Again, because  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: During the day?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: During the day, again, because the greater includes the lesser.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Quite right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: And you can't  -- but you can't do that at night?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Night, correct, because, at night, during over --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: It's unrestricted because Geders says that. So there's no --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Well  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: You can't have a line at night?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Well, Geders says that  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: You can have a line during the day but not at night, right?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Yeah, because Geders says that, but Geders -- Geders was correct in saying that, right?  Geders  --Geders pointed out correctly that overnight recesses are  -- have always been times of intense strategizing, discussion, and so on and -- and whereas Perry said, well, not so for -- for -- for brief daytime recesses. Let me, if I could  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Mr. Banner, can I ask you  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent

speaker: KAVANAUGH

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent

text: Overnight recess.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Well, a trial  -- a trial could barely go on if -- if a --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Okay. I'm going to  -- I'm going to quarrel twice with the  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Okay.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: -- the framing of your question. First, he  --he never -- doesn't have a right to coach him in the sense of impermissible coaching. He has a right to give  advice about the wording of his testimony, not the  -- not the right to coach him.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: So he can't do it in a 15- --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: That's Perry.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Well  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- that it's 15 minutes versus overnight?  If the Constitution says that a defendant has a right to be counseled with respect to his answers while he's testifying, I don't understand what difference it makes that we have a recess  or not or whatever.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Thank you.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Stuart Banner
text: Thank you.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Mr. Warthen.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  When a defendant's testimony is paused for a long break, the trial court may tell defense counsel not to either manage the ongoing testimony, as we propose, or not to  discuss the testimony altogether, as the United States proposes. Both rules are supported by this Court's precedents. In Geders versus United States, this Court barred absolute no conferral orders during long breaks, but it never opined on qualified orders. Indeed, Geders himself would have been fine with such an order. In Perry versus Leeke, this Court allowed both absolute and qualified orders during short breaks, emphasizing the importance of untainted cross-examination to uncovering the truth. Perry reconciled its holding with Geders by noting that there is a constitutional difference between discussing ongoing testimony, which is not protected, and discussing other trial -related matters, which is protected. And as long as protected matters can be discussed, the right to counsel is preserved. Moreover, by allowing qualified orders, Perry necessarily recognized that  counsel can indeed navigate such orders during short breaks, and there is no logical reason  why they could not do so during long breaks as well. Accordingly, qualified orders allow  trial courts to balance what the Constitution actually protects with the integrity of trial, and that's exactly what happened here. I welcome the Court's questions.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: After the night passed and -- and the  -- the --there was no -- you had testimony by Petitioner, was there some objection to the judge's order in -- in the sense that Petitioner said or his lawyer said that they were not allowed to discuss the matters other than testimony?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Not at all, Your Honor. When they came back the next day, the trial court asked them if there was anything to bring up. They never -- they said nothing from the defense, Your -- Your Honor. And they neve r filed a motion for a new trial. And, in fact, not only that, on top of that, my friends on the other side, they say the only way to enforce these orders is to say, well, what did you talk about last night. But  that didn't even happen. The trial court -- the trial court just started his testimony up the next day and everybody went on. It was assumed that they followed the court's order.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Mr. Warthen, I appreciate the subtlety of Texas's position as compared to the Solicitor General's more absolute rule, and I just have a couple of questions about that distinction.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Yes, Your Honor.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: First, is there any reason why the Court needs to reach the Solicitor General's more absolute rule in this case?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: The only reason you would have to do that, Your Honor, is if you read the order actually given in this case more broadly.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I think that's right. That would be the only reason why we'd have to reach the government's position.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: You agree with that?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Yes.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. And then, when  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: If you read it the way we read it, it would only be a managing order -- no managing order and not a -- not a  no-testimony order.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And when we come to that, you've got, I think, the relevant language at page 23 in your brief, where the court says that -- well, actually, where we said in Perry that an overnight recess that would encompass matters that go beyond the content of defendant's own testimony, matters that the defendant does have a constitutional right, those are protected. If we understand the trial court's order in this case to be consistent with that standard, is there any reason why we need to address the Solicitor General's proposal?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: No, I don't believe so.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: If you believe it was just a -- if this is a -- a small, like, I guess you can conceptualize like this, if the  --if this is broad, this is a  --a narrower kind of order.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And give me your best reason why that's the case here.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: That this is a narrow order?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Well, so, if you look at page 7A of the appendix, he says:  I don't want you discussing what you couldn't discuss with him if he was on the stand in front of the jury, his testimony. I'm not sure whatever else you would like to talk to him about when he's on the stand, but ask yourself before you talk to him about something, is this something that manages testimony in front of the jury?  And I think what he's saying here is the only thing you'd want to do while he's on the stand testifying is go up there and say you need to slow down, you need to stop shifting, you need to look at the jury in the eye, you need to remember the things that we talked about as far as the things you should say, here are the questions I'm going to ask you next. That's all managing in the way we define it. And then he tells him:  Just ask yourself when you're talking to him tonight, you can talk to him about something  --and even gives him an example of potentially if they go  into a punishment phase -- you can talk to him about something, but, if  -- if -- if you're going to be managing his testimony, that's a -- you can't do that.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And, as Justice Thomas pointed out, there were no questions or follow -up clarification  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Exactly.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- requests from counsel on that.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Exactly. He gave a little bit more clarification on his own after that, but there was no question about, well, can we talk about perjury if that -- if that's maybe a thing, can we talk about a potential plea bargain?  They di dn't ask any of that.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Thank you, Mr. Warthen.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Counsel  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Counsel, let  -- let -- let's say the defendant and the lawyer go into their, you know, wherever for  the evening recess, and the defendant says something like:  Counsel, you remember when we  were preparing for this, we both agreed we should try to get the jury to focus on Fred, and whenever it's reasonable, I should mention  Fred, and I've been doing that, and I notice every time I do that, you know, Juror Number 8 gets a big frown and shakes his head. He doesn't look to me like he likes the idea of talking about Fred at all. So I think that's a bad idea. Now talking about Fred was your idea. Do you still think it's a good idea?  Can the lawyer respond to that question?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: No. They would have to tell them I'm under a court order not to  -- not to answer that.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: So, at that point, he tells the defendant, who's facing a capital sentence, I'm not going to tell you? It's a very simple thing. Don't talk about -- he's not saying particular things, but let's  -- let's stop talking about Fred whenever we can.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Yes, that would be managing his testimony. That would be coaching and strategizing with him.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Counsel  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Do you think that the  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: No, go ahead.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Do you think that counsel can say, listen, I've been noticing that you've been mumbling and you're also not making eye contact with the questioner, and it would just be a good idea if you'd stop mumbling and made eye contact?  Can the lawyer do that in an overnight recess?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: No. I would consider that to be coaching their testimony. As far as how you present yourself to the jury, I would say that's also the same as the substance of what  --what you're saying.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Yeah. So the -- the  -- the line that you're drawing -- and you draw this on page 14, and I just want to make sure that -- that you're still saying what you're saying on page 14, where you say direct discussion, i.e., testimonial management, that  is, direct discussion of the testimony, right --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: -- can be prohibited. So whether it's the Chief Justice's question or my mumbling question, that's direct discussion. But counsel can still discuss a range of issues related to the testimony, including calling additional witnesses, plea bargains, legal objections, court orders, excluded evidence, and the implications of perjury, among others.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Yes.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: So that's still the line that you're drawing?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Yes. The touchstone is always the lawyer should contemplate for a moment and ask themselves is this going to cause me to manage their testimony. That -- the way we define that is coaching, regrouping, strategizing about the testimony itself, not about other things related to the -- the -- you could strategize all you want about should we still bring in the expert witness,  things like that. But, as far as the -- how the testimony is ongoing, that would not be allowed.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: And when Mr. Banner says that's not a line at all --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: -- what is your response to that?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: I think that's a very real line because, I mean, one, the case law draws that line. And I think the logic of Perry is very strong. They say it's an empirical predicate of our system of justice that an uncounseled witness is more likely to tell the truth than one who has time to pause and consult with their attorney. And they  --they say this -- this r ule applies for both witnesses generally and defense  --defendant witnesses. They don't draw a distinction between the two. And I think there's a lot of logic to that because, if it wasn't logical, then we would have to get rid of this rule for all witnesses. I mean, all witnesses would have to be  --let's say this  --we flip it around. Let's just say it's the state's star witness. Let's say the victim had lived in this case and it was an aggravated assault case. Why  wouldn't the state be able to talk to the witness overnight and coach their testimony if  -- if the -- if the --if the victim is not doing very well on the stand?  The same logic would apply the other way.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Thank you.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Counsel, I -- I think I might have missed the  --the answer. You  -- the -- the question was like, can you tell the witness to stop mumbling?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: You said he can't say that?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: No. I would consider  -- how you present yourself to the  --the jury, I consider that to be  also coaching, a form of coaching. Look him in the eye, stop mumbling, don't talk as quickly, things of that nature.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: What's the exact formulation, if you have one, of what the judge should say to the counsel before an overnight recess?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Well, I would say something like this, if  -- for a managing order or testimony generally?  A managing order?  I would  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Yeah.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: If I were the judge, I would say:  Okay, I'm not going to go through  an entire list of everything you can talk about, but whenever you're sitting there talking to your client, I want you to ask yourself, is this directly talking about the testimony or is this talking -- is -- conceptually, is this something that's a derivative matter from it, and, in any event, regardless of what you're talking about, does this require you to coach, regroup, or strategize about the testimony itself?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Don't you think lawyers are going to have very different answers to that question when they ask themselves that question?  I guess the  point being, is that line really able to be applied in a neutral and equal manner?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: They  --they might have some differences of opinion, but we do trust lawyers to use their judgment whenever they are complying with any kind of court order. And our rule also allows any lawyer, if they're just not sure and they  -- they really don't want to run afoul of the court's order, to come back and ask the trial court and to say:  Your Honor, I wasn't sure about this, can I get some clarification or even maybe some reconsideration?  And let's say it's, like, 5 in the morning or something like that and they don't want to bother the trial court judge at 5 in the morning. They can wait to the morning and they can explain the problem that they were having and then they can ask for a continuance.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: So that's -- that's important. That's your solution to ambiguity for the lawyers, is just come back and ask if there's something you want to talk about?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: That's right.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Counsel, let me ask you about the government's -- the -- the Solicitor General's position, which we've now established is much broader. It's a no-testimony order.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: What are your thoughts on the workability of that?  I mean, the  -- the -- the counsel on the other side suggests that there are all kinds of discussions that involve trial strategy that are going to be related to the defendant's testimony, so a no-testimony order might be sweeping too broadly, or at least that's the argument. Do you have an opinion about that?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: I think that it fits with the Court's case law. I do -- ours -- our rule  --their rule is a much more bright-line rule. So, in a way, it would be easier to comply with. But it's not as flexible. What our rule -- the -- the benefit of our rule is it maximizes the amount of conferral that an attorney could possibly have about the matters they do have a constitutional right to talk about. But, at the same time, it -- it excises as much as possible to protect the integrity of trial the things that they don't have the right to talk about, which is the ongoing  -- the substance of the ongoing testimony.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Counsel, Justice Gorsuch asked you the facts of this case are  really your position in this case, which is the judge's order only limited management. But the  SG wants us to announce a greater -- a bigger rule.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Do you agree with that rule?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Their rule would -- you're asking if I agree with it. I think it would be supported by the case law, yes.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. How would it be supported by logic?  Putting aside -- you agree that under any circumstance a lawyer has an obligation, even we've said it in Nix, to not suborn perjury.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: If a client is suborning -- is perjuring him or herself  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- the lawyer just can't sit there and not do something about that.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So that's the close case here, what can they do.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You would say they can say to the  --to the defendant:  If you commit perjury, these are the consequences. Correct?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Yes.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: If the government says no, that's really dangerous. How about plea bargain?  The government said no in its brief to saying: Your testimony is really bad.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You should reconsider taking this. If the lawyer doesn't do that, he or she is not supporting their ethical obligation to give the defendant information, adequate information, to consider a plea, correct?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Well, I think, in order to comply with court orders, you are able to --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Excuse  the ethical obligation?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Well, to  --yes, to a certain extent. I  --I -- I would be surprised about that.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. But putting that aside, at what point do we accept the SG's position?  Because an order that says don't talk to the person at all we said in Geders -- in Perry was wrong. In -- I'm sorry -- in Geders, we said:  Don't talk to the defendant at all.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: That's correct. And that  --that  --that  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So the question is where to draw the line. Should we ignore that line here?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Well, I think, in Perry, they drew the line at -- between testimony and not testimony. I mean, they even go so far in Perry as to say:  You can tell them not to talk at all because we're so worried that yo u're going to go talk to them about their testimony.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Right. But we said  --we said in Geders you can't do it overnight.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen
text: Not  -- not -- they say over  --that was the context, although I would say they say a long break. But the problem with  -- as --as was brought up earlier, drawing the temporal line between the two is a problem.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent

text: All right. Thank you.

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Counsel  --

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: I want to just read you a potential instruction, and tell me if you agree with it or if you see any kind of difference between your position and what I'm going to say and what the SG says. What if the court says  --or what if we were to say that qualified conferral orders are okay if they tell the lawyer:  Listen, you  can't talk about the content of the testimony or the manner of its delivery, but you can discuss any strategic consequences of the defendant's testimony, such as whether to take a plea, whether to call another witness, et cetera?  Are you okay with that?

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
speaker: Andrew N. Warthen

case_name: David Asa Villarreal, Petitioner, V. Texas, Respondent
